title: Scalable continuous-space crystal optimality certificates
open: Develop computationally practical certificates that a candidate lies within a chosen energy tolerance of the global minimum over continuous atomic positions and variable cell geometry, for a stated class of realistic many-body potentials and bounded cell sizes. Control discretization error explicitly.
status: Gusev et al. demonstrated integer-programming optimality guarantees and assumption-dependent relaxed structures in 2023. Practical scaling, grid-to-continuum error bounds, and wider potential classes remain extension targets.
why: Separates reliable ground-state predictions from search-algorithm preferences.
key_works: Oganov, Pickard, Zhu and Needs (2019), “Structure prediction drives materials discovery,” [DOI:10.1038/s41578-019-0101-8](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41578-019-0101-8); V. V. Gusev et al. (2023), “Optimality guarantees for crystal structure prediction,” [DOI:10.1038/s41586-023-06071-y](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-023-06071-y).

title: Near-degenerate polymorph free energies
open: Predict temperature- and pressure-dependent ordering of experimentally competing polymorphs, including anharmonic, electronic, magnetic, and configurational contributions, with uncertainty smaller than their free-energy separation.
status: Documented for decades; inexpensive Gibbs-energy descriptors enable screening, while rigorous calculations remain demanding and material dependent.
why: Prevents selecting a functional phase that is unstable under actual operating conditions.
key_works: Bartel et al. (2018), “Physical descriptor for the Gibbs energy of inorganic crystalline solids and temperature-dependent materials chemistry,” [DOI:10.1038/s41467-018-06682-4](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-018-06682-4).

title: Absolute homogeneous crystal-nucleation rates
open: Predict absolute nucleation rates across supersaturation or undercooling without fitting the barrier or kinetic prefactor to the same rate measurements.
status: Classical nucleation theory is nearly a century old; rare-event simulations succeed selectively, but quantitative agreement remains system dependent.
why: Makes crystallization processing predictable and distinguishes incorrect mechanisms from incorrect force fields.
key_works: Sosso et al. (2016), “Crystal Nucleation in Liquids: Open Questions and Future Challenges in Molecular Dynamics Simulations,” [DOI:10.1021/acs.chemrev.5b00744](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.chemrev.5b00744).

title: Heterogeneous nucleation-site potency
open: Predict which chemically heterogeneous surface sites nucleate a chosen phase, and their rate distribution, from measured local chemistry, defects, and topography.
status: Active for decades; selected substrates are understood, but lattice matching alone does not explain general nucleation potency.
why: Enables reproducible coatings, inoculants, and crystallization control.
key_works: Sosso et al. (2016), “Crystal Nucleation in Liquids: Open Questions and Future Challenges in Molecular Dynamics Simulations,” [DOI:10.1021/acs.chemrev.5b00744](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.chemrev.5b00744).

title: Predicting particle-attachment crystallization
open: Determine when crystals grow through monomer addition, oriented particle attachment, or precursor transformation, and predict the resulting defect population before synthesis.
status: Particle-attachment pathways are experimentally established; the unresolved problem is quantitative pathway selection and defect inheritance across chemistries.
why: Controls nanocrystal shape, biomineral structure, and functional interfaces.
key_works: De Yoreo et al. (2015), “Crystallization by particle attachment in synthetic, biogenic, and geologic environments,” [DOI:10.1126/science.aaa6760](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aaa6760).

title: Metastable-phase lifetime prediction
open: Predict a metastable solid’s survival-time distribution under specified temperature, stress, atmosphere, and defect population, including competing transformation pathways.
status: Energy-above-hull statistics are available; induction-time models exist, but thermodynamic metastability alone does not determine practical lifetime.
why: Makes metastable materials usable in durable products.
key_works: Sun et al. (2016), “The thermodynamic scale of inorganic crystalline metastability,” [DOI:10.1126/sciadv.1600225](https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.1600225); Sun and Ceder (2017), “Induction time of a polymorphic transformation,” [DOI:10.1039/C7CE00766C](https://doi.org/10.1039/C7CE00766C).

title: Transferable solid-state reaction-path prediction
open: Predict intermediate phases, phase fractions, and reaction times for previously unseen powder recipes while accounting for particle contacts, interphase transport, and atmosphere.
status: Karan et al. (2026) reproduced four Ba–Ti–O reaction histories using correlated transport; transfer beyond this demonstrated chemistry remains open.
why: Turns predicted compounds into reproducible synthesis instructions.
key_works: Karan et al. (2026), “Ion correlations explain kinetic selectivity in diffusion-limited solid-state synthesis reactions,” [DOI:10.1038/s41563-026-02596-5](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41563-026-02596-5).

title: Recoverability of high-pressure phases
open: Predict which functional high-pressure phases can survive decompression, and design defect, interface, or compositional constraints that preserve a specified useful phase fraction at ambient pressure.
status: Many phases are recoverable and others transform; recent zirconia work identifies domain-wall stabilization, without establishing a general recoverability rule.
why: Converts extreme-pressure discoveries into usable materials.
key_works: Oganov et al. (2019), “Structure prediction drives materials discovery,” [DOI:10.1038/s41578-019-0101-8](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41578-019-0101-8); Solomon et al. (2025), “Atomic-scale structure of ZrO2: Formation of metastable polymorphs,” [DOI:10.1126/sciadv.adq5943](https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.adq5943).

title: Three-dimensional Kauzmann transition
open: Establish whether realistic three-dimensional glass formers have a thermodynamic ideal-glass transition at positive temperature, with controlled thermodynamic and equilibration limits.
status: Posed in 1948; Jung et al. find a zero-temperature transition in a two-dimensional model, which leaves the three-dimensional question unresolved.
why: Determines whether ordinary glass formation hides an equilibrium phase transition.
key_works: Kauzmann (1948), “The Nature of the Glassy State and the Behavior of Liquids at Low Temperatures,” [DOI:10.1021/cr60135a002](https://doi.org/10.1021/cr60135a002); Jung et al. (2025; journal 2026), “Numerical investigation of the equilibrium Kauzmann transition in a two-dimensional atomistic glass,” [arXiv:2507.03590](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.03590).

title: Static order versus dynamical facilitation
open: Make discriminating predictions for relaxation times and spatial correlations that distinguish thermodynamic ordering, facilitation, and elastic mechanisms across independently chosen glass formers.
status: Competing frameworks developed over decades reproduce overlapping observations; deeply supercooled simulations improve access without settling universal mechanism.
why: Provides transferable predictions of viscosity and kinetic arrest.
key_works: Berthier and Biroli (2011), “Theoretical perspective on the glass transition and amorphous materials,” [DOI:10.1103/RevModPhys.83.587](https://doi.org/10.1103/RevModPhys.83.587).

title: Gardner transition in physical dimensions
open: Determine when the mean-field Gardner transition survives as a true transition in three-dimensional glasses, and distinguish it from a crossover or localized defects.
status: Proposed in spin-glass theory in 1985; mean-field amorphous-solid results and finite-system signatures exist, with dimensional and preparation dependence unresolved.
why: Connects glass stability, anomalous elasticity, and marginality.
key_works: Berthier et al. (2019), “Gardner physics in amorphous solids and beyond,” [DOI:10.1063/1.5097175](https://doi.org/10.1063/1.5097175).

title: Chemical identity of tunnelling defects
open: Identify the atomic rearrangements responsible for tunnelling two-level systems in representative amorphous oxides and predict their density and coupling from preparation history.
status: Phenomenological tunnelling models date to the 1970s; individual defects are measurable, but no universal microscopic account spans glass chemistries.
why: Reduces dielectric loss, mechanical noise, and quantum-device decoherence.
key_works: Yu and Carruzzo (2021), “Two-Level Systems and the Tunneling Model: A Critical View,” [arXiv:2101.02787](https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.02787).

title: Realizable ideal glass in three dimensions
open: Construct and physically prepare a three-dimensional amorphous solid with demonstrably vanishing configurational entropy under a precisely specified ensemble, or establish why proposed preparation routes cannot achieve it.
status: Bolton-Lum et al. constructed special two-dimensional ideal packings; this does not establish a physical preparation route for three-dimensional atomic glasses.
why: Tests ideal-glass predictions independently of extrapolated relaxation times.
key_works: Bolton-Lum et al. (2024, revised 2025; journal 2026), “The Ideal Glass and the Ideal Disk Packing in Two Dimensions,” [arXiv:2404.07492](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.07492).

title: Sound attenuation near ideal-glass stability
open: Determine whether the longitudinal-to-transverse Ioffe–Regel frequency ratio approaches one or falls below one as glass stability increases, and derive the controlling structural quantity.
status: A September 2026 preprint reports ratios decreasing to about 2.4 in its three-dimensional models and 1.6 in its two-dimensional models. Whether further stabilization reaches or crosses unity remains unresolved.
why: Improves predictions of vibrational damping and anomalous glass heat transport.
key_works: Fu et al. (2026), “On the ratio between longitudinal and transverse Ioffe-Regel frequencies in glasses,” [arXiv:2609.22386](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22386).

title: Frictional-jamming universality
open: Determine which jamming exponents and state variables remain universal for particles with friction, shape anisotropy, adhesion, and preparation-dependent contact histories.
status: Frictionless spherical-particle scaling is mature; frictional and nonspherical systems require additional history variables and exhibit distinct transition behavior.
why: Predicts powder handling, granular support, and dense suspension arrest.
key_works: van Hecke (2010), “Jamming of soft particles: geometry, mechanics, scaling and isostaticity,” [DOI:10.1088/0953-8984/22/3/033101](https://doi.org/10.1088/0953-8984/22/3/033101).

title: Defect-tolerant hyperuniform materials
open: Quantify how finite size, vacancies, polydispersity, and processing noise destroy useful hyperuniformity, and design scalable preparation that preserves a specified optical or transport benefit.
status: Hyperuniform constructions and self-organized examples exist; universal tolerance-to-performance relations across material classes remain undeveloped.
why: Makes disordered photonic and transport materials manufacturable.
key_works: Torquato (2018), “Hyperuniform states of matter,” [DOI:10.1016/j.physrep.2018.03.001](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.physrep.2018.03.001).

title: Predictive thermal boundary conductance
open: Predict thermal conductance across a chemically realistic rough interface from its measured structure, including intermixing, contamination, bonding, and inelastic scattering.
status: Acoustic/diffuse mismatch models and atomistic calculations capture selected interfaces; the general structure-to-conductance map remains incomplete.
why: Enables reliable thermal design of layered devices and composites.
key_works: Cahill et al. (2014), “Nanoscale thermal transport. II. 2003–2012,” [DOI:10.1063/1.4832615](https://doi.org/10.1063/1.4832615).

title: Heat transfer across subnanometre gaps
open: Establish a quantitatively tested crossover theory combining radiation, phonon coupling, electron tunnelling, and actual surface chemistry as separated solids approach contact.
status: Near-field radiative transfer and conductive mechanisms are individually established; their experimentally resolved crossover remains material and geometry dependent.
why: Sets the limits of nanoscale cooling and energy conversion.
key_works: Cahill et al. (2014), “Nanoscale thermal transport. II. 2003–2012,” [DOI:10.1063/1.4832615](https://doi.org/10.1063/1.4832615); Miller, Johnson and Rodriguez (2015), “Shape-Independent Limits to Near-Field Radiative Heat Transfer,” [DOI:10.1103/PhysRevLett.115.204302](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.115.204302).

title: Heat transport beyond weak anharmonicity
open: Predict conductivity in strongly anharmonic, dynamically disordered solids when well-defined phonon quasiparticles and perturbative scattering cease to suffice.
status: Wigner transport unifies particle-like and coherence contributions; strongly nonperturbative, temperature-changing structures remain a demanding frontier.
why: Enables reliable design of complex thermal barriers and thermoelectrics.
key_works: Simoncelli, Marzari and Mauri (2022), “Wigner Formulation of Thermal Transport in Solids,” [DOI:10.1103/PhysRevX.12.041011](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevX.12.041011).

title: Useful room-temperature phonon hydrodynamics
open: Demonstrate reproducible hydrodynamic heat transport in patterned room-temperature materials with realistic boundaries and defects, and show a practical thermal-control advantage.
status: Graphite measurements progressed from above 100 K in 2019 to room-temperature second sound in isotopically purified specimens in 2026. Robust patterned-device operation with realistic disorder and boundaries remains open.
why: Offers new means to route and time heat pulses.
key_works: Huberman et al. (2019), “Observation of second sound in graphite at temperatures above 100 K,” [DOI:10.1126/science.aav3548](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aav3548); Ding et al. (2022), “Observation of second sound in graphite over 200 K,” [DOI:10.1038/s41467-021-27907-z](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-021-27907-z); Z. Xie et al. (2026), “Room-temperature second sound in isotopically pure graphite,” [DOI:10.1038/s41467-026-70807-3](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-70807-3).

title: Sharp thermal-diffusivity bounds
open: Establish sharp lower bounds for thermal diffusivity in specified classes of interacting materials, with explicit assumptions and treatment of criticality, disorder, and quantum statistics.
status: Proposed bounds describe many liquids; the 2021 liquid bound explicitly excludes the critical-point neighborhood, leaving generality and optimality unresolved.
why: Distinguishes feasible insulation targets from limits imposed by physics.
key_works: Trachenko, Baggioli, Behnia and Brazhkin (2021), “Universal lower bounds on energy and momentum diffusion in liquids,” [DOI:10.1103/PhysRevB.103.014311](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevB.103.014311).

title: Long-life high-temperature phase-change stores
open: Develop salt-based thermal-storage composites that retain latent heat, shape, containment integrity, and heat-transfer performance through an application-representative service life.
status: Encapsulation and conductive scaffolds improve laboratory performance; coupled segregation, corrosion, and cycling stability remain scale-dependent barriers.
why: Makes dispatchable industrial heat and solar thermal storage more economical.
key_works: Wang et al. (2025), “A review of the performance and application of molten salt-based phase change materials in sustainable thermal energy storage at medium and high temperatures,” [DOI:10.1016/j.apenergy.2025.125766](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.apenergy.2025.125766).

title: Transferable density functionals for strong correlation
open: Construct a computationally practical density functional that simultaneously treats charge localization, static correlation, and bond breaking in solids while respecting relevant exact constraints.
status: A decades-old challenge; hybrid, range-separated, and correction schemes help selected regimes without providing uniform reliability.
why: Improves predictions of redox, magnetism, defects, and phase stability.
key_works: Cohen, Mori-Sánchez and Yang (2012), “Challenges for Density Functional Theory,” [DOI:10.1021/cr200107z](https://doi.org/10.1021/cr200107z).

title: Universal potentials beyond equilibrium configurations
open: Develop broadly transferable interatomic potentials that predict defects, transition states, surfaces, and high-energy configurations without systematic curvature or barrier bias.
status: Deng et al. (2025) document systematic softening in three foundation potentials and show efficient corrections; broad unseen-regime reliability remains open.
why: Prevents confident but incorrect simulations of failure, diffusion, and reaction.
key_works: Deng et al. (2025), “Systematic softening in universal machine learning interatomic potentials,” [DOI:10.1038/s41524-024-01500-6](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41524-024-01500-6).

title: Scalable reactive potentials with nonlocal charge transfer
open: Predict charge redistribution and reactive forces across heterogeneous metal–insulator–electrolyte systems under changing boundary conditions, with accuracy and scaling suitable for large simulations.
status: Fourth-generation neural potentials address nonlocal charge transfer in demonstrated systems; reactive transferability and large-scale boundary-condition handling remain incomplete.
why: Enables realistic interface chemistry and electrically driven materials processing.
key_works: Ko et al. (2021), “A fourth-generation high-dimensional neural network potential with accurate electrostatics including non-local charge transfer,” [DOI:10.1038/s41467-020-20427-2](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-020-20427-2).

title: Predicting long-trajectory model failure
open: Predict before deployment whether an interatomic model will remain physically faithful during long simulations, including rare excursions absent from held-out static tests.
status: A 2026 CdSe nanocluster benchmark finds low force error does not rank dynamical robustness; its findings do not yet establish general diagnostics.
why: Prevents unstable trajectories from corrupting calculated material properties.
key_works: Usman et al. (2026), “Benchmarking Machine-Learning Interatomic Potentials for Dynamical Stability in Inorganic Semiconductor Nanocrystals: A CdSe Case Study,” [arXiv:2609.15299](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15299).

title: Uncertainty on material observables
open: Propagate model uncertainty into calibrated intervals for free energies, diffusion constants, nucleation rates, and phase boundaries, including biased sampling and correlated errors.
status: Ensembles and Bayesian approaches quantify local prediction uncertainty; calibrated uncertainty on nonlinear trajectory-derived observables remains substantially harder.
why: Makes simulation-driven decisions quantitatively defensible.
key_works: Grasselli et al. (2025), “Uncertainty in the era of machine learning for atomistic modeling,” [DOI:10.1039/D5DD00102A](https://doi.org/10.1039/D5DD00102A).

title: Rare-event simulations without missing pathways
open: Accelerate atomistic kinetics over experimental times while preserving rate distributions and detecting important transitions omitted from the learned or enumerated event catalogue.
status: Hyperdynamics, parallel replicas, and kinetic Monte Carlo extend timescales; validity depends on basin separation and event coverage.
why: Predicts aging, segregation, corrosion, and phase changes before long experiments finish.
key_works: Voter, Montalenti and Germann (2002), “Extending the Time Scale in Atomistic Simulation of Materials,” [DOI:10.1146/annurev.matsci.32.112601.141541](https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev.matsci.32.112601.141541).

title: Predictive phase-field kinetic coefficients
open: Derive coarse-grained interface mobilities and evolution laws from atomistics that transfer across composition, temperature, and driving force without refitting each microstructure experiment.
status: Phase-field modeling is mature for many processes; kinetic inputs, coarse-graining choices, and memory effects often remain phenomenological.
why: Connects atomic mechanisms to manufacturing-scale microstructure prediction.
key_works: Chen (2002), “Phase-Field Models for Microstructure Evolution,” [DOI:10.1146/annurev.matsci.32.112001.132041](https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev.matsci.32.112001.132041).

title: Cross-code precision beyond equations of state
open: Establish reproducible cross-code reference results for defects, magnetic states, forces, response tensors, and excited-state quantities, with equivalent physical assumptions and convergence criteria.
status: Large equation-of-state verification exercises demonstrate substantial agreement; that success does not certify every materials observable.
why: Distinguishes numerical implementation disagreement from physical-model error.
key_works: Bosoni et al. (2024; online 2023), “How to verify the precision of density-functional-theory implementations via reproducible and universal workflows,” [DOI:10.1038/s42254-023-00655-3](https://doi.org/10.1038/s42254-023-00655-3).

title: Reusable negative-synthesis data
open: Build interoperable datasets of failed and partially successful syntheses with complete recipes, detection limits, precursor history, and reasons for failure, enabling prospective cross-laboratory learning.
status: Raccuglia et al. demonstrated the value of failed experiments in 2016; broad, comparable failure coverage remains sparse.
why: Reveals the boundaries of synthesizability and reduces repeated failed experiments.
key_works: Raccuglia et al. (2016), “Machine-learning-assisted materials discovery using failed experiments,” [DOI:10.1038/nature17439](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature17439).

title: Prospective materials-discovery benchmarks
open: Evaluate discovery algorithms on genuinely unseen chemistry and prospective synthesis outcomes, separating stable-crystal prediction, novelty, synthesizability, and useful measured performance.
status: Matbench Discovery provides a concrete stability benchmark; database leakage, experimental validation, and broader discovery utility need additional evaluation layers.
why: Prevents benchmark gains from being mistaken for practical discovery gains.
key_works: Riebesell et al. (2025), “A framework to evaluate machine learning crystal stability predictions,” [DOI:10.1038/s42256-025-01055-1](https://doi.org/10.1038/s42256-025-01055-1).

title: Specimen-to-process provenance across databases
open: Link a physical specimen’s composition, processing history, microstructure, measurements, uncertainty, and subsequent modifications across databases using machine-readable identities and semantics.
status: OPTIMADE standardizes access to materials databases; comprehensive experimental process and specimen provenance remains a wider interoperability task.
why: Enables reproducibility and learning from actual manufactured materials.
key_works: Andersen et al. (2021), “OPTIMADE, an API for exchanging materials data,” [DOI:10.1038/s41597-021-00974-z](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41597-021-00974-z); Wilkinson et al. (2016), “The FAIR Guiding Principles for scientific data management and stewardship,” [DOI:10.1038/sdata.2016.18](https://doi.org/10.1038/sdata.2016.18).

title: Laboratory-independent executable recipes
open: Transfer a materials synthesis protocol between laboratories and robotic platforms while preserving the relevant thermal, mixing, atmosphere, and precursor-state histories within measured tolerances.
status: Autonomous laboratories execute specialized workflows; translating nominal recipe settings into equivalent physical histories remains unresolved.
why: Turns one laboratory’s success into repeatable production knowledge.
key_works: Tom et al. (2024), “Self-Driving Laboratories for Chemistry and Materials Science,” [DOI:10.1021/acs.chemrev.4c00055](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.chemrev.4c00055).

title: Autonomous phase identification with unknown phases
open: Automatically quantify phase purity and identify genuinely unmodeled phases from noisy characterization, while distinguishing texture, disorder, mixtures, and instrument artifacts.
status: A-Lab integrates powder synthesis and diffraction analysis; robust identification beyond known structural libraries remains a separate unresolved requirement. Its 2026 correction acknowledges concerns about structural identification and the interpretation of novelty.
why: Prevents autonomous discovery systems from accepting misidentified products.
key_works: Szymanski et al. (2023), “An autonomous laboratory for the accelerated synthesis of inorganic materials” (current corrected title), [DOI:10.1038/s41586-023-06734-w](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-023-06734-w); Szymanski et al. (2026), “Author Correction: An autonomous laboratory for the accelerated synthesis of inorganic materials,” [DOI:10.1038/s41586-025-09992-y](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-025-09992-y).

title: Tenfold cheaper validated discovery
open: Demonstrate a tenfold reduction in total cost per independently reproduced, application-qualified material against a declared contemporary manual baseline across multiple chemistry families.
status: A proposed census moonshot: individual automated tasks accelerate, but component speedups do not establish this complete discovery-cost target.
why: Makes materials exploration accessible beyond highly equipped laboratories.
key_works: Tom et al. (2024), “Self-Driving Laboratories for Chemistry and Materials Science,” [DOI:10.1021/acs.chemrev.4c00055](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.chemrev.4c00055).

title: Atomic tomography of intact buried interfaces
open: Map metal and oxygen atomic positions in three dimensions across an intact buried metal–oxide interface within a micrometre-thick specimen, without sectioning. Establish independently validated atom-recovery, false-assignment, and probe-induced structural-change bounds.
status: Yang et al. mapped 23,196 Fe/Pt atom positions and species in a nanoparticle in 2017; 2021 ptychography reached lattice-vibration-limited resolution. Intact thick mixed-element interfaces impose substantially stronger penetration, inversion, and dose constraints.
why: Measures the actual structures underlying materials properties.
key_works: Y. Yang et al. (2017), “Deciphering chemical order/disorder and material properties at the single-atom level,” [DOI:10.1038/nature21042](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature21042); Chen et al. (2021), “Electron ptychography achieves atomic-resolution limits set by lattice vibrations,” [DOI:10.1126/science.abg2533](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.abg2533).

title: Continuous atomic movies of working materials
open: Follow three-dimensional atomic rearrangements continuously during a nonrepeating reaction or deformation event under realistic conditions, with sufficient chemical and temporal resolution to infer mechanisms.
status: Four-dimensional atomic tomography has reconstructed nucleation at successive annealing states; continuous operando observation is a more demanding target.
why: Resolves transient intermediates and causal defect evolution.
key_works: Zhou et al. (2019), “Observing crystal nucleation in four dimensions using atomic electron tomography,” [DOI:10.1038/s41586-019-1317-x](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-019-1317-x).

title: Atomic chemistry below the damage threshold
open: Measure local bonding and composition in beam-sensitive materials with independently quantified uncertainty before the probe changes the structure being measured.
status: Low-dose, cryogenic, and dose-fractionated methods mitigate damage; damage-free information acquisition at useful resolution remains specimen dependent.
why: Makes observations of polymers, soft interfaces, and reactive solids trustworthy.
key_works: Egerton (2019), “Radiation damage to organic and inorganic specimens in the TEM,” [DOI:10.1016/j.micron.2019.01.005](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.micron.2019.01.005).

title: Artifact-controlled hydrogen atom-probe maps
open: Quantify hydrogen occupancy at specific defects while separating original sample hydrogen from preparation contamination, residual gas, field-driven migration, and detection artifacts.
status: Isotope labeling and cryogenic transfer enable valuable observations; accurate site populations remain difficult to establish across materials and instruments.
why: Tests hydrogen-embrittlement and hydrogen-storage mechanisms directly.

title: Identifiable electric-field and strain maps
open: Infer local electric fields and strain from scanning diffraction while separating thickness, tilt, dynamical scattering, probe aberrations, and charging with validated uncertainty.
status: 4D-STEM provides multiple quantitative imaging modes; distinct physical causes can still generate similar measured contrast.
why: Prevents structural or electrostatic artifacts from becoming false mechanism claims.
key_works: Ophus (2019), “Four-Dimensional Scanning Transmission Electron Microscopy (4D-STEM): From Scanning Nanodiffraction to Ptychography and Beyond,” [DOI:10.1017/S1431927619000497](https://doi.org/10.1017/S1431927619000497).

title: Unique structure inference for disordered nanomaterials
open: Determine what combination of scattering, spectroscopy, and microscopy identifies the relevant atomic correlations of an amorphous or nanocrystalline material, including defensible equivalence classes when uniqueness is impossible.
status: Pair-distribution analysis and joint modeling constrain structures; multiple configurations can fit the same limited measurements.
why: Establishes which structural claims the data can actually support.
key_works: Billinge and Levin (2007), “The Problem with Determining Atomic Structure at the Nanoscale,” [DOI:10.1126/science.1135080](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1135080).

title: Causal mechanical effect of chemical short-range order
open: Determine how much changing chemical short-range order alone changes yield stress, slip localization, and work hardening in CrCoNi, while holding grain size, dislocation density, segregation, and contamination fixed. A solution requires independently measured ordering and blinded predictions for matched heat-treated specimens.
status: An explicit controversy since at least 2020; 2024 atom-probe measurements quantify heat-treatment-dependent ordering, but measuring order does not itself establish its mechanical contribution.
why: Makes atomic chemical order a controllable alloy-design variable.
key_works: M. He et al. (2024), “Quantifying short-range order using atom probe tomography,” [DOI:10.1038/s41563-024-01912-1](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41563-024-01912-1); Y. Cao, K. Sheriff, R. Freitas (2024), “Capturing short-range order in high-entropy alloys with machine learning potentials,” [arXiv:2401.06622](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.06622).

title: Cross-instrument short-range-order ground truth
open: Build reference specimens and a common inference benchmark that recover the same species-resolved pair correlations from atom-probe, electron, X-ray, and neutron measurements, with uncertainties and identifiable detection limits.
status: The 2024 atom-probe approach explicitly maps regimes where neighborhood information survives detection losses and trajectory errors; equivalent reliable comparisons across measurement modalities remain a separate target.
why: Prevents incompatible definitions or instrument artifacts from becoming alloy-design labels.
key_works: M. He et al. (2024), “Quantifying short-range order using atom probe tomography,” [DOI:10.1038/s41563-024-01912-1](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41563-024-01912-1).

title: Equilibrium ordering versus segregation in refractory multicomponent alloys
open: Predict the stable ordered phases, decomposition products, and transition temperatures of non-equiatomic Ti–Nb–Mo–Ta–W alloys, then distinguish genuine equilibrium from slow decomposition experimentally over the intended service-temperature range.
status: A 2024 electronic-structure study resolves competing ordering and segregation tendencies in specific Ti-containing systems; complete experimentally validated composition–temperature maps are still lacking.
why: Avoids selecting strong alloys that decompose during prolonged service.
key_works: C. D. Woodgate and J. B. Staunton (2024), “Competition between phase ordering and phase segregation in the TiₓNbMoTaW and TiₓVNbMoTaW refractory high-entropy alloys,” [arXiv:2401.16243](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.16243).

title: Grain-boundary segregation beyond dilute binary spectra
open: Predict temperature-dependent occupancy of competing solutes on the full distribution of boundary sites in real multicomponent polycrystals, including solute interactions and boundary structural changes, without fitting a separate segregation constant for each alloy.
status: Tuchinda and Schuh computed entropy spectra for 155 dilute binary systems in 2024; non-dilute interactions and dynamically changing boundaries extend beyond that benchmark.
why: Connects alloy chemistry to embrittlement, grain growth, and corrosion through actual interfaces.
key_works: N. Tuchinda and C. A. Schuh (2024), “Computed entropy spectra for grain boundary segregation in polycrystals,” [DOI:10.1038/s41524-024-01260-3](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41524-024-01260-3).

title: Nanocrystalline stability under simultaneous heat and load
open: Design nanocrystalline alloys whose grain-size distribution and ductility remain stable during combined prolonged heating and cyclic deformation, accounting for segregation at boundaries and triple junctions rather than annealing stability alone.
status: A 2024 Pt–Au study demonstrates a strong role for triple-junction segregation in grain coarsening. Its model-system result does not establish long-term stability across alloy chemistries and mechanical histories.
why: Preserves nanoscale strengthening in operating components.
key_works: A. K. Barnett et al. (2024), “Triple Junction Segregation Dominates the Stability of Nanocrystalline Alloys,” [DOI:10.1021/acs.nanolett.4c02395](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.nanolett.4c02395).

title: Long-life strength–ductility balance in refractory alloys
open: Retain useful tensile ductility and fracture resistance in a refractory concentrated alloy after prolonged high-temperature exposure, creep, and realistic oxygen uptake; qualify the same composition across this service envelope.
status: Huang et al. reported Nb₄Ta₄V₃Ti with about 1 GPa room-temperature yield strength, nearly 20% uniform strain, and 500 MPa tensile strength at 1,000 °C in 2026. These are tensile benchmarks, with long-life service qualification remaining open.
why: Enables hotter load-bearing components without sacrificing manufacturability.
key_works: H. Huang et al. (2026), “Achieving high tensile strength and ductility in refractory alloys by tuning electronic structure,” [DOI:10.1038/s41563-025-02464-8](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41563-025-02464-8).

title: Copper removal from scrap-derived steel at industrial throughput
open: Remove dissolved copper from realistic scrap-steel melts to the specification of demanding sheet products, with demonstrated industrial throughput, iron yield, reagent recycling, and cost competitiveness against dilution with primary iron.
status: Copper accumulation remains a circular-steel bottleneck. Souza Filho et al. demonstrated a promising oxygen-controlled metallurgical removal route in 2024; economically qualified industrial operation across variable scrap streams remains open.
why: Expands high-value steel recycling without continually adding primary iron.
key_works: I. R. Souza Filho et al. (2024), “Sustainable Ironmaking Toward a Future Circular Steel Economy: Exploiting a Critical Oxygen Concentration for Metallurgical Cu Removal from Scrap-Based Melts,” [DOI:10.1002/srin.202300785](https://doi.org/10.1002/srin.202300785).

title: Repeated high-grade aluminium recycling with variable impurities
open: Demonstrate repeated closed recycling loops for mixed automotive aluminium, with controlled fracture, fatigue, corrosion, and forming performance despite changing Fe, Cu, Zn, and Si inventories, without increasing primary-metal dilution each cycle.
status: Krall et al. demonstrated direct whole-vehicle-scrap upcycling under industrially relevant processing conditions in 2026. Repeated-loop impurity evolution and the full product-property envelope are the remaining targets here.
why: Converts a successful upcycling route into a durable circular material system.
key_works: P. Krall et al. (2026), “Direct aluminium-alloy upcycling from entire end-of life vehicles,” [DOI:10.1038/s41467-026-69492-z](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-69492-z).

title: Recrystallization prediction with competing solute drag and precipitation
open: Predict recrystallized fraction and grain-size distributions in microalloyed steels across changing thermomechanical schedules using independently determined boundary mobilities, segregation, and precipitation kinetics.
status: Physically based models couple precipitation and recrystallization in 2025, but rely on difficult-to-measure mobilities and interaction parameters. Transfer across residual-element inventories remains an open validation problem.
why: Allows recycled steel chemistry to be accommodated through controlled processing.
key_works: M.-I. T. Tzini and G. N. Haidemenopoulos (2025), “A Physically Based Mean Field Model for Strain-Induced Precipitation and Recrystallization in High-Strength Low-Alloy Steels,” [DOI:10.1002/srin.202400493](https://doi.org/10.1002/srin.202400493).

title: Site-resolved martensite nucleation under deformation
open: Predict which measured defects nucleate martensite, the selected crystallographic variants, and onset stresses in metastable stainless steel across temperature and strain-rate changes, without prescribing embryos from the eventual observed microstructure.
status: Atomic observations and simulations in 316L at 15 and 173 K identified different transformation pathways and defect associations in 2025; prospectively selecting actual nucleation sites remains harder than explaining observed ones.
why: Makes transformation-induced strengthening and ductility more reliably designable.
key_works: S. Li, P. J. Withers, W. Chen, K. Yan (2025), “Atomic-scale investigation of the mechanisms of deformation-induced martensitic transformation at ultra-cryogenic temperatures,” [DOI:10.1016/j.jmst.2024.04.067](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jmst.2024.04.067).

title: Full-stress-tensor screw-dislocation mobility
open: Derive and validate screw-dislocation mobility laws for body-centred-cubic alloys over the full applied stress tensor, temperature, and solute distributions, including non-Schmid effects at experimentally relevant rates.
status: Non-Schmid behavior is longstanding. Allera et al. calculated activation free energies in Fe and W in 2025, but explicitly restricted their treatment to resolved shear stress in the glide plane.
why: Improves predictions of low-temperature brittleness and rate-dependent plastic flow.
key_works: A. Allera et al. (2025), “Activation entropy of dislocation glide in body-centered cubic metals from atomistic simulations,” [DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-62390-w](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-62390-w).

title: Closure of three-dimensional dislocation-network dynamics
open: Obtain tractable continuum evolution equations that preserve dislocation topology and predict multiplication, junction formation, annihilation, and pattern length scales from initial microstructure, without regime-specific fitted closure rules.
status: Phase-field formulations with conserved dislocation variables demonstrated pattern formation in 2025; deriving broadly valid correlation and reaction closures remains distinct from demonstrating selected patterns.
why: Connects microscopic dislocation motion to component-scale constitutive models.
key_works: Y. Zhang, R. Wu, M. Zaiser (2025), “Continuum dislocation dynamics as a phase field theory with conserved order parameters: formulation and application to dislocation patterning,” [DOI:10.1088/1361-651X/adc31f](https://doi.org/10.1088/1361-651X/adc31f); [arXiv:2410.17177](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.17177).

title: Slip transmission through chemically complex grain boundaries
open: Predict whether an incident dislocation is absorbed, transmitted, or re-emitted at a measured three-dimensional boundary, including its segregation state and local stress, and validate the outgoing slip system in situ.
status: Stricker and Weygand implemented explicit transmission through planar boundaries in 2024. Curved, chemically heterogeneous boundaries and evolving boundary dislocation content extend beyond that controlled setting.
why: Connects grain-boundary design to strain localization and crack initiation.
key_works: M. Stricker and D. Weygand (2024), “A model for physical dislocation transmission through grain boundaries and its implementation in a discrete dislocation dynamics tool,” [DOI:10.1186/s41313-024-00065-7](https://doi.org/10.1186/s41313-024-00065-7).

title: Intrinsic inverse Hall–Petch crossover
open: Determine the intrinsic grain-size crossover between dislocation strengthening and boundary-mediated softening for a specified nanocrystalline metal, separating grain growth, porosity, impurities, and strain-rate effects through stable specimens and matched measurements.
status: Atomistic softening predictions date to 1998; recent models still predict condition-dependent crossovers. There is no composition- and rate-independent critical grain size to insert into a universal law.
why: Identifies the usable lower grain-size limit for strengthening.
key_works: J. Schiøtz, F. D. Di Tolla, K. W. Jacobsen (1998), “Softening of nanocrystalline metals at very small grain sizes,” [DOI:10.1038/35328](https://doi.org/10.1038/35328); A. K. Barnett et al. (2024), “Triple Junction Segregation Dominates the Stability of Nanocrystalline Alloys,” [DOI:10.1021/acs.nanolett.4c02395](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.nanolett.4c02395).

title: Quantitative competition among hydrogen-embrittlement mechanisms
open: Predict crack-initiation location, growth rate, and ductility loss in a specified steel from measured hydrogen, microstructure, stress, and loading rate, resolving the competing contributions of decohesion, localized plasticity, and vacancy generation.
status: More than a century of research has produced multiple mechanisms. Interface protection demonstrated in 2025 improves resistance, but does not supply a generally validated mechanism-selection law.
why: Replaces broad susceptibility labels with usable failure predictions.
key_works: G. Hachet et al. (2025), “Protection of metal interfaces against hydrogen-assisted cracking,” [DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-67310-6](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-67310-6).

title: Hydrogen-trap protection after saturation and cycling
open: Determine when deliberately introduced traps remain protective under repeated charging, unloading, and temperature cycling, versus saturating or releasing hydrogen into crack-critical regions; demonstrate predictive limits for actual microstructures.
status: Atomic-scale trapping measurements and interface-engineering strategies exist. A reduction in initial hydrogen uptake, including the approximately twofold reduction reported by Hachet et al., does not establish lifetime protection.
why: Prevents mitigation strategies from failing after apparently successful short tests.
key_works: G. Hachet et al. (2025), “Protection of metal interfaces against hydrogen-assisted cracking,” [DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-67310-6](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-67310-6).

title: Stress-corrosion initiation under heterogeneous salt deposits
open: Predict the distribution of crack-initiation times and locations beneath spatially heterogeneous salt deposits during wet–dry cycling, accounting for local electrolyte chemistry, residual stress, and surface microstructure.
status: The 2025 study by Elsherkisi et al. isolates deposit-pattern effects; extrapolating from uniformly coated laboratory coupons to irregular service deposits remains a separate problem.
why: Makes exposure-specific corrosion management possible for real components.
key_works: M. Elsherkisi et al. (2025), “Effect of salt deposition patterns on stress corrosion cracking,” [DOI:10.1038/s41529-025-00650-2](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41529-025-00650-2).

title: Rare-event fatigue initiation from measured microstructure
open: Predict the low-probability tail of fatigue-initiation life for components containing measured microtextured regions, inclusions, and residual stresses, with calibration retained when component volume or loading waveform changes.
status: A 2026 multiscale platform connects location-specific microstructure to probabilistic dwell-fatigue nucleation in titanium. General tail calibration across manufactured populations remains the target.
why: Reduces uncertainty in allowable lifetimes without overlooking rare early failures.
key_works: S. Ghosh and collaborators (2026), “Parametrically upscaled model-based predictive platform for fatigue with location-specific microstructural linkages,” [DOI:10.1038/s41467-026-72037-z](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-72037-z).

title: Microstructurally short-crack arrest under changing loads
open: Predict whether a short fatigue crack arrests, deflects, or escapes a grain-scale barrier under variable-amplitude loading, using the actual microstructure and evolving crack closure rather than a long-crack threshold alone.
status: Short cracks have long been known to grow below long-crack thresholds. In 2025, surface-strain and roughness indicators improved prospective path prediction in nickel; load-history-dependent arrest remains an additional requirement.
why: Connects inspection-sized defects to early fatigue damage that controls life.
key_works: Valiollahi et al. (2025), “Combining Effective Plastic Strain and Surface Roughness for Predicting Future Propagation Path of Microstructure-Sensitive Crack (MSC) in Polycrystalline Nickel,” [DOI:10.1111/ffe.14462](https://doi.org/10.1111/ffe.14462).

title: Ductile fracture after non-proportional loading
open: Predict failure strain and fracture location after compression–tension and changing shear histories from evolving void populations, particle cracking, and strain localization, without recalibrating a separate fracture locus for each path.
status: A 2025 computational study shows why growth from an initial void fraction alone misses some compression-before-tension behavior. Void nucleation and loading history remain essential unresolved ingredients for transfer.
why: Improves forming limits, crashworthiness, and assessment of dented structures.
key_works: M. Kristoffersen et al. (2025), “Ductile failure by strain localisation: A computational study of materials and structures subjected to highly non-proportional load histories,” [DOI:10.1016/j.ijsolstr.2024.113128](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijsolstr.2024.113128).

title: Creep-cavity nucleation over service timescales
open: Predict the emergence and coalescence of creep cavities from grain-boundary character, precipitates, local stress, and aging, and transfer predictions from accelerated tests to long low-stress exposures.
status: Correlative microscopy in 2024 linked cavities in ex-service 316H steel to local microstructure statistically. Correlation maps still need validated nucleation rates and time extrapolation.
why: Supports defensible life extension for high-temperature structures.
key_works: T. L. Martin and collaborators (2024), “A correlative approach to evaluating the links between local microstructural parameters and creep initiated cavities,” [DOI:10.1016/j.matdes.2024.112905](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.matdes.2024.112905).

title: Material-specific onset of dynamic crack microbranching
open: Predict the onset velocity, branch spacing, and three-dimensional morphology of dynamic microbranching from independently measured dissipation and process-zone physics across brittle material classes.
status: Controlled experiments established microbranching in the 1990s; contemporary simulations generate branching, but reproducing it does not by itself validate transferable onset and length-scale predictions.
why: Determines rapid-fracture resistance and fragmentation beyond quasistatic toughness.
key_works: E. Sharon, S. P. Gross, J. Fineberg (1995), “Local crack branching as a mechanism for instability in dynamic fracture,” [DOI:10.1103/PhysRevLett.74.5096](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.74.5096); E. Sharon and J. Fineberg (1996), “Microbranching instability and the dynamic fracture of brittle materials,” [DOI:10.1103/PhysRevB.54.7128](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevB.54.7128).

title: Adhesive-wear transition with real surface chemistry
open: Predict the transition between plastic asperity smoothing and debris detachment for oxidized, chemically heterogeneous engineering surfaces, using measurable interfacial properties rather than tuned model potentials.
status: Aghababaei et al. established a critical-junction-length framework in 2016; realistic oxidation, lubrication, and evolving tribomaterial layers were outside its explicit simulation scope.
why: Identifies when contact causes permanent material loss.
key_works: R. Aghababaei, D. H. Warner, J.-F. Molinari (2016), “Critical length scale controls adhesive wear mechanisms,” [DOI:10.1038/ncomms11816](https://doi.org/10.1038/ncomms11816); T. Brink and J.-F. Molinari (2019), “Adhesive wear mechanisms in the presence of weak interfaces: Insights from an amorphous model system,” [arXiv:1901.07466](https://arxiv.org/abs/1901.07466).

title: Predictive steady-state wear without an empirical wear coefficient
open: Predict macroscopic wear volume and debris-size distributions from contact geometry and material properties while accounting for debris aggregation, recirculation, escape, and surface renewal.
status: Archard-type coefficients remain useful empirical quantities. Pham-Ba and Molinari modeled formation and aggregation regimes in a third-body layer in 2023; scale and dimensionality limit direct component transfer.
why: Permits material selection without repeating every sliding experiment.
key_works: J. F. Archard (1953), “Contact and Rubbing of Flat Surfaces,” [DOI:10.1063/1.1721448](https://doi.org/10.1063/1.1721448); S. Pham-Ba and J.-F. Molinari (2023), “Role of minimum adhesive wear particle size in third-body layer properties,” [arXiv:2304.14783](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.14783).

title: Separating chemical and mechanical frictional aging
open: Quantify the separate contributions of bond formation, contact-area creep, and capillary bridges to frictional aging over controlled humidity, temperature, and load histories, then predict the resulting rate-and-state parameters.
status: Li et al. directly demonstrated chemical-bond contributions in 2011. Later nanoindentation and humidity studies show that the operative mechanism depends on material and contact conditions.
why: Connects friction laws to surface treatments and environmental control.
key_works: Q. Li, T. E. Tullis, D. Goldsby, R. W. Carpick (2011), “Frictional ageing from interfacial bonding and the origins of rate and state friction,” [DOI:10.1038/nature10589](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature10589).

title: Load-bearing superlubricity in contaminated ambient conditions
open: Maintain structural superlubricity over macroscopic travel and practical loads despite particles, humidity cycling, misalignment, and wear, with specified lifetime and independently repeated friction measurements.
status: A 2026 graphite–silica device reported friction coefficient 0.0034 and stable electrical operation beyond 110,000 cycles at a specially prepared microscopic interface. General macroscopic-bearing performance remains open.
why: Reduces frictional energy losses and wear in practical moving interfaces.
key_works: C. Chen et al. (2026), “Structural superlubricity triboelectric nanogenerator with negligible wear and high triboelectrification efficiency,” [DOI:10.1038/s41467-026-74450-w](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-74450-w).

title: Predicting protective tribofilm growth and failure
open: Predict when a lubricant chemistry forms, repairs, or loses a protective tribofilm under realistic pressure, temperature, and intermittent sliding histories, including antagonistic interactions among additives.
status: Single-asperity experiments resolve tribofilm growth, and 2025 diester experiments generated graphitic films with reduced friction and wear. These are mechanistic building blocks for a still-incomplete formulation-to-lifetime prediction method.
why: Enables lubricant design that predicts service protection and depletion.
key_works: N. N. Gosvami et al. (2015), “Mechanisms of antiwear tribofilm growth revealed in situ by single-asperity sliding contacts,” [DOI:10.1126/science.1258788](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1258788); W. Song et al. (2025), “In-situ catalysis of green lubricants into graphitic carbon by iron single atoms to reduce friction and wear,” [DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-58292-6](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-58292-6).

title: Coupled fretting wear and fatigue across slip regimes
open: Predict crack-initiation life as a contact transitions between partial and gross slip while wear continuously changes its geometry, friction, and residual stress; validate on previously unseen joint geometries.
status: Comparative 2024 critical-plane studies and coupled damage models improve selected fretting tests, but rankings and predictive accuracy depend on the contact regime and model choices.
why: Improves lifetime prediction for joints, connectors, and contacting structural components.
key_works: Shu et al. (2024), “A comparative study of several life prediction models based on the critical plane approach for fretting fatigue crack initiation,” [DOI:10.1111/ffe.14256](https://doi.org/10.1111/ffe.14256).

title: Preventing keyhole pores by closed-loop control
open: Detect incipient keyhole instability and adjust the laser before pore entrapment across scan turns, accumulated heat, and changing surface angles, demonstrating lower defect rates on entire builds with measured false-alarm rates.
status: A 2025 acoustic study correlated frequency signatures with keyhole depth and porosity onset across several alloys. Generalized prevention requires control action and full-build validation beyond detection.
why: Prevents internal defects during manufacture and reduces dependence on later inspection.
key_works: L. Galiègue et al. (2025), “Acoustic emission monitoring reveals keyhole formation and evolution,” [DOI:10.1038/s41598-025-27232-1](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-27232-1).

title: Detecting crack-like lack-of-fusion defects in complex parts
open: Establish calibrated detection probabilities for thin, irregular lack-of-fusion defects throughout thick or geometrically inaccessible metal-AM parts, including unfavorable defect orientations and realistic surface roughness.
status: NIST’s ongoing 2026 program explicitly targets reference anomaly images, nondestructive testing, and probability-of-detection measurements; nominal density alone does not certify defect absence.
why: Makes inspection results usable in component qualification and reliability calculations.
key_works: NIST (updated 2026), “Measurement Science for Additive Manufacturing Program,” [program](https://www.nist.gov/programs-projects/measurement-science-additive-manufacturing-program).

title: Hot-cracking-resistant AM alloys without lost service performance
open: Co-design alloy chemistry and processing to eliminate solidification cracking in demanding multicomponent alloys while retaining the required creep, corrosion, or fatigue properties after heat treatment.
status: Sheikh et al. screened 3,876 Co–Cr–Fe–Mn–Ni compositions in 2025 using printability and phase criteria; validation concentrated on a particular alloy and simplified processing conditions.
why: Expands the range of high-performance alloys that can be reliably printed.
key_works: S. Sheikh et al. (2025), “High-throughput alloy and process design for metal additive manufacturing,” [DOI:10.1038/s41524-025-01670-x](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41524-025-01670-x); [arXiv:2304.04149](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.04149).

title: Predicting residual stress through cutting and heat treatment
open: Predict spatial residual-stress tensors and distortion through the complete sequence of deposition, support removal, machining, and heat treatment, with uncertainty verified on new part geometries.
status: AM Bench provides measured stresses and released-part deflections, including 2025 synchrotron measurements of IN718 artifacts. These validate selected stages; full-sequence transfer remains open.
why: Enables dimensional control and meaningful structural-integrity predictions after manufacture.
key_works: T. Phan et al. (2025), “Elastic residual strain measurements of 3D additively manufactured builds of nickel alloy 718 AM Bench 2022 artifacts using energy dispersive synchrotron X-ray diffraction,” [NIST bibliography and data](https://www.nist.gov/ambench/direct-am-bench-data-links-and-referencing-guidance).

title: Joint surface–pore control of AM fatigue
open: Predict fatigue life from interacting surface valleys, near-surface pores, microstructure, and residual stress, and determine when polishing or pore removal stops improving life because another initiation mechanism dominates.
status: Qu et al. demonstrated high fatigue resistance through near-void-free titanium printing in 2024. Transferable defect-to-fatigue relations across surfaces and component volumes remain incomplete.
why: Directs processing and finishing effort toward the defects that actually limit lifetime.
key_works: Z. Qu et al. (2024), “High fatigue resistance in a titanium alloy via near-void-free 3D printing,” [DOI:10.1038/s41586-024-07048-1](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-024-07048-1).

title: Powder-reuse retirement criteria based on properties
open: Determine when reused Ti–6Al–4V powder must be refreshed or retired using oxygen, morphology, contamination, and process signatures that predict fracture and fatigue properties, rather than a fixed reuse count.
status: Zhuo et al. tracked morphology, oxygen uptake, and mechanical changes in 2025. Reuse-count results depend on handling history and cannot automatically transfer among machines or replenishment policies.
why: Reduces powder waste without accepting unmeasured loss of component reliability.
key_works: Z. Zhuo, R. Ji, L. Wang, J. Mao (2025), “Reusability of Ti-6Al-4V powder in laser powder bed fusion: Influence on powder morphology, oxygen uptake, and mechanical properties,” [DOI:10.1016/j.jmatprotec.2024.118672](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jmatprotec.2024.118672).

title: Transferable AM qualification across machines
open: Demonstrate which calibrated machine observables and material descriptors suffice to transfer a qualified process between machines and sites while preserving property distributions, without repeating the entire original qualification campaign.
status: NIST’s 2026 program still identifies machine calibration, variability, and process/part qualification as research needs. Parameter-name equivalence alone does not establish process equivalence.
why: Reduces qualification cost and makes distributed production credible.
key_works: NIST (updated 2026), “Measurement Science for Additive Manufacturing Program,” [program](https://www.nist.gov/programs-projects/measurement-science-additive-manufacturing-program).

title: Shared AM sensor-to-defect-to-lifetime benchmarks
open: Assemble interoperable, time-registered monitoring, tomography, microstructure, and lifetime data for the same manufactured specimens, with machine and powder histories and reserved cross-site evaluation cohorts.
status: AM Bench 2025 adds public tensile and rotating-bending fatigue datasets; the remaining target is joined evidence spanning monitoring through failure across sites and alloys.
why: Tests whether manufacturing observations actually predict useful component properties.
key_works: NIST (2025), “AMB2025-03 High-Cycle Rotating Bending Fatigue Tests of PBF-L Ti-6Al-4V,” [DOI:10.18434/mds2-3734](https://doi.org/10.18434/mds2-3734); NIST, [AM Bench data and referencing guidance](https://www.nist.gov/ambench/direct-am-bench-data-links-and-referencing-guidance).

title: Simultaneous closed-loop geometry and microstructure control
open: Control melt-pool geometry and the final microstructure simultaneously during printing, with explicit constraints preventing a correction that improves dimensions from worsening porosity, texture, or mechanical properties.
status: Bayesian controller autotuning was demonstrated for LPBF in 2025. A melt-pool control objective is still an imperfect proxy for the final material state.
why: Makes real-time process control optimize component function as well as geometry.
key_works: B. Kavas et al. (2025), “In-situ controller autotuning by Bayesian optimization for closed-loop feedback control of laser powder bed fusion process,” [DOI:10.1016/j.addma.2025.104641](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.addma.2025.104641); [arXiv:2406.19096](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.19096).

title: Predictable steel–copper interfaces in multimaterial printing
open: Design a printed 316L–copper-alloy interface with reproducible bonding and fatigue resistance, predicting dilution, cracking, and brittle-phase formation across interface orientations and thermal histories.
status: Bulloch et al. combined depth profiling, microscopy, and thermodynamic modeling for 316L–CuSn10 interfaces in 2025. Transferable prediction across orientations and processing histories remains open.
why: Enables integrated structures combining strength, thermal conduction, and electrical function.
key_works: A. Bulloch et al. (2025), “Fundamental Investigation of the Interface Formation of Multi-material Additive Manufactured 316L-CuSn10 Structures,” [DOI:10.1007/s11661-025-07817-1](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11661-025-07817-1).

title: Weld-local hydrogen-cracking prediction
open: Predict the weakest crack path and failure load in a heterogeneous steel weld from its thermal history, local phases, residual stress, and hydrogen transport, including uncertainty in the heat-affected zone.
status: Wijnen and collaborators linked welding simulations to heterogeneous phase-field integrity analysis in 2025. Broad experimental validation across weld procedures and hydrogen histories remains the target.
why: Makes weld qualification sensitive to the actual local failure mechanisms.
key_works: J. Wijnen and collaborators (2025), “A computational framework to predict weld integrity and microstructural heterogeneity: Application to hydrogen transmission,” [arXiv:2412.08217](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.08217); [paper](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0264127524009080).

title: Hot tearing from evolving mushy-zone topology
open: Predict casting hot-tear nucleation and coalescence from measured dendrite/intermetallic geometry, liquid feeding, and imposed contraction, including changes in local permeability as solidification proceeds.
status: Han et al. directly imaged hot-tear formation in Al–Cu and Al–Cu–Fe in 2024; conventional susceptibility correlations did not capture the influence of second phases.
why: Reduces casting defects and supports robust use of more complex recycled alloys.
key_works: I. Han, S. Feng, F. Wilde, P. S. Grant, E. Liotti (2024), “Revealing hot tear formation dynamics in Al–Cu alloys with X-ray radiography,” [DOI:10.1016/j.actamat.2023.119421](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.actamat.2023.119421).

title: Room-temperature tensile ductility in bulk structural ceramics
subfield: Structural ceramics, ceramic composites, and refractories
open: Produce macroscopic hard oxide or covalent ceramic specimens with reproducible distributed tensile plasticity at room temperature while retaining useful stiffness, hardness, and resistance to subcritical cracking.
status: Room-temperature deformation has been demonstrated in selected ceramics, micropillars, and nanofibers; 2025 ceramic-nanofiber results do not establish bulk tensile ductility in general structural ceramics.
why: Combines ceramic environmental resistance with substantially improved damage tolerance.
key_works: S. Qiang et al. (2025), “Integration of high strength, flexibility, and room-temperature plasticity in ceramic nanofibers,” [DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-58240-4](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-58240-4); L. Liu et al. (2025), “Nanotwinned CrN ceramics with enhanced plasticity,” [DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-61275-2](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-61275-2).

title: True toughness design for high-entropy carbides
subfield: Structural ceramics, ceramic composites, and refractories
open: Predict and improve measured crack-growth resistance of dense multicomponent carbides from composition and bonding while retaining hardness, and verify predictions with fracture-mechanics tests rather than elastic-modulus proxies alone.
status: Valence-electron tuning has provided computational design directions since 2021; 2025 UHTC potential studies broaden compositional screening, but elastic constants alone do not determine fracture toughness.
why: Makes compositional screening predict resistance to actual crack growth.
key_works: D. G. Sangiovanni et al. (2021), “Enhancing plasticity in high-entropy refractory ceramics via tailoring valence electron concentration,” [DOI:10.1016/j.matdes.2021.109932](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.matdes.2021.109932); S. J. Magorrian et al. (2025), “Computational tuning of the elastic properties of low- and high-entropy ultra-high temperature ceramics,” [arXiv:2512.13204](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.13204).

title: Ceramic strength tails from actual flaw populations
subfield: Structural ceramics, ceramic composites, and refractories
open: Predict component failure probabilities from independently measured surface and volume flaw populations when defects are clustered, multimodal, or correlated with processing, with defensible extrapolation beyond coupon sizes.
status: Weibull statistics provide a longstanding baseline. Lamon’s 2024 SiC study shows variability among inferred flaw-strength distributions and testing configurations; tail transfer requires more than fitting a distribution.
why: Makes reliability claims credible for large, brittle components.
key_works: J. Lamon (2024), “Investigation of Variability of Flaw Strength Distributions on Brittle SiC Ceramic,” [DOI:10.3390/ceramics7020050](https://doi.org/10.3390/ceramics7020050).

title: Thermal-shock damage with an evolving flaw network
subfield: Structural ceramics, ceramic composites, and refractories
open: Predict residual strength after repeated thermal shocks using the evolving three-dimensional crack population, heat-transfer boundary conditions, and crack interactions, rather than a single critical temperature difference.
status: Classical thermal-shock criteria distinguish initiation and propagation. Current ceramic-composite experiments additionally reveal coupled oxidation and thermal-shock degradation, making repeated-exposure prediction a separate challenge.
why: Supports reusable furnaces, heat exchangers, and rapidly cycled ceramic components.
key_works: D. P. H. Hasselman (1969), “Unified Theory of Thermal Shock Fracture Initiation and Crack Propagation in Brittle Ceramics,” [DOI:10.1111/j.1151-2916.1969.tb15848.x](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1151-2916.1969.tb15848.x); R. Mitra and collaborators (2025), “Resistance to cyclic oxidation and evolution of oxide scale in 2.5D and 3D Cf/SiC composites with Si-B-C added matrix,” [paper](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S095522192500487X) (2026 corrigendum should also be consulted).

title: Zirconia aging-front kinetics under coupled stress and moisture
subfield: Structural ceramics, ceramic composites, and refractories
open: Predict the depth and mechanical consequences of tetragonal-to-monoclinic transformation in engineered zirconia under combined humid exposure and cyclic stress, including grain-boundary dopant segregation and heterogeneous grain sizes.
status: A 2024 study resolved multiple kinetic regimes in strong, tough 1.5Y-TZP using water vapor and air exposure. A single accelerated-aging conversion factor cannot represent all these conditions.
why: Preserves transformation toughening without unexpected aging damage.
key_works: H. Reveron and collaborators (2024), “Aging behavior of a 1.5 mol% yttria doped zirconia exhibiting optimized toughness and strength,” [paper](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0955221923007422).

title: Uniform flash sintering of complex thick ceramics
subfield: Structural ceramics, ceramic composites, and refractories
open: Densify complex, thick ceramic shapes by flash sintering while bounding temperature, density, grain-size, and stoichiometry gradients throughout the part, including near electrodes and geometric constrictions.
status: Ong et al. achieved over 99% relative density in 1.5YSZ at furnace temperatures as low as 600 °C using controlled current ramps in 2025. Furnace temperature differs from specimen temperature; shape-independent uniformity remains unestablished.
why: Reduces ceramic-processing time and furnace demands while preserving quality.
key_works: Ong et al. (2025), “Low-furnace-temperature flash sintering of tetragonal 1.5-mol% YSZ: Role of particle necking on grain growth,” [DOI:10.1111/jace.20490](https://doi.org/10.1111/jace.20490).

title: Long-duration UHTC recession under realistic oxidizing flow
subfield: Structural ceramics, ceramic composites, and refractories
open: Predict and suppress recession of an ultrahigh-temperature ceramic above 2,000 °C under high-enthalpy oxidizing flow and repeated heating, including oxide volatilization, shear removal, and changing emissivity.
status: Tsuganezawa et al. conducted greater-than-2,000 °C arc-jet exposures for 60 seconds in 2025 and linked protection to oxide chemistry. Long-duration reusable-service qualification remains open.
why: Enables durable extreme-heat components and reusable thermal protection.
key_works: M. Tsuganezawa, Y. Arai, R. Inoue (2025), “Thermodynamic Analysis on Complex Oxides Formed by Aerodynamic Heating for Ultrahigh-Temperature Ceramic Matrix Composites,” [DOI:10.3390/jcs9020087](https://doi.org/10.3390/jcs9020087).

title: Environmental-barrier coatings against combined steam and molten deposits
subfield: Structural ceramics, ceramic composites, and refractories
open: Preserve adhesion and low recession in a ceramic-composite coating under simultaneous steam, molten calcium–magnesium–aluminosilicate deposits, thermal cycling, and erosion; validate the coupled failure map rather than isolated exposure resistance.
status: Rare-earth silicate coatings and chemically modified bond coats provide substantial protection. Lee’s 2019 work addresses bond-coat oxidation, one of several interacting failure processes.
why: Makes ceramic composites reliable in contaminated high-temperature gas flows.
key_works: K. N. Lee (2019; online 2018), “Yb2Si2O7 Environmental barrier coatings with reduced bond coat oxidation rates via chemical modifications for long life,” [DOI:10.1111/jace.15978](https://doi.org/10.1111/jace.15978).

title: Oxidation-tolerant crack-deflecting CMC interphases
subfield: Structural ceramics, ceramic composites, and refractories
open: Design a fiber–matrix interphase that remains sufficiently weak for crack deflection and fiber pull-out while resisting oxidation and volatilization through service-induced matrix cracks.
status: SiC/BN/SiBCN studies in 2025 show that steam can consume BN and form glassy products that bond fibers to the matrix. Initial toughness therefore does not guarantee retained toughness after exposure.
why: Preserves the damage tolerance that makes ceramic-matrix composites useful.
key_works: Z. Li, Z. Gao, X. Zhang, Y. Liu, P. J. Withers, P. Xiao (2025), “Oxidation behavior and subsequent mechanical properties of SiC/BN/SiBCN composite after exposure to steam at high temperature,” [institutional paper record](https://research.manchester.ac.uk/en/publications/oxidation-behavior-and-subsequent-mechanical-properties-of-sicbns/).

title: Multiaxial matrix-cracking laws in woven ceramic composites
subfield: Structural ceramics, ceramic composites, and refractories
open: Predict crack multiplication, fiber bridging, and residual stiffness under combined tension and shear in measured woven CMC architectures, including off-axis loading and changing interface friction.
status: Fiber-bridging theory dates to the 1980s and remains foundational; general loading in three-dimensional architectures requires more than the original aligned-fiber tensile model.
why: Allows component design without treating every layup and load path as a new material.
key_works: B. Budiansky, J. W. Hutchinson, A. G. Evans (1986), “Matrix fracture in fiber-reinforced ceramics,” [DOI:10.1016/0022-5096(86)90035-9](https://doi.org/10.1016/0022-5096(86)90035-9).

title: Defect-free dimensional compensation in printed ceramics
subfield: Structural ceramics, ceramic composites, and refractories
open: Predict and compensate anisotropic shrinkage during drying, debinding, and sintering or pyrolysis so that a complex ceramic part meets geometric tolerances without generating internal cracks or closed porosity.
status: Eckel et al. demonstrated complex printed polymer-derived ceramics in 2016. Subsequent processing advances reduce shrinkage in selected systems; transferable compensation across shapes and feedstocks remains the problem.
why: Makes ceramic additive manufacturing suitable for precision structural parts.
key_works: Z. C. Eckel et al. (2016), “Additive manufacturing of polymer-derived ceramics,” [DOI:10.1126/science.aad2688](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aad2688).

title: Rapid uniform densification of thick CMC preforms
subfield: Structural ceramics, ceramic composites, and refractories
open: Achieve a specified near-full matrix density throughout thick, complex fiber preforms in a single short infiltration campaign without prematurely sealing outer pores or damaging fibers, verified by three-dimensional porosity and mechanical measurements.
status: Venkatachalam et al. reported 90% theoretical density in 24 hours using radio-frequency-assisted CVI in 2024, at least ten times faster than their conventional comparison. Higher density, complex geometry, and validated properties remain separate hurdles.
why: Reduces a major time and cost barrier in ceramic-composite manufacturing.
key_works: V. Venkatachalam, B. Esser, J. Binner (2024), “Processing and performance of ultra high temperature ceramic matrix composite (UHTCMCs) using radio frequency assisted chemical vapour infiltration (RF-CVI),” [DLR paper record](https://elib.dlr.de/205288/).

title: Slag–refractory corrosion rates under evolving microstructure
subfield: Structural ceramics, ceramic composites, and refractories
open: Predict refractory penetration, dissolution, and spalling in contact with changing industrial slags from pore connectivity, wetting, reaction-layer growth, and thermal stress, with measurements that separate these mechanisms in situ.
status: Recent rotating-finger and high-temperature imaging studies resolve parts of the process; 2026 digital-image-correlation work measures coupled corrosion severity, but a severity index is not yet a transferable kinetic law.
why: Extends furnace-lining life and reduces contamination and shutdowns.
key_works: C. Liu et al. (2026), “In-situ assessment of slag corrosion on refractories based on HT-DIC: A novel multi-dimensional index with corrosion severity,” [paper](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0010938X26000569); S. C. Duan et al. (2025), “Effect of tundish fluxes on the degradation of MgO-based refractory linings in continuous casting process,” [DOI:10.1016/j.jmrt.2025.09.274](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jmrt.2025.09.274).

title: Composition-resolved calcium-silicate-hydrate structure
subfield: Cement, concrete, earthen materials, and glass durability
open: Determine predictive ensembles of C–S–H atomic and mesoscale structures across Ca/Si ratio, aluminium substitution, water activity, and age that jointly reproduce scattering, spectroscopy, density, and mechanical properties.
status: Pellenq et al.’s 2009 model supplied a validated structural archetype; it does not uniquely determine the full heterogeneous, composition-dependent ensemble present in practical binders.
why: Connects binder chemistry to transport, shrinkage, and mechanical performance.
key_works: R. J.-M. Pellenq et al. (2009), “A realistic molecular model of cement hydrates,” [DOI:10.1073/pnas.0902180106](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.0902180106).

title: Mechanistic concrete creep under changing humidity
subfield: Cement, concrete, earthen materials, and glass durability
open: Predict long-term creep and recovery during humidity and stress cycling from C–S–H rearrangement, water transport, and chemical aging, distinguishing irreversible structural change from reversible poroelastic effects.
status: Vandamme and Ulm linked creep to nanogranular packing in 2009; large-scale environmental tests continue to show the importance of moisture history. Prediction across changing lifetime histories remains incomplete.
why: Improves dimensional stability and service-life estimates of concrete structures.
key_works: M. Vandamme and F.-J. Ulm (2009), “Nanogranular origin of concrete creep,” [DOI:10.1073/pnas.0901033106](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.0901033106); W. Bachofner et al. (2025; online 2024), “Influence of environmental conditions on the creep behavior of large-scale concrete specimens,” [DOI:10.1002/suco.202401042](https://doi.org/10.1002/suco.202401042).

title: Alkali–silica reaction swelling pressure from gel chemistry
subfield: Cement, concrete, earthen materials, and glass durability
open: Predict expansive pressure and resulting cracking from ASR-product composition, nanoscale confinement, water uptake, and restraint, resolving when colloidal osmotic pressure versus other gel-swelling mechanisms dominates.
status: ASR chemistry is established, but its expansion mechanism remains debated. Giebson and Seyfarth’s 2025 study quantifies colloidal properties and osmotic potential in synthetic products.
why: Enables aggregate-specific prevention and assessment of damaged structures.
key_works: C. Giebson and K. Seyfarth (2025; online 2024), “The colloidal nature and osmotic potential of alkali-silica reaction products and their role for the ASR expansion mechanism,” [DOI:10.1617/s11527-024-02542-4](https://doi.org/10.1617/s11527-024-02542-4).

title: Transport-law transfer across carbonated low-clinker binders
subfield: Cement, concrete, earthen materials, and glass durability
