open: Predict changes in water, oxygen, and chloride transport after carbonation for low-clinker binder compositions from independently measured pore structure and chemistry, including partial carbonation and realistic curing histories.
status: Dudi and collaborators compared several low-clinker binders and water/binder ratios in 2025; general relationships that remain valid across binder families and exposure states are still being established.
why: Prevents lower initial emissions from being offset by unpredicted durability loss.
key_works: L. Dudi and collaborators (2025), “Revealing the relationships between transport properties and microstructure characteristics in low-clinker binders before and after carbonation,” [paper](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S000888462500225X).

title: Steel-interface moisture and carbonation-induced corrosion
subfield: Cement, concrete, earthen materials, and glass durability
open: Predict corrosion rates and cumulative section loss from the actual moisture and oxygen state at the steel–concrete interface under wet–dry cycling in carbonated low-clinker concrete.
status: Albert and collaborators’ 2025 experiments identify moisture as a key controller across binder types. Carbonation-front position alone is therefore an insufficient proxy for corrosion kinetics.
why: Supports durability design that can accommodate low-carbon binders.
key_works: C. Albert and collaborators (2025), “Moisture as a key factor in the corrosion of steel in carbonated low-clinker materials,” conference contribution, [ETH repository record](https://www.research-collection.ethz.ch/entities/publication/012f55e9-29d9-4fef-a4a3-1e859df5b979).

title: Repeated autonomous concrete healing with structural recovery
subfield: Cement, concrete, earthen materials, and glass durability
open: Demonstrate repeated crack healing that restores specified permeability and mechanical performance after multiple damage events under realistic wet–dry exposure, without exhausting healing capacity or causing harmful expansion.
status: Seymour et al.’s 2023 experiments support lime-clast-mediated healing inspired by Roman concrete. Repeatable recovery in reinforced structural service remains beyond one-time laboratory crack closure.
why: Reduces repair needs and extends material service life.
key_works: L. M. Seymour et al. (2023), “Hot mixing: Mechanistic insights into the durability of ancient Roman concrete,” [DOI:10.1126/sciadv.add1602](https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.add1602).

title: Water-durable earthen construction with genuine recyclability
subfield: Cement, concrete, earthen materials, and glass durability
open: Develop an earthen material that retains specified structural properties after repeated rain and wet–dry exposure and can subsequently be reprocessed into equivalent material without progressive binder addition or thermal firing.
status: A 2025 study recycled cement- or lime-stabilized compressed-earth blocks but found residual cement no longer supplied the original water resistance. Strong initial stabilization and repeated equivalent recycling remain different achievements.
why: Preserves the low-energy and circular advantages of locally available earth.
key_works: M. Audren, S. Guihéneuf, T. Le Borgne, D. Rangeard, A. Perrot (2025), “Recycling or downcycling? The difference between raw and stabilised earth explained,” [DOI:10.1617/s11527-025-02721-x](https://doi.org/10.1617/s11527-025-02721-x); A. Perrot, D. Rangeard, E. Courteille (2018), “3D printing of earth-based materials: Processing aspects,” [DOI:10.1016/j.conbuildmat.2018.04.017](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.conbuildmat.2018.04.017).

title: Glass crack-growth kinetics under realistic humidity histories
subfield: Cement, concrete, earthen materials, and glass durability
open: Predict lifetime distributions of stressed silicate glass from evolving surface flaws under variable humidity, temperature, and aqueous chemistry, including crack arrest and restart after changing exposure.
status: Wiederhorn established water-vapor-dependent crack propagation in 1967. Extrapolation from steady laboratory environments to arbitrary fluctuating exposure and flaw populations remains a practical mechanistic problem.
why: Improves reliability of glass structures, containers, and protective surfaces.
key_works: S. M. Wiederhorn (1967), “Influence of Water Vapor on Crack Propagation in Soda-Lime Glass,” [DOI:10.1111/j.1151-2916.1967.tb15145.x](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1151-2916.1967.tb15145.x).

title: Durable reversible protection of unstable heritage glass
subfield: Cement, concrete, earthen materials, and glass durability
open: Prevent atmospheric leaching and crizzling in chemically unstable heritage glass through a removable treatment that preserves appearance and remains effective under long humidity cycles, without trapping damaging salts or water.
status: Centenaro et al. compared inorganic and hybrid silica protective films under artificial aging in 2025. Long-term compatibility and reversibility across historical compositions remain separate conservation targets.
why: Preserves irreplaceable glass objects without irreversible alteration by conservation treatments.
key_works: Centenaro et al. (2025), “Sol–Gel Thin Films for the Protection of Ancient Glass Artifacts: A Performance Comparison Between Inorganic and Hybrid Silica Compositions,” [DOI:10.1002/admi.202500061](https://doi.org/10.1002/admi.202500061).

title: Lithium-metal efficiency that predicts practical cell life
open: Make lithium deposition and stripping sufficiently reversible in cells with limited lithium inventory, lean electrolyte, and commercially relevant areal capacity, and predict cell life from independently measured loss mechanisms.
status: A decades-old problem. Xiao and colleagues established improved coulombic-efficiency protocols in 2020; apparently excellent efficiency in excess-lithium laboratory cells still does not establish the required full-cell lifetime.
why: Enables the energy-density benefit of lithium metal without rapid inventory exhaustion.
key_works: J. Xiao et al. (2020), “Understanding and applying coulombic efficiency in lithium metal batteries,” [DOI:10.1038/s41560-020-0648-z](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41560-020-0648-z).

title: Operando accounting of inactive lithium
open: Quantify, spatially and during operation, lithium lost to electronically isolated metal separately from lithium bound in interphase products, without perturbing the buried electrode. Close the lithium mass balance in realistic multilayer cells.
status: Fang et al. introduced destructive titration–gas chromatography in 2019. Later imaging and recovery studies establish that isolated lithium can move or reconnect; a generally applicable operando inventory remains a distinct target.
why: Identifies which loss process an electrolyte or charging intervention actually fixes.
key_works: C. Fang et al. (2019), “Quantifying inactive lithium in lithium metal batteries,” [DOI:10.1038/s41586-019-1481-z](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-019-1481-z).

title: Stripping-induced void suppression at solid–lithium interfaces
open: Prevent contact loss when lithium is removed faster than interfacial creep and diffusion can replenish it, at useful current and capacity with low external pressure. Predict the safe operating window from measured interface properties.
status: Kasemchainan et al. directly connected stripping-current limits, voids, and subsequent dendrites in 2019. Pressure and interlayers mitigate particular interfaces; transferable criteria across electrolyte, temperature, and lithium thickness remain incomplete.
why: Addresses a failure mechanism that can precede short circuits even when plating initially appears uniform.
key_works: J. Kasemchainan et al. (2019), “Critical stripping current leads to dendrite formation on plating in lithium anode solid electrolyte cells,” [DOI:10.1038/s41563-019-0438-9](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41563-019-0438-9).

title: Predictive grain-boundary failure maps for ceramic electrolytes
open: Determine which grain-boundary structures, impurities, electronic leakage, and space-charge states initiate lithium penetration, then manufacture boundary populations that remain resistant throughout cycling.
status: Penetration and intergranular transport have been studied for years; a 2025 review still identifies unresolved connections among boundary chemistry, transport, void formation, and dendrite failure. No single conductivity or stiffness metric settles all mechanisms.
why: Makes electrolyte processing specifications predictive of battery reliability.
key_works: M. S. R. Limon, A. F. Navid, C. W. Duffee and Z. Ahmad (2025), “Grain Boundaries in Ceramic Solid-State Lithium Metal Batteries: A Review,” [arXiv:2508.06866](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.06866).

title: Thin solid-state separators that tolerate manufacturing defects
open: Produce large-area, thin solid-electrolyte separators whose defect distribution permits high yield, low stack pressure, and long-life high-loading cells. Establish how acceptable defect statistics change with area and layer count.
status: The 2016 solid-state roadmap and its 2023 reassessment describe substantial conductivity advances alongside unresolved mechanical, manufacturing, and economic constraints. A successful small pellet does not determine multilayer manufacturing yield.
why: Converts laboratory solid-state performance into a scalable cell architecture.
key_works: J. Janek and W. G. Zeier (2023), “Challenges in speeding up solid-state battery development,” [DOI:10.1038/s41560-023-01208-9](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41560-023-01208-9).

title: Reversible oxygen redox without cumulative voltage loss
open: Obtain substantial anionic-redox capacity while avoiding oxygen release, irreversible cation rearrangement, and accumulating charge–discharge hysteresis over practical cycling. Identify structural rules that work across compositions rather than one special material.
status: Oxygen-redox cathodes have been developed for decades. House et al. demonstrated superstructure control of first-cycle hysteresis in 2020; first-cycle improvements do not by themselves establish stable lifetime energy efficiency.
why: Unlocks cathode capacity beyond transition-metal redox without sacrificing delivered energy.
key_works: R. A. House et al. (2020), “Superstructure control of first-cycle voltage hysteresis in oxygen-redox cathodes,” [DOI:10.1038/s41586-019-1854-3](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-019-1854-3).

title: Silicon-anode calendar stability at high silicon fraction
open: Stabilize silicon interphases during months and years of storage across state of charge and temperature, while retaining high silicon loading and useful cycling performance. Separate interphase dissolution, cracking, and lithium consumption quantitatively.
status: Calendar aging was highlighted explicitly in 2021. Zhang et al. in 2026 connected particle size and interphase chemistry to distinct aging modes and improved microsilicon stability; broad lifetime extrapolation remains unresolved.
why: Prevents stored or intermittently used silicon-rich batteries from losing their energy-density advantage.
key_works: W. Zhang et al. (2026), “Mechanistic understanding of interphase-driven ageing in silicon anodes,” [DOI:10.1038/s41560-026-01967-1](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41560-026-01967-1).

title: Rotational-stacking-fault control in layered cathodes
open: Predict and suppress synthesis-generated rotational stacking faults that promote oxygen dimerization, transition-metal migration, and intraparticle cracking, without losing rate capability or increasing manufacturing cost excessively.
status: Eum et al. identified these faults and demonstrated thermal defect annihilation in 2024. General synthesis controls and quantitative lifetime predictions across layered-oxide families remain open.
why: Offers a specific route to preventing mechanical degradation inside cathode particles.
key_works: D. Eum et al. (2024), “Electrochemomechanical failure in layered oxide cathodes caused by rotational stacking faults,” [DOI:10.1038/s41563-024-01899-9](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41563-024-01899-9).

title: Lithium–sulfur cycling with lean electrolyte and thick cathodes
open: Simultaneously maintain sulfur utilization, fast conversion, and long cycle life with high sulfur loading, little electrolyte, and limited lithium. Count host, binder, separator, and electrolyte masses in the demonstrated energy density.
status: A long-standing practical Li–S bottleneck. The 2023 assessment documents why porous hosts that capture polysulfides often consume too much electrolyte; isolated high-capacity or high-loading demonstrations do not resolve the joint constraint.
why: Makes inexpensive sulfur useful in genuinely high-energy rechargeable cells.
key_works: Y. Gong et al. (2023), “Towards Practical Application of Li–S Battery with High Sulfur Loading and Lean Electrolyte: Will Carbon-Based Hosts Win This Race?,” [DOI:10.1007/s40820-023-01120-7](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40820-023-01120-7).

title: A transferable sodium-storage mechanism for hard carbon
open: Determine when adsorption, interlayer insertion, pore filling, and metallic-cluster formation dominate the sloping and plateau capacities of hard carbon. Predict these contributions from measurable structure and electrolyte properties across precursor families.
status: Competing mechanisms remain after decades of research. Wang et al. used EPR in 2024 to connect electronic signatures with storage regions; those correlations do not yet constitute a universal structure–capacity model.
why: Replaces precursor trial-and-error with rational sodium-anode design.
key_works: B. Wang et al. (2024), “Electron paramagnetic resonance as a tool to determine the sodium charge storage mechanism of hard carbon,” [DOI:10.1038/s41467-024-45460-3](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-024-45460-3).

title: Air- and water-stable sodium layered oxides without energy penalties
open: Establish composition and surface-design rules that preserve high usable capacity while preventing proton exchange, hydration, carbonate formation, and detrimental phase transitions during ambient handling and aqueous processing.
status: Jia et al. demonstrated an air/water-stable titanium-substituted manganese oxide and practical pouch-cell implementation in 2025. The open task is extending simultaneous processing stability and performance across high-energy compositions and manufacturing variability.
why: Reduces dry-room requirements and processing costs for sodium-ion batteries.
key_works: X.-B. Jia et al. (2025), “Design principles of practical industrial-scale layered oxide cathodes with air/water stability for sustainable sodium-ion batteries,” [DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-65480-x](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-65480-x).

title: Magnesium interfaces compatible with high-energy full cells
open: Create an electronically passivating yet Mg-ion-conducting interface that supports efficient metal cycling and a high-voltage, high-loading cathode in the same electrolyte, including realistic impurity tolerance.
status: Son et al. demonstrated an artificial interphase enabling reversible magnesium chemistry in carbonate electrolyte in 2018. This resolves a proof-of-principle incompatibility; a broadly practical cathode–electrolyte–anode combination remains unfinished.
why: Allows abundant magnesium to compete on full-cell energy and cost.
key_works: S.-B. Son et al. (2018), “An artificial interphase enables reversible magnesium chemistry in carbonate electrolytes,” [DOI:10.1038/s41557-018-0019-6](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41557-018-0019-6).

title: Practical calcium-metal battery chemistry
open: Couple efficient calcium plating with a high-loading cathode and affordable electrolyte that preserves energy efficiency and cycle life under limited calcium inventory. Establish which passivation chemistry can satisfy both electrodes.
status: Ye et al. reported a room-temperature calcium–oxygen cell rechargeable for 700 cycles in 2024. That important demonstration leaves practical electrolyte cost, electrode loading, and full-cell operating constraints to be jointly established.
why: Opens another abundant-metal route to rechargeable energy storage.
key_works: L. Ye et al. (2024), “A rechargeable calcium–oxygen battery that operates at room temperature,” [DOI:10.1038/s41586-023-06949-x](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-023-06949-x).

title: Durable galvanic-corrosion control in anode-less aqueous zinc
open: Prevent corrosion between deposited zinc and its current collector during both storage and cycling, while retaining uniform nucleation and low resistance with limited zinc inventory.
status: Aqueous-zinc corrosion is longstanding; Zhao et al. isolated the current-collector galvanic pathway and demonstrated mitigation in 2026. General collector/interphase designs with validated long calendar life remain open.
why: Makes low-cost, nonflammable zinc storage compatible with energy-dense anode-less designs.
key_works: Y. Zhao et al. (2026), “Minimizing galvanic corrosion for durable anode-less aqueous zinc batteries,” [DOI:10.1038/s41467-026-74166-x](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-74166-x).

title: Regenerable organic flow-battery molecules
open: Design inexpensive redox molecules whose dominant degradation products can be returned to active material in situ with little energy or reagent consumption, without accumulating irreversible contaminants.
status: Organic-electrolyte decomposition has constrained the field for years. Jing et al. demonstrated electrochemical recomposition of a decomposed anthraquinone electrolyte in 2022; broadly applicable regeneration across both electrolytes and repeated aging remains open.
why: Makes electrolyte lifetime repairable instead of requiring continual chemical replacement.
key_works: Y. Jing et al. (2022), “In situ electrochemical recomposition of decomposed redox-active species in aqueous organic flow batteries,” [DOI:10.1038/s41557-022-00967-4](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41557-022-00967-4).

title: Comparable lifetime–cost data for organic flow electrolytes
open: Build an openly reproducible dataset separating calendar decomposition, crossover, state-of-charge imbalance, and cycling losses, alongside measured synthesis costs and regeneration requirements under matched protocols.
status: Emmel et al. introduced lifetime–cost benchmarking in 2023. Literature-derived comparisons provide a start; they do not replace interlaboratory measurements with complete provenance and standardized operating conditions.
why: Prevents unstable or costly molecules from looking competitive because of favorable reporting conventions.
key_works: D. Emmel et al. (2023), “Benchmarking organic active materials for aqueous redox flow batteries in terms of lifetime and cost,” [DOI:10.1038/s41467-023-42450-9](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-023-42450-9).

title: Singlet-oxygen-resistant lithium–oxygen chemistry
open: Suppress or harmlessly quench singlet oxygen during oxygen reduction and evolution without sacrificing useful capacity or adding consumable scavengers. Demonstrate closed oxygen and electrolyte mass balances over extended cycling.
status: Mahne et al. identified singlet oxygen as a major parasitic-reaction source in 2017. Quenchers and mediator redesign help individual pathways, but reversible aprotic oxygen cycling with durable components remains unresolved.
why: Addresses chemical destruction that otherwise masquerades as rechargeable oxygen capacity.
key_works: N. Mahne et al. (2017), “Singlet oxygen generation as a major cause for parasitic reactions during cycling of aprotic lithium–oxygen batteries,” [DOI:10.1038/nenergy.2017.36](https://doi.org/10.1038/nenergy.2017.36).

title: Lifetime suppression of mixed-halide phase segregation
open: Keep wide-bandgap mixed-halide absorbers compositionally uniform under simultaneous illumination, bias, heat, and cycling, while maintaining efficient charge extraction. Predict segregation thresholds from composition and microstructure.
status: Light-induced segregation has been investigated since the mid-2010s. Wang et al. demonstrated suppression suitable for triple-junction cells in 2023; establishing a durable, transferable suppression mechanism remains open.
why: Preserves the bandgaps and voltages needed for efficient multijunction solar cells.
key_works: Z. Wang et al. (2023), “Suppressed phase segregation for triple-junction perovskite solar cells,” [DOI:10.1038/s41586-023-06006-7](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-023-06006-7).

title: Reverse-bias-tolerant perovskite tandem materials
open: Design absorber, transport-layer, and electrode interfaces that survive repeated partial-shading reverse bias after normal environmental aging, without hotspots, irreversible ion redistribution, or a large efficiency penalty.
status: Several mitigation routes now exist, including graded dielectric layers reported by Wang et al. in 2026. The remaining issue is reliable combined-stress performance at module scale, not the first demonstration of mitigation.
why: Prevents ordinary shading events from becoming irreversible module failures.
key_works: L. Wang et al. (2026), “Improving the stability of monolithic perovskite/silicon tandems against reverse-bias stress using graded dielectric layers,” [DOI:10.1038/s41560-026-02067-w](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41560-026-02067-w).

title: Tin-perovskite oxidation and self-doping control
open: Suppress Sn(II) oxidation, vacancy-driven self-doping, and film inhomogeneity through fabrication and prolonged outdoor operation, while preserving the favorable narrow bandgap and efficient carrier collection of lead-free tin absorbers.
status: He et al. reported certified 16.65% efficiency in 2025 and 1,500-hour illumination stability in nitrogen; the reported endurance test was at open circuit. Air exposure, power-producing operation, and module lifetime remain distinct challenges.
why: Enables competitive lead-free thin-film photovoltaics.
key_works: D. He et al. (2025), “Homogeneous 2D/3D heterostructured tin halide perovskite photovoltaics,” [DOI:10.1038/s41565-025-01905-4](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41565-025-01905-4).

title: Transferable acceleration laws for perovskite outdoor lifetime
open: Infer long-term field degradation from accelerated tests with calibrated uncertainty across climates, cell stacks, and encapsulants. The model must capture interacting light, humidity, temperature, bias, and thermal-cycle mechanisms.
status: Jiang et al. linked accelerated testing to six months of outdoor aging in a particular stack in 2023. That is a valuable partial result; general multi-decade extrapolation and independent cross-climate validation remain open.
why: Makes durability claims and warranties scientifically defensible.
key_works: Q. Jiang et al. (2023), “Towards linking lab and field lifetimes of perovskite solar cells,” [DOI:10.1038/s41586-023-06610-7](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-023-06610-7).

title: Lead immobilization through damage and end of life
open: Develop lead-binding materials that retain released lead after realistic breakage, weathering, and disposal exposures, while permitting efficient module recycling. Quantify capture saturation and leaching products rather than only intact-module leakage.
status: Adsorption, complexation, grain isolation, and encapsulation approaches were assessed comprehensively in 2023. The unresolved target is durable containment across failure modes with demonstrated recovery, not merely the existence of lead sorbents.
why: Reduces environmental release and simplifies responsible deployment of lead-containing absorbers.
key_works: H. Zhang et al. (2023), “Lead immobilization for environmentally sustainable perovskite solar cells,” [DOI:10.1038/s41586-023-05938-4](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-023-05938-4).

title: Predictive suppression of organic-photovoltaic triplet voltage loss
open: Predict donor–acceptor structures that suppress nonradiative recombination through triplets while retaining efficient charge generation at small energy offsets. Validate the rule across molecular families and device processing conditions.
status: Gillett et al. identified dominant triplet recombination in important non-fullerene blends and demonstrated a suppression strategy in 2021. This makes the open problem a transferable materials-design principle rather than proving that suppression is possible.
why: Raises voltage without giving back the gain through poor photocurrent.
key_works: A. J. Gillett et al. (2021), “The role of charge recombination to triplet excitons in organic solar cells,” [DOI:10.1038/s41586-021-03840-5](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-021-03840-5).

title: Predictive photochemical lifetime of organic absorber blends
open: Connect excited-state populations and molecular packing to irreversible photochemical products and efficiency loss, then design blends that remain chemically and morphologically stable under realistic spectra, oxygen ingress, and temperature cycling.
status: Organic-cell instability has been studied for decades. Ramirez et al. established a spin-dependent fullerene degradation pathway in 2021; chemistry-specific mechanisms still lack a generally predictive lifetime framework.
why: Makes flexible photovoltaics durable enough to realize their low-material-use advantages.
key_works: I. Ramirez et al. (2021), “The role of spin in the degradation of organic photovoltaics,” [DOI:10.1038/s41467-020-20601-6](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-020-20601-6).

title: Kesterite voltage deficit from disorder and deep traps
open: Remove the dominant nonradiative losses in Cu2ZnSn(S,Se)4 while controlling antisite disorder, secondary phases, and band tails during scalable processing. Establish which defect populations causally determine the residual voltage deficit.
status: A long-standing kesterite limitation. Wu et al. reported oxygen-assisted suppression of deep traps and 11.51% certified efficiency for sulfur-only Cu2ZnSnS4 in 2025; this is not a record claim for mixed sulfur–selenium kesterites.
why: Improves a photovoltaic family based on comparatively abundant elements.
key_works: T. Wu et al. (2025), “Heat treatment in an oxygen-rich environment to suppress deep-level traps in Cu2ZnSnS4 solar cell with 11.51% certified efficiency,” [DOI:10.1038/s41560-025-01756-2](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41560-025-01756-2).

title: Earth-abundant catalysts for durable acidic oxygen evolution
subfield: Catalysts, membranes, and porous energy materials
open: Achieve industrially useful oxygen-evolution current and lifetime in strongly acidic membrane electrolysis without relying on substantial platinum-group-metal content. Measure dissolution and retained active-site population during realistic dynamic operation.
status: Acidic water oxidation is a decades-old activity–stability problem. Wan et al. reviewed promising nonprecious compositions in 2024, while identifying durability and device translation as continuing limitations.
why: Removes an important materials-supply constraint on large-scale hydrogen electrolysis.
key_works: R. Wan et al. (2024), “Earth-abundant electrocatalysts for acidic oxygen evolution,” [DOI:10.1038/s41929-024-01266-6](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41929-024-01266-6).

title: Durable Fe–N–C oxygen-reduction sites in acidic fuel cells
subfield: Catalysts, membranes, and porous energy materials
open: Preserve active Fe–Nx sites, carbon support structure, and gas accessibility under realistic acidic fuel-cell potentials, peroxide exposure, and humidity cycling without sacrificing initial activity.
status: Fe–N–C has been pursued for decades. Bae et al. disentangled coupled degradation causes in 2023 and demonstrated stabilization using isolated platinum ions; achieving comparable durability without introducing a precious-metal dependency remains open.
why: Enables lower-cost fuel-cell cathodes with predictable lifetime.
key_works: G. Bae et al. (2023), “Unravelling the complex causality behind Fe–N–C degradation in fuel cells,” [DOI:10.1038/s41929-023-01039-7](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41929-023-01039-7).

title: Carbon-efficient CO2 electrolysis without prohibitive energy losses
subfield: Catalysts, membranes, and porous energy materials
open: Develop electrode–electrolyte–membrane combinations that suppress carbonate loss while retaining high CO2-reduction selectivity, useful current density, and low total energy demand including separation and CO2 recovery.
status: Rabinowitz and Kanan quantified the basic carbonate penalty in 2020. Acidic operation and bipolar membranes provide partial routes, but introduce hydrogen competition or additional voltage costs.
why: Determines whether electrochemical carbon conversion uses captured carbon and electricity efficiently.
key_works: J. A. Rabinowitz and M. W. Kanan (2020), “The future of low-temperature carbon dioxide electrolysis depends on solving one basic problem,” [DOI:10.1038/s41467-020-19135-8](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-020-19135-8).

title: Stable copper active structures for multicarbon electrosynthesis
subfield: Catalysts, membranes, and porous energy materials
open: Identify and maintain the copper surface ensembles that produce a chosen multicarbon product, despite dissolution, redeposition, alloy segregation, and adsorbate-driven restructuring during operation.
status: Copper selectivity has been studied for decades. Kim et al. reported predictive reconstruction principles for bimetallic copper catalysts in 2025; sustaining a desired active structure and selectivity through long operation remains open.
why: Makes catalyst design relevant to the operating state and downstream product purity.
key_works: I. Kim et al. (2025), “Unveiling the reconstruction of copper bimetallic catalysts during CO2 electroreduction,” [DOI:10.1038/s41929-025-01368-9](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41929-025-01368-9).

title: Flood- and salt-resistant CO2 gas-diffusion electrodes
subfield: Catalysts, membranes, and porous energy materials
open: Maintain stable gas, liquid, and ion pathways in catalyst layers over prolonged high-current operation despite electrowetting, carbonate crystallization, and changing local composition. Predict failure from pore-scale measurements.
status: Flooding and salt precipitation have constrained high-rate cells for years. Li et al. demonstrated non-isothermal mitigation in 2025; robust materials and operating windows across feed conditions remain unresolved.
why: Prevents transport failures from erasing promising catalyst performance.
key_works: J. Li et al. (2025), “Non-isothermal CO2 electrolysis enables simultaneous enhanced electrochemical and anti-precipitation performance,” [DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-59604-6](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-59604-6).

title: Energy-efficient lithium-mediated nitrogen reduction
subfield: Catalysts, membranes, and porous energy materials
open: Control the reactive lithium interphase and proton delivery so that sustained ammonia synthesis combines high selectivity, high production rate, and low full-cell energy consumption without accumulating electrolyte damage.
status: Lithium-mediated nitrogen reduction is established experimentally. Li et al. demonstrated long-term continuous electrosynthesis in 2024; the remaining material challenge is simultaneously optimizing interphase lifetime, proton transport, and energy efficiency.
why: Could support distributed ammonia production using electricity and nitrogen.
key_works: S. Li et al. (2024), “Long-term continuous ammonia electrosynthesis,” [DOI:10.1038/s41586-024-07276-5](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-024-07276-5).

title: Selective nitrate-to-ammonia catalysts across dilute real feeds
subfield: Catalysts, membranes, and porous energy materials
open: Sustain selective nitrate conversion at low and fluctuating concentration in the presence of realistic competing ions and contaminants, while suppressing hydrogen and nitrite byproducts and enabling economical ammonia recovery.
status: Zhang et al. reported defect-engineered copper effective across a wide concentration range in 2024. Performance under changing real effluents, catalyst fouling, and integrated low-concentration product recovery remains a broader unresolved target.
why: Joins pollutant removal with useful nitrogen recovery.
key_works: B. Zhang et al. (2024), “Defect-induced triple synergistic modulation in copper for superior electrochemical ammonia production across broad nitrate concentrations,” [DOI:10.1038/s41467-024-47025-w](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-024-47025-w).

title: Oxidation-resistant ionomers for pure-water alkaline electrolysis
subfield: Catalysts, membranes, and porous energy materials
open: Design hydroxide-conducting ionomer cations and backbones that resist oxidative attack at the anode while preserving catalyst adhesion, water transport, and conductivity in pure-water-fed devices.
status: Alkaline chemical stability alone has proved insufficient. Jin et al. traced device failure to cation oxidation in 2026 and proposed design guidance; a broadly validated conductivity–oxidation–mechanics solution remains open.
why: Enables inexpensive catalysts without requiring continual concentrated-alkali feed.
key_works: Y. Jin et al. (2026), “Oxidative stability as a guiding principle for durable ionomer cations in pure-water electrolysis,” [DOI:10.1038/s41467-026-73209-7](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-73209-7).

title: Low-loss, durable bipolar-membrane junctions
subfield: Catalysts, membranes, and porous energy materials
open: Catalyse water dissociation at bipolar junctions with low added voltage at high current while preventing delamination, salt leakage, and catalyst redistribution. Demonstrate performance under sustained pH gradients and repeated start–stop operation.
status: Bipolar membranes are established technology; Prats Vergel et al. quantified how water-dissociation efficiency constrains CO2-electrolysis viability in 2025. Joint voltage, crossover, and lifetime targets remain material-specific challenges.
why: Allows incompatible optimal electrode environments to coexist efficiently in one cell.
key_works: G. Prats Vergel et al. (2025), “Water dissociation efficiencies control the viability of reverse-bias bipolar membranes for CO2 electrolysis,” [DOI:10.1038/s44286-025-00306-7](https://doi.org/10.1038/s44286-025-00306-7).

title: Direct-air-capture sorbents that survive realistic atmospheres
subfield: Catalysts, membranes, and porous energy materials
open: Combine rapid uptake at atmospheric CO2 concentration with low regeneration energy and durable performance through humidity, oxygen, pollutants, and temperature swings, after shaping the sorbent into a low-pressure-drop contactor.
status: Zhou et al. reported a COF retaining performance through more than 100 open-air adsorption–desorption cycles in 2024. This milestone leaves long service life, diverse atmospheres, shaping, and regeneration economics to be established jointly.
why: Reduces sorbent replacement and energy requirements for carbon removal.
key_works: Z. Zhou et al. (2024), “Carbon dioxide capture from open air using covalent organic frameworks,” [DOI:10.1038/s41586-024-08080-x](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-024-08080-x).

title: Defect-controlled MOF-glass separation membranes
subfield: Catalysts, membranes, and porous energy materials
open: Preserve designed molecular-scale pores while forming mechanically robust, large-area MOF-glass membranes, and maintain mixture selectivity after humid exposure, pressure cycling, and physical aging.
status: Li et al. demonstrated highly porous MOF glasses and gas-separation membranes in 2025. Precise pore control and reproducible integration remain more demanding than demonstrating favorable gas transport in individual specimens.
why: Combines molecular sieving with forms that can be manufactured and operated reliably.
key_works: S. Li et al. (2025), “Highly porous metal-organic framework glass design and application for gas separation membranes,” [DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-56295-x](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-56295-x).

title: Reversible hydrogen-storage materials meeting complete system requirements
subfield: Catalysts, membranes, and porous energy materials
open: Find sorbents or reversible hydrides that simultaneously deliver adequate usable gravimetric and volumetric capacity, rapid uptake and release, appropriate temperatures and pressures, hydrogen purity, and low cycling energy after system hardware is counted.
status: A multi-decade program. DOE's materials-based-storage program explicitly retains capacity, kinetics, impurities, and regeneration as research needs; material-only uptake measurements do not establish a complete storage-system solution.
why: Enables compact hydrogen storage without severe compression or cryogenic penalties.
key_works: U.S. Department of Energy (ongoing), [“Materials-Based Hydrogen Storage”](https://www.energy.gov/cmei/fuels/materials-based-hydrogen-storage); DOE (2024), [“Department of Energy Hydrogen Program Plan”](https://www.hydrogen.energy.gov/docs/hydrogenprogramlibraries/pdfs/hydrogen-program-plan-2024.pdf).

title: Durable high-yield particulate solar water splitting
subfield: Catalysts, membranes, and porous energy materials
open: Demonstrate a particulate-photocatalyst system of at least 100 m² with annual solar-to-hydrogen energy conversion of at least 7.6%, scalable catalyst manufacture, safe product separation, and no sacrificial reagents. This census-proposed moonshot sets the annual target at ten times the 2021 demonstration's reported peak efficiency.
status: Nishiyama et al. demonstrated a 100 m² system operated over several months in 2021, reaching a maximum 0.76% solar-to-hydrogen efficiency. Peak efficiency and year-long energy yield are different metrics; the proposed combined scale–efficiency–lifetime target remains open.
why: Could make solar hydrogen using simple, inexpensive semiconductor particle systems.
key_works: H. Nishiyama et al. (2021), “Photocatalytic solar hydrogen production from water on a 100-m² scale,” [DOI:10.1038/s41586-021-03907-3](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-021-03907-3).

title: Long-life electrical contacts for Mg3Sb2 thermoelectrics
open: Maintain low contact resistance and adhesion while preventing interdiffusion and reaction at Mg3Sb2-based thermoelectric legs through prolonged thermal gradients and repeated thermal cycling.
status: Fu et al. reported contact resistivity below 5 µΩ cm² and module efficiency up to 11% at a 440 K temperature difference in 2024. Lifetime extrapolation and repeatable large-batch contacts remain separate engineering challenges.
why: Converts strong bulk thermoelectric properties into durable generator performance.
key_works: Y. Fu et al. (2024), “Interface kinetic manipulation enabling efficient and reliable Mg3Sb2 thermoelectrics,” [DOI:10.1038/s41467-024-53598-3](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-024-53598-3).

title: Suppressing ionic segregation in superionic thermoelectrics
open: Prevent current- and temperature-driven copper migration, electrode deposition, and composition gradients in copper-chalcogenide thermoelectrics while retaining the low thermal conductivity responsible for their performance.
status: The superionic advantage and its stability cost have been recognized for years. Hu et al. demonstrated stabilized copper selenide in 2024; broadly predictive long-term stability under actual device gradients remains open.
why: Makes high thermoelectric figures of merit useful under continuous electrical load.
key_works: H. Hu et al. (2024), “Highly stabilized and efficient thermoelectric copper selenide,” [DOI:10.1038/s41563-024-01815-1](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41563-024-01815-1).

title: Air-stable n-type thermoelectric elastomers
open: Maintain electron doping, conductivity, thermopower, and mechanical recovery through prolonged air/humidity exposure and repeated strain, with matched durable contacts and scalable processing.
status: Liu et al. demonstrated n-type thermoelectric elastomers with substantial elastic recovery in 2025. The open target is the combined environmental, mechanical, and device lifetime rather than the existence of an n-type stretchable material.
why: Enables mechanically conformable thermoelectric pairs for sensing and energy harvesting.
key_works: K. Liu et al. (2025), “n-Type thermoelectric elastomers,” [DOI:10.1038/s41586-025-09387-z](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-025-09387-z).

title: Useful bulk p-type conductivity in beta-gallium oxide
open: Demonstrate reproducible, mobile-hole conduction in bulk beta-Ga2O3 at device-useful temperatures and densities, with compensation and parasitic phases excluded; alternatively establish the material-specific limits imposed by self-trapping and acceptor energetics.
status: Self-trapped holes were identified as a fundamental obstacle by Varley and colleagues in 2012. Reports of p-type behavior require distinguishing band transport from defect, surface, and secondary-phase conduction.
why: Would enable native bipolar architectures in an ultrawide-bandgap power material.
key_works: J. B. Varley, A. Janotti, C. Franchini and C. G. Van de Walle (2012), “Role of self-trapping in luminescence and p-type conductivity of wide-band-gap oxides,” [DOI:10.1103/PhysRevB.85.081109](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevB.85.081109).

title: Efficient room-temperature electron doping of diamond
open: Introduce electrically active donors into device-quality diamond with sufficiently shallow activation, low compensation, and controlled spatial profiles to support low-resistance room-temperature electron transport.
status: Diamond n-type doping has been pursued for decades and is not wholly absent: phosphorus-doped material exists. The 2025 review emphasizes deep levels, incorporation limitations, and room-temperature conductivity as continuing obstacles.
why: Complements diamond's established hole conduction for high-power bipolar devices.
key_works: M. Sultana, S. Karmakar and A. Haque (2025), [“N- and P-type doping of diamonds: A review”](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S136980012400920X).

title: High-conductivity p-type aluminum nitride
open: Achieve stable, reproducible hole injection and conduction in high-quality AlN without excessive compensation, optical absorption, or contact resistance. Validate the mechanism in functioning AlN-based bipolar structures.
status: Deep acceptors have constrained AlN devices for decades. Ma et al. reported Mg-doped p-type films in 2025, while identifying limited activation and mobility; detecting p-type character does not settle useful device conductivity.
why: Supports deep-ultraviolet emitters and ultrawide-bandgap bipolar electronics.
key_works: Y. Ma et al. (2025), “Mg-Doped P-Type AlN Thin Film Prepared by Magnetron Sputtering Using Mg-Al Alloy Targets,” [DOI:10.3390/mi16091035](https://doi.org/10.3390/mi16091035).

title: Reproducible nanoscale contacts to two-dimensional semiconductors
open: Preserve low contact resistance and reproducible carrier injection as contact length shrinks, across wafer-scale material variations, both carrier polarities, and subsequent processing. Resolve interfacial chemistry and Fermi-level pinning without fragile transfer steps.
status: Du et al. reported antimony contacts with 98 Ω µm resistance at 18 nm contact length in 2025. The remaining target includes distribution tails, p-type contacts, thermal stability, and manufacturing yield.
why: Prevents contacts from overwhelming the advantages of atomically thin channels.
key_works: M. Du et al. (2025), “Scaled crystalline antimony ohmic contacts for two-dimensional transistors,” [DOI:10.1038/s41928-025-01500-4](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41928-025-01500-4); [author correction, 2026](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41928-026-01563-x).

title: Scalable ultrathin dielectrics with clean 2D interfaces
open: Integrate uniform high-permittivity gate dielectrics on two-dimensional semiconductors with low trap density, low leakage, stable threshold voltage, and reliable breakdown at aggressively scaled thickness.
status: Zeng et al. demonstrated transferred single-crystalline alumina dielectrics in 2024. Demonstrating excellent devices is a partial result; reproducible low-temperature integration and wafer-level reliability remain separate material/process questions.
why: Enables strong gate control without introducing defects that destroy channel performance.
key_works: D. Zeng et al. (2024), “Single-crystalline metal-oxide dielectrics for top-gate 2D transistors,” [DOI:10.1038/s41586-024-07786-2](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-024-07786-2).

title: Wafer-scale 2D single crystals without stitched-boundary penalties
open: Grow device-grade monolayers with uniform thickness, orientation, and defect density over manufacturing wafers, avoiding electrically harmful translation boundaries where aligned domains merge. Establish reproducible yield across batches and substrates.
status: Jiang et al. demonstrated centimetre-scale single-domain MoS2 through two-dimensional Czochralski growth in 2025. Extending single-domain quality to manufacturing-scale wafers and compatible substrates remains open.
why: Makes large-area two-dimensional electronics predictable at the individual-device level.
key_works: H. Jiang et al. (2025), “Two-dimensional Czochralski growth of single-crystal MoS2,” [DOI:10.1038/s41563-024-02069-7](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41563-024-02069-7).

title: Deep-blue OLED efficiency–lifetime compatibility
open: Design emitters, sensitizers, and hosts that provide saturated deep-blue emission with high efficiency and long operating life at useful luminance, while resisting exciton-induced bond cleavage and electrical degradation.
status: The blue-lifetime problem is decades old. Zhang et al.'s 2026 review surveys sensitized-fluorescence progress and continuing efficiency–lifetime limitations; broadly manufacturable color, efficiency, and lifetime across demanding operating conditions remain unresolved.
why: Improves display lifetime and reduces the power cost of blue emission.
key_works: D. Zhang et al. (2026), “Stable deep-blue organic light-emitting diodes based on sensitized fluorescence,” [DOI:10.1038/s41566-025-01810-1](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41566-025-01810-1).

title: Color-stable blue perovskite electroluminescence
open: Maintain saturated blue emission, high efficiency, and long lifetime under sustained electrical injection and heat, without halide redistribution or progressive structural decomposition.
status: Wang et al. reported isomer-mediated hydrogen-bond networks and external quantum efficiencies up to 22.0% in 2026. High peak efficiency is a partial result; extended operation at practical luminance remains a separate target.
why: Completes the demanding blue component of perovskite full-color displays.
key_works: Y. Wang et al. (2026), “Isomeric multi-hydrogen-bonding enables blue perovskite LEDs,” [DOI:10.1038/s41586-026-10723-0](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-10723-0).

title: Continuous electrically pumped colloidal-quantum-dot lasing
open: Demonstrate sustained electrically pumped lasing with clear cavity-mode and coherence evidence, while controlling Auger recombination, charge imbalance, Joule heating, and optical loss in a solution-processable quantum-dot device.
status: Ahn et al. achieved electrically driven amplified spontaneous emission in 2023. That milestone establishes electrical gain, while continuous laser operation and durable devices impose additional materials constraints.
why: Enables chemically tunable, integrated laser sources fabricated from colloidal materials.
key_works: N. Ahn et al. (2023), “Electrically driven amplified spontaneous emission from colloidal quantum dots,” [DOI:10.1038/s41586-023-05855-6](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-023-05855-6).

title: Reproducible telecom spin–photon defects in silicon
open: Fabricate optically coherent silicon defects at controlled locations with reproducible charge states and sufficiently uniform optical frequencies for remote photon interference, while preserving spin coherence after nanofabrication and electrical excitation.
status: T-center cavity coupling and electrical excitation have advanced rapidly; Dobinson et al. reported electrically triggered devices in 2025. High-yield defect formation and reproducible coherence across many devices remain open.
why: Connects semiconductor manufacturing to scalable quantum-network nodes.
key_works: M. Dobinson et al. (2025), “Electrically triggered spin–photon devices in silicon,” [DOI:10.1038/s41566-025-01752-8](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41566-025-01752-8).

title: Predictive microscopic pairing theory for cuprates
open: Derive a quantitatively predictive account of pairing and superconducting transition temperatures across cuprate families from experimentally constrained electronic structure, including the competing roles of correlation, lattice coupling, and phase coherence.
status: Open since the 1986 discovery. D-wave pairing and extensive phase diagrams are established, but the 2015 synthesis and subsequent work leave the material-dependent microscopic origin of high transition temperatures unresolved.
why: Would turn a remarkable empirical materials family into a platform for directed superconductor design.
key_works: B. Keimer et al. (2015), “From quantum matter to high-temperature superconductivity in copper oxides,” [DOI:10.1038/nature14165](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature14165).

title: The superconducting order parameter of Sr2RuO4
open: Identify an order parameter consistent with spin susceptibility, strain response, time-reversal-symmetry tests, gap structure, and thermodynamics in comparably characterized samples, resolving conflicting interpretations among these probes.
status: Unsettled since superconductivity was discovered in 1994. Pustogow et al.'s 2019 oxygen-NMR results challenged the long-favored spin-triplet interpretation; a universally consistent experimental identification remains open.
why: Tests how multiorbital electronic correlations create unconventional superconductivity.
key_works: A. Pustogow et al. (2019), “Constraints on the superconducting order parameter in Sr2RuO4 from oxygen-17 nuclear magnetic resonance,” [DOI:10.1038/s41586-019-1596-2](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-019-1596-2).

title: Pairing symmetry in bilayer nickelate superconductors
open: Determine the sign and momentum structure of pairing in bilayer nickelates, and establish which orbital, interlayer, and oxygen-stoichiometry parameters control superconductivity. Require phase-sensitive or mutually constraining bulk probes on well-characterized phases.
status: High-pressure bilayer-nickelate superconductivity was reported in 2023. The 2026 review emphasizes continuing synthesis and sample-quality limits on decisive measurements, despite rapid progress across several nickelate families.
why: Distinguishes competing mechanisms in a new high-temperature superconductor family.
key_works: P. Puphal et al. (2026), “Superconductivity in infinite-layer and Ruddlesden–Popper nickelates,” [DOI:10.1038/s42254-025-00898-2](https://doi.org/10.1038/s42254-025-00898-2).

title: Recovering high-temperature superconducting hydrides at low pressure
open: Preserve a hydrogen-rich superconducting structure and its favorable electronic/phonon properties after decompression, with measured lifetime, reproducible synthesis, and independently verified superconductivity at the recovered pressure.
status: High-pressure hydrides have achieved major superconducting advances. Caussé et al. recovered Y3Fe4H20 at ambient pressure in 2026; structural recovery alone does not establish recovery of a high-temperature superconducting phase.
why: Connects high-pressure discovery to materials that can be handled and used.
key_works: M. Caussé et al. (2026), “Ambient pressure recovery of the structurally unconventional hydride Y3Fe4H20,” [DOI:10.1038/s41467-026-74232-4](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-74232-4).

title: Reproducible ambient-pressure room-temperature superconductivity
open: Produce a reproducible material superconducting near ordinary room temperature and atmospheric pressure, supported by consistent transport, magnetic, thermodynamic, and structural evidence and independent replication.
status: A century-scale ambition; the 2026 programmatic roadmap still treats it as an open grand challenge. High-pressure results, theoretical predictions, and disputed claims are partial context rather than a demonstrated solution to this target.
why: Removes refrigeration and pressure barriers to many superconducting applications.
key_works: R. P. Prasankumar et al. (2026), “The path to room-temperature superconductivity: A programmatic approach,” [DOI:10.1073/pnas.2520324123](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2520324123).

title: Disorder-tolerant material platforms for protected Majorana modes
open: Produce sufficiently uniform, hard-gap semiconductor–superconductor structures whose zero modes exhibit protection that strengthens with system size, while excluding ordinary Andreev states and controlling quasiparticle poisoning.
status: Bordin et al. demonstrated enhanced stability in a three-site Kitaev chain in 2025. Short-chain zero-mode signatures are partial progress toward a scalable, experimentally protected material platform.
why: Determines whether candidate topological states can provide useful physical protection.
key_works: A. Bordin et al. (2025), “Enhanced Majorana stability in a three-site Kitaev chain,” [DOI:10.1038/s41565-025-01894-4](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41565-025-01894-4).

title: Robust fractional Chern insulators beyond exceptional devices
open: Establish how disorder, twist variations, screening, and contacts control the fractional gap, then fabricate reproducible zero-field fractional Chern states that retain low dissipation over useful temperature and current ranges.
status: Fractionally quantized anomalous Hall transport was observed in 2023, and Park et al. reported a dissipationless fractional Chern insulator in 2026. Reproducibility and robust operating margins remain distinct unsolved materials problems.
why: Makes zero-field fractional topological matter a controlled experimental resource.
key_works: H. Park et al. (2026), “Observation of dissipationless fractional Chern insulator,” [DOI:10.1038/s41567-025-03167-2](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41567-025-03167-2).

title: Pairing mechanism in graphene moiré superconductors
open: Identify the dominant pairing interaction and symmetry, separating phonon, spin, valley, and correlation effects while accounting for twist disorder and dielectric environment. Predict how controlled material changes shift the superconducting dome.
status: Superconductivity emerged in magic-angle graphene experiments in 2018. Kim et al. resolved intervalley gaps and many-body resonances in 2026, but spectroscopic correlations alone do not uniquely determine the pairing mechanism.
why: Uses tunable quantum materials to test competing explanations of unconventional pairing.
key_works: Y. Cao et al. (2018), “Unconventional superconductivity in magic-angle graphene superlattices,” [DOI:10.1038/nature26160](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature26160); H. Kim et al. (2026), “Resolving intervalley gaps and many-body resonances in moiré superconductors,” [DOI:10.1038/s41586-025-10067-1](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-025-10067-1).

title: Identifying the heat carriers in field-tuned alpha-RuCl3
open: Separate phonon, magnon, and fractionalized-spin contributions to thermal Hall transport across relevant field geometries, and determine whether a distinct field-induced topological spin-liquid regime exists.
status: Quantum-spin-liquid interpretations have been debated for roughly a decade. Shragai et al. measured phonon Hall-viscosity effects in 2026; this adds a concrete competing heat-transport mechanism without by itself deciding every field regime.
why: Tests a prominent candidate realization of Kitaev fractionalization.
key_works: A. Shragai et al. (2026), “Phonon Hall viscosity and the intrinsic thermal Hall effect of α-RuCl3,” [DOI:10.1038/s41586-026-10420-y](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-10420-y).

title: Intrinsic spin gap and ground state of herbertsmithite
open: Determine the clean kagome-layer ground state and excitation gap while quantitatively separating intersite disorder and defect-spin contributions. Reconcile local probes, neutron spectra, and thermodynamic measurements on matched samples.
status: Herbertsmithite has been a leading spin-liquid candidate since the 2000s. Takahashi et al. reported new spin-dynamics evidence in 2026; defect-sensitive interpretation and the intrinsic low-energy spectrum remain open.
why: Anchors kagome quantum-spin-liquid theory to a chemically realized material.
key_works: H. Takahashi et al. (2026), “Spinon mediation of witness spin dynamics in herbertsmithite,” [DOI:10.1038/s41567-026-03303-6](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41567-026-03303-6).

title: Manufacturable air-stable room-temperature 2D magnets
open: Combine room-temperature magnetic order, ambient chemical stability, reproducible ultrathin growth, and reversible electrical control in an integrated material platform. Establish whether the observed magnetism is intrinsic rather than defect or secondary-phase dominated.
status: Deng et al. demonstrated gate-tunable room-temperature ferromagnetism in thin Fe3GeTe2 in 2018. The open target combines environmental stability and manufacturing reproducibility with useful magnetic control; room-temperature 2D ferromagnetism itself is not unobserved.
why: Enables atomically thin spin filters, memories, and magnetic heterostructures.
key_works: Y. Deng et al. (2018), “Gate-tunable room-temperature ferromagnetism in two-dimensional Fe3GeTe2,” [DOI:10.1038/s41586-018-0626-9](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-018-0626-9).

title: Predictable dense skyrmion motion in real multilayers
open: Engineer multilayer disorder and interfacial interactions so dense skyrmion populations can be created, moved, and annihilated reproducibly without pinning, uncontrolled lateral deflection, or collision-induced information loss.
status: Synthetic antiferromagnets offer fast motion and reduced Hall deflection. Bhukta et al. imaged interactions and demonstrated collective control in 2026; robust operation across realistic disorder and dense populations remains open.
why: Makes skyrmion dynamics useful for reproducible information-bearing devices.
key_works: M. Bhukta et al. (2026), “Time-resolved imaging of antiferromagnetic skyrmion interactions,” [DOI:10.1038/s41567-026-03383-4](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41567-026-03383-4).

title: Predicting hafnia ferroelectric phase stability and fatigue
open: Predict which polar phases form and survive from oxygen chemical potential, grain structure, stress, electrodes, and electrical history, then prevent wake-up, imprint, and fatigue without sacrificing scaled-film polarization.
status: Ferroelectric hafnia was discovered in 2011. Kelley et al. demonstrated control through the surface electrochemical state in 2023; a unified process-to-phase-to-lifetime model remains incomplete.
why: Makes hafnia-based memory manufacturing and endurance more predictable.
key_works: K. P. Kelley et al. (2023), “Ferroelectricity in hafnia controlled via surface electrochemical state,” [DOI:10.1038/s41563-023-01619-9](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41563-023-01619-9).

title: Low-field switching with high endurance in ultrathin AlScN
open: Lower the switching field and energy of ultrathin AlScN while retaining remanent polarization, a wide margin below dielectric breakdown, long retention, and endurance across manufacturing variations.
status: Wurtzite ferroelectricity has developed rapidly since 2019. Cho et al. reported over 10^10 cycles with controlled partial polarization switching in 45-nm AlScN in 2026; complete reversal sustained about 10^8 cycles. Simultaneous low-field operation, polarization, scaling, and reliability remain open.
why: Enables practical nitride ferroelectric memories and integrated electromechanical devices.
key_works: H. Cho et al. (2026), “Write cycling endurance exceeding 10^10 in sub-50 nm ferroelectric AlScN,” [DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-68221-2](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-68221-2).

title: Arbitrary-sequence synthetic polymers at production scale
open: Produce nonbiological-backbone polymers with long, individually specified monomer sequences while controlling chain length, stereochemistry, and sequence defects. A demanding census target is kilogram batches of prescribed 1,000-unit chains with independently measured whole-chain sequence fidelity above 99%.
status: Sequence control has advanced substantially since the 2000s through iterative synthesis, controlled polymerization, and biological templates; these capabilities do not establish this combined length–fidelity–throughput target for arbitrary synthetic backbones.
why: Enables reproducible synthetic catalysts, molecular information storage, and protein-like materials with new chemistries.
key_works: J.-F. Lutz, M. Ouchi, D. R. Liu, and M. Sawamoto (2013), “Sequence-Controlled Polymers,” [DOI:10.1126/science.1238149](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1238149); J.-F. Lutz (2017), “Defining the Field of Sequence-Controlled Polymers,” [DOI:10.1002/marc.201700582](https://doi.org/10.1002/marc.201700582).

title: Molecular pathway of primary polymer-crystal nucleation
open: Determine when polymer crystals nucleate directly versus through conformationally ordered, mesomorphic, or other intermediate states, and predict absolute nucleation rates from molecular structure and thermal history. Discriminating experiments must resolve ordering and density changes before crystals become detectable by conventional scattering.
status: Competing pathways remain under discussion decades after classical nucleation descriptions and Strobl’s intermediate-state proposal; chain connectivity and unequilibrated melts complicate identification of a universal mechanism.
why: Makes crystallinity and processing windows predictable instead of requiring empirical formulation trials.
key_works: G. Strobl (2000), “From the melt via mesomorphic and granular crystalline layers to lamellar crystallites: A major route followed in polymer crystallization?”, [DOI:10.1007/s101890070030](https://doi.org/10.1007/s101890070030); J. Xu, G. Reiter, and R. G. Alamo (2021), “Concepts of Nucleation in Polymer Crystallization,” [DOI:10.3390/cryst11030304](https://doi.org/10.3390/cryst11030304).

title: Processing-history prediction of shish–kebab morphology
open: Predict the density, orientation, lifetime, and subsequent lamellar growth of flow-induced polymer-crystallization precursors from a specified shear/extension and cooling history. The prediction must transfer across molecular-weight distributions and branching without refitting each processing experiment.
status: Flow-induced shish formation has been studied for decades; in situ scattering and microscopy resolve selected stages, while 2026 work still investigates the exceptional persistence of polypropylene precursors.
why: Enables reliable high-strength films, fibers, and molded parts from controlled processing histories.
key_works: B. Shen, Y. Liang, J. A. Kornfield, and C. C. Han (2013), “Mechanism for Shish Formation under Shear Flow: An Interpretation from an in Situ Morphological Study,” [DOI:10.1021/ma3023958](https://doi.org/10.1021/ma3023958); H. Seyed Khabbaz et al. (2026), “Extraordinary Longevity of Flow-Induced Crystallization Precursors in Isotactic Polypropylene,” [DOI:10.1021/acs.macromol.6c00315](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.macromol.6c00315).

title: Nonlinear rheology across the ionomer–polyelectrolyte crossover
open: Predict shear thinning, stress overshoot, and recovery when ionic clusters become connected networks in ionizable polymer melts. A solution must connect ionization pattern, counterion chemistry, solvent uptake, and chain motion to measured flow curves beyond one chemistry or simulation timescale.
status: Atomistic simulations in 2025 resolved selected sulfonated-polystyrene compositions and swelling conditions; transferable relations between cluster rearrangement and nonlinear viscosity remain incomplete.
why: Improves processing of ion-containing membranes, coatings, and mechanically strong ion-conducting polymers.
key_works: S. Meedin, G. S. Grest, and D. Perahia (2025), “Shear Response of Ionizable Polymer Melts at the Crossover from Ionomers to Polyelectrolytes,” [DOI:10.1021/acspolymersau.5c00041](https://doi.org/10.1021/acspolymersau.5c00041).

title: Network-level prediction of elastomer fatigue damage
open: Predict fatigue-crack growth from network topology, bond kinetics, and local damage accumulation under variable loading, temperature, and oxidation. The model must distinguish sacrificial-bond damage, irreversible backbone scission, and actual crack advance using independent molecular measurements.
status: Lake–Thomas theory dates to 1967; mechanophores now reveal where bonds break, but lifetime prediction for heterogeneous, aging networks remains substantially empirical.
why: Extends the life of tires, seals, soft robots, and flexible structures while reducing abrasion debris.
key_works: G. J. Lake and A. G. Thomas (1967), “The Strength of Highly Elastic Materials,” [DOI:10.1098/rspa.1967.0160](https://doi.org/10.1098/rspa.1967.0160); E. Ducrot et al. (2014), “Toughening elastomers with sacrificial bonds and watching them break,” [DOI:10.1126/science.1248494](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1248494).

title: Repeated autonomous restoration of elastomer fatigue resistance
open: Restore a damaged elastomer’s fatigue threshold repeatedly at ambient conditions, including contaminated interfaces and sustained load, without losing dimensional stability. Demonstrating tensile-strength recovery alone does not establish restoration of resistance to cyclic crack growth.
status: Self-healing has progressed from soft networks to stiff composites; Liu et al. reported an approximately 8.23 kJ/m² fatigue threshold and rapid near-infrared-triggered healing in 2025. Autonomous repair under realistic continuing service remains a stronger combined target.
why: Enables repairable load-bearing soft components with measurable service-life gains.
key_works: T. Liu et al. (2025), “Multiscale interlinked structures limit fatigue crack propagation in a MXene-polyurethane composite,” [DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-64611-8](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-64611-8).

title: Durable service and rapid reprocessing in industrial vitrimers
open: Establish exchange chemistries and network designs that retain specified creep resistance throughout realistic service aging, yet repeatedly reprocess rapidly without accumulating defects or losing crosslink density. Qualification must include air, moisture, additives, and recycled-feedstock variability.
status: Vitrimers date to 2011; latent catalysts and heterogeneous networks have reduced creep. Debsharma et al. demonstrated strongly suppressed creep using temperature-resilient siloxane exchange in 2025, leaving broad industrial qualification and repeated-aging transfer unresolved.
why: Makes repairable and recyclable thermosets viable in demanding structural applications.
key_works: D. Montarnal et al. (2011), “Silica-Like Malleable Materials from Permanent Organic Networks,” [DOI:10.1126/science.1212648](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1212648); T. Debsharma et al. (2025), “Eliminating creep in vitrimers using temperature-resilient siloxane exchange chemistry and N-heterocyclic carbenes,” [DOI:10.1039/D4SC06278G](https://doi.org/10.1039/D4SC06278G).

title: Tenfold lower-field dielectric-elastomer actuation
open: Reduce required electric field by an order of magnitude at matched useful stress, strain, bandwidth, and cycling lifetime, including electrodes and encapsulation. Determine whether increased permittivity can deliver this gain without offsetting dielectric loss, stiffening, or breakdown.
status: Large-strain artificial muscles are established; Mao et al. reported 125% operable strain at 25 MV/m over 150,000 cycles in 2026. This is a specific experimental baseline, not proof of the combined lower-field target.
why: Enables compact, efficient soft actuators with simpler drive electronics.
key_works: J. Mao et al. (2026), “A self healable dielectric elastomer artificial muscle,” [DOI:10.1038/s41467-026-72611-5](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-72611-5).

title: Recombinant silk with native performance and industrial economics
open: Couple high-yield spidroin production to continuous aqueous spinning that reproducibly matches the selected natural silk’s toughness, strength, and humidity response. Report finished-fiber yield, energy, solvent recovery, and cost rather than protein-expression titer alone.
status: Biomimetic spinning from chimeric minispidroins was demonstrated in 2017; subsequent recombinant and hybrid fibers improve individual properties. Simultaneously reproducing hierarchical assembly and economical, consistent production remains an engineering target.
why: Supplies high-performance renewable fibers without farming spiders or using harsh spinning processes.
key_works: M. Andersson et al. (2017), “Biomimetic spinning of artificial spider silk from a chimeric minispidroin,” [DOI:10.1038/nchembio.2269](https://doi.org/10.1038/nchembio.2269).

title: Predictable wash lifetime of electronic textiles
open: Predict electrical and mechanical failure across repeated laundering, drying, sweat exposure, and abrasion from fiber, coating, junction, and textile architecture. Establish transferable qualification protocols that identify failure at connectors and integrated components as well as conductive yarns.
status: Washable fibers and circuits exist; Rotzler et al. systematically compared substrate–circuit combinations in 2025. Many device demonstrations still validate limited, non-equivalent washing histories.
why: Turns wearable textile prototypes into maintainable everyday garments.
key_works: S. Rotzler et al. (2025), “Washability of E-Textiles: Washing Behavior of Textile Integrated Circuits Depending on Textile Substrate, Circuit Material and Integration Method,” [DOI:10.1002/adfm.202417344](https://doi.org/10.1002/adfm.202417344).

title: Device-quality colloidal diamond
subfield: Colloids, liquid crystals, gels, and active soft materials
open: Assemble large, orientationally controlled colloidal-diamond domains with sufficiently low vacancy, stacking, and grain-boundary defect densities for a specified complete photonic bandgap. Preserve the architecture during conversion into a useful high-index material and demonstrate reproducible optical performance.
status: Colloidal diamond itself was experimentally assembled by He et al. in 2020 after decades of effort; scalable, defect-controlled assembly plus device-material conversion is the remaining integrated problem.
why: Offers an inexpensive route to three-dimensional photonic materials.

title: Inverse design of assembly pathways
subfield: Colloids, liquid crystals, gels, and active soft materials
open: Given a target colloidal structure and practical interactions, find a temperature, concentration, or field protocol that maximizes finite-time yield while avoiding competing structures. The method must predict kinetic failures, not only identify a favorable equilibrium phase.
status: Established by the 2010s as a distinct problem; simulations and selected controlled protocols outperform fixed conditions, but transferable inverse design for realistic hydrodynamics and polydispersity remains limited.
why: Makes self-assembly a reliable manufacturing method for complex structures.
key_works: S. Whitelam and R. L. Jack (2015), “The Statistical Mechanics of Dynamic Pathways to Self-Assembly,” [DOI:10.1146/annurev-physchem-040214-121215](https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-physchem-040214-121215); W. M. Jacobs, A. Reinhardt, and D. Frenkel (2015), “Rational design of self-assembly pathways for complex multicomponent structures,” [arXiv:1502.01351](https://arxiv.org/abs/1502.01351).

title: Error scaling in addressable multicomponent assembly
subfield: Colloids, liquid crystals, gels, and active soft materials
open: Determine how assembly yield and incorrect bonding scale with the number of distinct building blocks, interaction specificity, stoichiometric error, and target connectivity. Establish experimentally realizable design rules or lower bounds for assembling very large structures with individually addressed components.
status: DNA-addressable assembly and nucleation theory provide important finite-system demonstrations; the robust large-system limit under realistic cross-binding and concentration errors remains unresolved.
why: Enables programmable nanostructures with many distinct functional sites.
key_works: W. M. Jacobs, A. Reinhardt, and D. Frenkel (2015), “Rational design of self-assembly pathways for complex multicomponent structures,” [arXiv:1502.01351](https://arxiv.org/abs/1502.01351).

title: Predictive microscopic closure for active-nematic turbulence
subfield: Colloids, liquid crystals, gels, and active soft materials
open: Derive measurable continuum coefficients and fluctuations from motor kinetics, filament length, crosslinking, and fuel concentration, then predict flows and defect statistics across preparations. Validation should distinguish genuine parameter transfer from refitting each active-nematic movie.
status: Hydrodynamic models reproduce major phenomena; experimental feedback control can regulate mean flow speed, including in the presence of aging. Microscopic-to-continuum parameter prediction remains incomplete.
why: Makes active fluids programmable materials rather than preparation-specific demonstrations.
key_works: A. Doostmohammadi et al. (2018), “Active nematics,” [DOI:10.1038/s41467-018-05666-8](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-018-05666-8); K. Nishiyama et al. (2024), “Closed-loop control of active nematic flows,” [arXiv:2408.14414](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.14414).

title: Controlled three-dimensional active-defect networks
subfield: Colloids, liquid crystals, gels, and active soft materials
open: Create, transport, reconnect, and erase specified three-dimensional disclination loops or networks using local actuation while predicting their lifetimes. Establish which topological structures remain controllable when activity, confinement, and flow jointly deform the director field.
status: Duclos et al. visualized dynamic three-dimensional active-nematic defects in 2020; two-dimensional feedback strategies have advanced, including 2025 reinforcement-learning studies. General three-dimensional manipulation remains substantially less developed.
why: Enables active microfluidics and materials whose internal topology encodes function.
key_works: G. Duclos et al. (2020), “Topological structure and dynamics of three-dimensional active nematics,” [DOI:10.1126/science.aaz4547](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aaz4547); C. Floyd, A. R. Dinner, and S. Vaikuntanathan (2025), “Tailoring interactions between active nematic defects with reinforcement learning,” [DOI:10.1039/D5SM00063G](https://doi.org/10.1039/D5SM00063G).

title: Sustained useful work from chemically fueled soft materials
subfield: Colloids, liquid crystals, gels, and active soft materials
open: Maintain a specified mechanical or transport function through many fuel cycles with measured energy efficiency, controlled waste removal, and stable composition. The unresolved target is autonomous operation with a useful load and realistic fuel supply, beyond repeated appearance and disappearance of assemblies.
status: Transient gels, transport, and waste-avoiding activation routes exist; a 2025 assessment identifies waste accumulation, compatibility, and useful performance as continuing constraints.
why: Enables materials that adapt and do work through local chemistry.
key_works: K. Rajawasam et al. (2025), “Autonomous Changes in Polymer Materials Driven by Chemical Fuels,” [DOI:10.1002/syst.202400090](https://doi.org/10.1002/syst.202400090); K. Liu et al. (2025), “Molecular-scale dissipative chemistry drives the formation of nanoscale assemblies and their macroscale transport,” [DOI:10.1038/s41557-024-01665-z](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41557-024-01665-z).

title: Heritable composition during coacervate growth and division
subfield: Colloids, liquid crystals, gels, and active soft materials
open: Engineer fuel-maintained droplets that repeatedly grow and divide while preserving a specified multicomponent composition and catalytic function in daughter droplets. Establish when partition noise, fusion, and chemical turnover prevent reliable inheritance.
status: Active-droplet size control and oscillations are established: Sastre et al. observed hundreds of oscillation periods in 2025. Oscillating populations do not yet establish compositionally faithful multigeneration reproduction.
why: Connects synthetic compartment materials to autonomous biochemical factories.
key_works: D. Zwicker et al. (2017), “Growth and division of active droplets,” [DOI:10.1038/nphys3984](https://doi.org/10.1038/nphys3984); J. Sastre et al. (2025), “Size control and oscillations of active droplets in synthetic cells,” [DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-57240-8](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-57240-8).

title: Cycling lifetime of programmed liquid-crystal elastomers
subfield: Colloids, liquid crystals, gels, and active soft materials
open: Predict and maximize actuation lifetime when director reorientation, viscoelastic creep, thermal cycling, and crack growth occur together. Demonstrate retention of a prescribed three-dimensional trajectory and output work, not only unloaded shape recovery.
status: Programmed morphing is well established; 2025 fracture and fatigue studies distinguish monodomain and polydomain behavior. Actuation-specific lifetime laws across director patterns and realistic boundary loads remain incomplete.
why: Enables reliable soft engines, valves, and deployable structures.
key_works: M. Hu, L. Wang, Z. Wei, R. Xiao, and J. Qian (2025; online 2024), “Fracture and fatigue characteristics of monodomain and polydomain liquid crystal elastomers,” [DOI:10.1039/D4SM01042F](https://doi.org/10.1039/D4SM01042F); Y. Zhou, C. Wei, and L. Jin (2025), “Fracture of liquid crystal elastomers,” [DOI:10.1073/pnas.2510727122](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2510727122).

title: Fatigue-resistant hydrogels under changing hydration
subfield: Colloids, liquid crystals, gels, and active soft materials
open: Preserve a specified fatigue threshold and compliance through drying–rewetting, salt exchange, freezing, and long loading histories. Determine how crystallites or aligned fibrils that arrest cracks survive these coupled environmental cycles.
status: Lin et al. demonstrated trained hydrogels with a 1,250 J/m² fatigue threshold and 84 wt% water in 2019. Such hydrated-state benchmarks do not establish reliability under repeated environmental excursions.
why: Makes durable water-rich components possible outside controlled laboratory hydration.
key_works: S. Lin, J. Liu, X. Liu, and X. Zhao (2019), “Muscle-like fatigue-resistant hydrogels by mechanical training,” [DOI:10.1073/pnas.1903019116](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1903019116).

title: Predicting ionic-screening effects in ferroelectric nematics
subfield: Colloids, liquid crystals, gels, and active soft materials
