open: Predict domain patterns and switching from molecular polarization, ionic impurities, electrode chemistry, and anchoring, including slow ion redistribution. A solution should separate intrinsic ferroelectric response from screening artifacts across cell thicknesses and materials.
status: Ferroelectric nematic phases are established; Lavrentovich, Kumari, and Lavrentovich showed quantitative domain-size effects and suppression by ionic screening in 2025. Transferable dynamic electrochemical–orientational models remain incomplete.
why: Enables reproducible polar-fluid electro-optic materials and meaningful property measurements.
key_works: M. O. Lavrentovich, P. Kumari, and O. D. Lavrentovich (2025), “Twist, splay, and uniform domains in ferroelectric nematic liquid crystals,” [DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-61840-9](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-61840-9).

title: Predicting the foreign-body response from material design
open: Predict long-term capsule formation and inflammatory cell states from material chemistry, mechanics, geometry, implantation site, and host condition. A successful model must generalize across species and distinguish surgical injury effects from material-induced immune responses.
status: Studied for decades; material size and shape affect responses, and adhesive interfaces prevented observable capsules for 12 weeks in several animal settings in 2024. General host- and site-transferable prediction remains open.
why: Reduces failure of implants, biosensors, and drug-delivery devices.
key_works: O. Veiseh et al. (2015), “Size- and shape-dependent foreign body immune response to materials implanted in rodents and non-human primates,” [DOI:10.1038/nmat4290](https://doi.org/10.1038/nmat4290); J. Wu et al. (2024), “Adhesive anti-fibrotic interfaces on diverse organs,” [DOI:10.1038/s41586-024-07426-9](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-024-07426-9).

title: Durable immunoisolating cell-encapsulation materials
open: Build retrievable, clinically sized cell implants that jointly maintain immune isolation, oxygen and nutrient delivery, rapid product transport, and low fibrosis for years. Demonstrate the complete function at therapeutic cell density without systemic immunosuppression.
status: Encapsulation has been investigated for decades; Pham et al. demonstrated oxygenated high-density encapsulation and diabetes reversal for up to three months in allogeneic rats in 2025. Multiyear human-scale performance remains a stronger target.
why: Makes replaceable cell therapies feasible without chronic immunosuppression.
key_works: T. T. Pham et al. (2025), “A continuously oxygenated macroencapsulation system enables high-density packing and delivery of insulin-secreting cells,” [DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-62271-2](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-62271-2).

title: Long-lived small-diameter vascular grafts
open: Produce readily available small-diameter grafts that maintain physiological compliance, endothelial function, and patency without progressive thrombosis, intimal hyperplasia, or aneurysm. Confirm long-term performance in anatomically and hemodynamically demanding graft configurations and comparative human studies.
status: A decades-old challenge; Zhang et al. reported 100% patency in their allogeneic rhesus-macaque experiment in 2025. That study-specific result does not establish universal or multiyear clinical durability.
why: Provides vascular replacements when suitable autologous vessels are unavailable.
key_works: J. Zhang et al. (2025), “Small-diameter artery grafts engineered from pluripotent stem cells maintain 100% patency in an allogeneic rhesus macaque model,” [DOI:10.1016/j.xcrm.2025.102002](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.xcrm.2025.102002).

title: Organ-scale hierarchical perfusion after bioprinting
open: Fabricate thick, dense tissues with connected artery-to-capillary-to-vein networks that remain endothelialized, perfusable, and exchange-competent after implantation. Validate spatial oxygenation and tissue function throughout the construct, including its least-perfused regions.
status: Embedded vascular channels were demonstrated in dense tissues in 2019, and hybrid printing reached sub-10-µm channel resolution in 2026. Channel resolution alone does not establish organ-scale network function and durable host integration.
why: Removes a central transport barrier to replacement organs and realistic tissue models.
key_works: M. A. Skylar-Scott et al. (2019), “Biomanufacturing of organ-specific tissues with high cellular density and embedded vascular channels,” [DOI:10.1126/sciadv.aaw2459](https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.aaw2459); Y. Liao et al. (2026), “Hybrid bioprinting of hierarchical vascular networks at capillary-scale resolution,” [DOI:10.1038/s44286-026-00396-x](https://doi.org/10.1038/s44286-026-00396-x).

title: Functional innervation of engineered tissues
open: Design scaffolds and guidance cues that establish correctly targeted sensory, motor, and autonomic innervation in an engineered tissue. Demonstrate durable bidirectional host integration and the appropriate physiological response, rather than neuronal-marker expression alone.
status: Innervated muscle constructs and organ models exist; Santoso et al. showed enhanced muscle-bundle differentiation with human motor neurons in 2025. Reliable organ-specific wiring and integration remain incomplete.
why: Enables tissues that sense, coordinate, and respond through their native control pathways.
key_works: J. W. Santoso et al. (2025), “Human iPSC-Derived Motor Neuron Innervation Enhances the Differentiation of Muscle Bundles Engineered with Benchtop Fabrication Techniques,” [DOI:10.1021/acsbiomaterials.4c02225](https://doi.org/10.1021/acsbiomaterials.4c02225).

title: Reconstructing functional lymphatic tissue networks
open: Engineer materials that support durable lymph uptake, directional drainage, and appropriate immune trafficking after transplantation. Establish how scaffold architecture and matrix mechanics coordinate lymphatic capillaries, collecting vessels, and lymph-node-like structures at clinically relevant scale.
status: Obana et al. reconstructed lymphatic tissue and suppressed lymphedema for 100 days in mice in 2025. Scaled, durable drainage and immune functionality across disease states remain open.
why: Addresses lymphedema and improves fluid homeostasis in engineered tissues.
key_works: S. Obana et al. (2025), “Reconstruction of the lymphatic system by transplantation of a centrifuge-based bioengineered lymphatic tissue,” [DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-65121-3](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-65121-3).

title: Regenerating the graded tendon–bone enthesis
open: Recreate the spatial mineral, collagen, cell, and mechanical gradients that transfer load from tendon to bone without stress concentration. Demonstrate durable restoration of native-like failure strength and fatigue resistance after biological remodeling.
status: Multiphasic and gradient scaffolds are established research approaches; dual gradients of biological effectors promoted relevant cell phenotypes in 2025. Durable reproduction of the complete attachment remains an unresolved translational target.
why: Improves rotator-cuff and other soft-to-hard tissue repairs.
key_works: Hao et al. (2025), “Biomimetic Scaffolds with Dual Gradients of Biological Effectors for Tendon-to-Bone Repair,” [DOI:10.1002/adhm.202503171](https://doi.org/10.1002/adhm.202503171).

title: Integrated load bearing and lubrication in cartilage replacements
open: Create a cartilage substitute that simultaneously sustains long cyclic contact loading, low friction, wear resistance, and secure biological integration. Validate performance after aging in synovial-like environments with inflammatory conditions and realistic opposing surfaces.
status: Tough and lubricating hydrogels have improved substantially; Liu et al. demonstrated injectable, self-lubricating extracellular-matrix-loaded hydrogels in 2024. Coupon strength and short tribology tests do not resolve lifetime joint performance.
why: Enables durable cartilage repair and reduces the need for whole-joint replacement.
key_works: Z. Liu et al. (2024), “Robust, self-lubricating and injectable dECM-loaded hydrogels based on rapid photo-crosslinking for articular cartilage regeneration,” [DOI:10.1016/j.apmt.2024.102462](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.apmt.2024.102462).

title: Defined dynamic matrices across organoid lineages
open: Replace variable animal-derived matrices with chemically defined materials that support reproducible expansion, differentiation, and maturation across specified human organoid lineages. Determine which time-dependent mechanical and ligand changes are necessary for each developmental transition.
status: Gjorevski et al. demonstrated dynamic synthetic matrices for intestinal organoids in 2016; later matrices extend selected tissue systems. A transferable recipe covering diverse lineages and mature function remains open.
why: Improves reproducibility of disease models, drug testing, and tissue manufacture.
key_works: N. Gjorevski et al. (2016), “Designer matrices for intestinal stem cell and organoid culture,” [DOI:10.1038/nature20168](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature20168).

title: Biofilm-resistant implants after conditioning and wear
open: Maintain resistance to multispecies biofilms after protein conditioning, abrasion, sterilization, and long implantation while supporting the required host-cell integration. Quantify whether organisms adapt to the surface during repeated exposure.
status: Hook et al. identified attachment-resistant polymers in 2012, with strong in vitro reductions and mouse-model benefit. Reliable performance against evolving, conditioned multispecies communities over implant lifetimes remains unresolved.
why: Prevents chronic implant infection without relying entirely on antimicrobial release.
key_works: A. L. Hook et al. (2012), “Combinatorial discovery of polymers resistant to bacterial attachment,” [DOI:10.1038/nbt.2316](https://doi.org/10.1038/nbt.2316).

title: Matching scaffold resorption to patient-specific tissue formation
open: Predict and control the loss of polymer-scaffold strength so that regenerating tissue assumes load without collapse or prolonged obstruction. Models must include hydrolysis, autocatalysis, stress, inflammation, geometry, and patient-dependent healing rates.
status: A longstanding tissue-engineering objective; 2025 studies still identify in vivo degradation prediction as a bottleneck, while permanent polymer scaffolds provide a demonstrated alternative for selected bone defects.
why: Enables temporary implants that safely disappear after completing their function.
key_works: H. Ramaraju et al. (2025), “Investigation of the biodegradation kinetics and associated mechanical properties of 3D-printed polycaprolactone during long-term preclinical testing,” [DOI:10.1016/j.biomaterials.2025.123257](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.biomaterials.2025.123257); J. R. Clark et al. (2025), “Mechanobiologically-optimized non-resorbable artificial bone for patient-matched scaffold-guided bone regeneration,” [DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-64466-z](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-64466-z).

title: Functional longevity with containment in engineered living materials
open: Maintain material-producing or sensing cells inside a useful composite for a specified service lifetime while preventing undesired escape and genetic loss of function. Quantify survival, mechanical performance, containment, and metabolic resource demand together under realistic environmental perturbations.
status: Programmable bacterial-cellulose and microbial co-culture materials were demonstrated by 2021. Coupled evolutionary, ecological, and mechanical stability remains less mature than short-term functional demonstrations.
why: Enables self-maintaining environmental sensors and locally manufactured functional materials.
key_works: C. Gilbert and T. Ellis (2019), “Biological Engineered Living Materials: Growing Functional Materials with Genetically Programmable Properties,” [DOI:10.1021/acssynbio.8b00423](https://doi.org/10.1021/acssynbio.8b00423); C. Gilbert et al. (2021), “Living materials with programmable functionalities grown from engineered microbial co-cultures,” [DOI:10.1038/s41563-020-00857-5](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41563-020-00857-5).

title: Fatigue prediction for imperfect polymer lattices
open: Predict the distribution of cyclic lifetime in architected polymer materials from measured manufacturing defects, local material properties, and multiaxial loading. Validate transfer between lattice families and build conditions rather than calibrating one geometry’s stress–life curve.
status: Geometry-specific fatigue models exist, including a 2026 methodology for functional polymer metamaterials. Manufacturing variability, environmental aging, and unfamiliar topologies remain substantial limits to transferable qualification.
why: Enables dependable compliant mechanisms, cushioning systems, and lightweight polymer structures.
key_works: L. Trávníček et al. (2026), “A methodology for fatigue lifetime prediction of functional mechanical metamaterials,” [publisher record](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1350630726003018).

title: Joint bounds on architected stiffness, strength, and toughness
open: Determine the attainable combinations of stiffness, strength, and crack resistance for a fixed constituent material, density, minimum feature size, and defect distribution. Provide sharp bounds and realizable constructions instead of optimizing each property independently.
status: Classical elastic bounds and near-optimal stiffness architectures are established, including Berger et al.’s 2017 work. Their existence does not settle simultaneous failure-sensitive bounds under fabrication constraints.
why: Reveals which proposed property combinations are achievable and which require different constituents or architectures.
key_works: J. B. Berger, H. N. G. Wadley, and R. M. McMeeking (2017), “Mechanical metamaterials at the theoretical limit of isotropic elastic stiffness,” [DOI:10.1038/nature21075](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature21075).

title: Realizable inverse design of multistage shape morphing
open: Given a sequence of loaded target shapes, design an architected material and actuation pattern that traverses them without collision, unintended buckling, or inaccessible intermediate states. Include manufacturing tolerance and finite material strain in the feasibility test.
status: Origami, kirigami, and frustrated-cell architectures realize many transformations; the 2025 shape-morphing review identifies continuing inverse-design and implementation challenges. Arbitrary compatible trajectories remain unsolved.
why: Enables deployable structures and soft robots whose complete motion is designed into their material.
key_works: K. K. Dudek, M. Kadic, C. Coulais, and K. Bertoldi (2025), “Shape-morphing metamaterials,” [DOI:10.1038/s41578-025-00828-9](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41578-025-00828-9); [arXiv:2501.14804](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.14804).

title: Topological mechanical function at large strain
open: Identify which topological invariants, protected responses, or replacements remain predictive during large deformation, dissipation, contact, and damage. Demonstrate designs whose desired transport or localization survives a specified finite-strain operating cycle.
status: Linear topological mechanics and nonlinear soliton mechanisms have been demonstrated since 2014. Extending protection claims to realistic nonlinear, degrading materials remains an active theoretical and experimental problem.
why: Enables mechanical signal routing and localization robust to operating conditions.
key_works: C. L. Kane and T. C. Lubensky (2014), “Topological boundary modes in isostatic lattices,” [DOI:10.1038/nphys2835](https://doi.org/10.1038/nphys2835); B. G.-g. Chen, N. Upadhyaya, and V. Vitelli (2014), “Nonlinear conduction via solitons in a topological mechanical insulator,” [DOI:10.1073/pnas.1405969111](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1405969111).

title: Capacity and interference in material memory
open: Determine how many independently readable mechanical memories a finite material can store, how training order causes interference, and how noise or wear limits retention. Demonstrate selective rewriting without erasing unrelated stored responses.
status: Mechanical memories and trainable metamaterials exist; Du et al. demonstrated materials that learn shape changes, with the work published in 2026. General capacity, retention, and selective-update laws remain incomplete.
why: Enables physical computation and adaptive structures with predictable learning behavior.
key_works: Y. Du, J. Veenstra, R. van Mastrigt, and C. Coulais (2026), “Metamaterials that learn to change shape,” [DOI:10.1038/s41567-026-03226-2](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41567-026-03226-2); [arXiv:2501.11958](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.11958).

title: Scalable self-assembly of load-bearing nanoarchitectures
open: Manufacture macroscopic volumes of prescribed nanoscale load-bearing architecture by self-assembly while controlling connectivity, defects, and material conversion. Verify bulk strength and toughness distributions after infiltration, removal of templates, and joining.
status: Copolymer and colloidal self-assembly offer feature-size and throughput advantages; Jin and Espinosa’s 2023 perspective identifies fabrication and characterization barriers. Small ordered domains do not establish structural-scale manufacturing.
why: Makes nanoscale architectural strengthening accessible beyond serial lithographic fabrication.
key_works: H. Jin and H. D. Espinosa (2023), “Mechanical Metamaterials Fabricated from Self-assembly: A Perspective,” [arXiv:2311.06734](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.06734).

title: Sharp absorption bounds with ventilation and structural constraints
open: Determine the best passive broadband sound absorption achievable when thickness, mass, airflow resistance, structural load, and available material losses are all constrained. Identify jointly infeasible targets and construct designs approaching the remaining attainable boundary.
status: Causal thickness–absorption bounds and near-optimal backed absorbers are established; Yang et al. demonstrated a 10.86-cm specimen against a 10.36-cm causal minimum in 2017. Those assumptions do not settle all ventilated, load-bearing configurations.
why: Prevents impossible acoustic specifications and guides compact noise-control materials.
key_works: M. Yang, S. Chen, C. Fu, and P. Sheng (2017), “Optimal sound-absorbing structures,” [DOI:10.1039/C7MH00129K](https://doi.org/10.1039/C7MH00129K).

title: Practical broadband three-dimensional elastic cloaking
open: Reduce scattering of both longitudinal and shear elastic waves over a specified finite band and range of incidence using finite, manufacturable material parameters. Include support loads, losses, and imperfections in the demonstrated performance specification.
status: Transformation elasticity gives exact idealized designs, and restricted-wave demonstrations exist. Simultaneous three-dimensional, multipolarization, broadband performance under practical constitutive constraints remains unresolved; unlimited perfect passive cloaking is not the target.
why: Enables vibration protection and unobtrusive structural supports.
key_works: A. N. Norris and A. L. Shuvalov (2011), “Elastic cloaking theory,” [arXiv:1103.6045](https://arxiv.org/abs/1103.6045).

title: Manufacturable large-aperture broadband achromatic metalenses
open: Achieve a specified aperture, numerical aperture, field of view, broadband efficiency, and fabrication yield within physically allowed dispersion bounds. Co-design materials and geometry so that measured large-area devices retain performance despite process variations.
status: Achromatic metalenses and fundamental delay–bandwidth bounds exist; wide-field bounds were extended in 2022. Joint large-aperture, broadband, high-efficiency, high-yield manufacture remains a harder target than demonstrating any one metric.
why: Enables compact imaging with predictable performance and manufacturing cost.
key_works: F. Presutti and F. Monticone (2020), “Focusing on Bandwidth: Achromatic Metalens Limits,” [arXiv:2001.10899](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.10899); K. Shastri and F. Monticone (2022), “Bandwidth bounds for wide-field-of-view dispersion-engineered achromatic metalenses,” [arXiv:2204.09154](https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.09154).

title: Active metasurfaces with joint efficiency, speed, and endurance
open: Produce addressable metasurface materials with large reversible optical modulation while jointly meeting useful switching speed, low loss, low energy, and high cycle life over a large area. Report aging and pixel-to-pixel drift alongside the initial optical response.
status: Electrical, thermal, mechanical, and phase-change tuning are established; the speed, modulation depth, loss, and integration tradeoffs identified in 2019 continue to motivate distinct material platforms. No single tuning mechanism settles the combined specification.
why: Enables practical dynamic holography, beam steering, and adaptive optics.
key_works: A. M. Shaltout, V. M. Shalaev, and M. L. Brongersma (2019), “Spatiotemporal light control with active metasurfaces,” [DOI:10.1126/science.aat3100](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aat3100).

title: Wet adhesion with reliable, tissue-safe selective release
subfield: Surfaces, wetting, adhesion, and functional coatings
open: Bond strongly to moving, blood- or mucus-contaminated tissue, then release on command without residual material or tissue injury. Establish the usable window between service adhesion and triggered detachment across different tissues and healing stages.
status: Tough wet-tissue adhesives were demonstrated in 2017, and reversible chemistries exist. Combining robust contaminated-surface adhesion, prolonged mechanical loading, and safe removal remains an application-specific materials challenge.
why: Enables removable wound closures, temporary implants, and repeatable surgical sealing.
key_works: J. Li et al. (2017), “Tough adhesives for diverse wet surfaces,” [DOI:10.1126/science.aah6362](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aah6362).

title: Predicting charge transfer between insulating surfaces
subfield: Surfaces, wetting, adhesion, and functional coatings
open: Predict charge sign, magnitude, and evolution from the measured chemistry, adsorbates, contact mechanics, and history of two insulating surfaces. Determine when electrons, ions, or transferred material dominate, using experiments that distinguish these mechanisms quantitatively.
status: The general mechanism has resisted explanation for decades. Grosjean et al. identified adventitious carbon as a symmetry-breaking factor for same-material oxide charging in 2026; a quantitative framework spanning insulators and environmental conditions remains open.
why: Improves powder handling, electrostatic reliability, dust control, and triboelectric devices.
key_works: G. Grosjean et al. (2026), “Adventitious carbon breaks symmetry in oxide contact electrification,” [DOI:10.1038/s41586-025-10088-w](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-025-10088-w).

title: Chemistry-based closure of moving-contact-line dynamics
subfield: Surfaces, wetting, adhesion, and functional coatings
open: Predict a moving liquid contact line from independently measured surface chemistry and molecular dynamics, including speed-dependent contact angle and transitions to film deposition. Bridge microscopic slip, adsorption, and contact-line friction to macroscopic flow without refitting an effective parameter for each experiment.
status: Slip and diffuse-interface models regularize the classical moving-contact-line singularity. The 2013 review by Snoeijer and Andreotti documents established regimes and remaining microscopic-to-continuum matching questions; real heterogeneous surfaces add unresolved history dependence.
why: Makes coating, printing, immersion lithography, and fluid deposition quantitatively predictable.
key_works: J. H. Snoeijer and B. Andreotti (2013), “Moving Contact Lines: Scales, Regimes, and Dynamical Transitions,” [DOI:10.1146/annurev-fluid-011212-140734](https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-fluid-011212-140734).

title: Transferable prediction of hydrodynamic slip
subfield: Surfaces, wetting, adhesion, and functional coatings
open: Predict slip length and interfacial friction across chemically heterogeneous, charged, curved, and deformable solid–liquid interfaces from independently characterized material properties. Reconcile methods when apparent slip can also arise from gas layers, contamination, confinement, or instrument response.
status: Molecular and continuum connections were synthesized by Bocquet and Barrat in 2007; controlled interfaces support quantitative models. A transferable treatment of realistic surface states and coupled electrokinetic effects remains incomplete.
why: Determines pumping losses and separation performance in nanofluidic materials.
key_works: L. Bocquet and J.-L. Barrat (2007), “Flow boundary conditions from nano- to micro-scales,” [DOI:10.1039/B616490K](https://doi.org/10.1039/B616490K).

title: Predicting contact-angle hysteresis from surface maps
subfield: Surfaces, wetting, adhesion, and functional coatings
open: Calculate advancing and receding contact angles, metastable states, and depinning statistics from measured multiscale roughness and chemical heterogeneity. Include correlations, droplet size, and preparation history so that predictions transfer between specimens without fitted defect distributions.
status: Joanny and de Gennes established a defect-pinning framework in 1984. Specific patterned surfaces can be modeled, but general quantitative inversion from realistic three-dimensional surface maps remains unresolved.
why: Enables reproducible droplet transport, ink placement, water harvesting, and anti-fouling surfaces.
key_works: J. F. Joanny and P.-G. de Gennes (1984), “A model for contact angle hysteresis,” [DOI:10.1063/1.447337](https://doi.org/10.1063/1.447337).

title: Long-lived submerged gas layers on superhydrophobic surfaces
subfield: Surfaces, wetting, adhesion, and functional coatings
open: Sustain a useful gas-covered fraction under specified water depth, gas undersaturation, turbulence, abrasion, and contamination for the intended service interval. Predict when gas dissolution or wetting nucleation causes failure, and quantify any gas-replenishment energy.
status: Jones et al. connected roughness scale to submerged gas/vapor stability in 2015. Thermodynamic stability arguments and laboratory plastron retention do not alone establish durability under combined field conditions.
why: Makes submerged drag reduction and corrosion isolation more dependable.
key_works: P. R. Jones et al. (2015), “Sustaining dry surfaces under water,” [DOI:10.1038/srep12311](https://doi.org/10.1038/srep12311).

title: Lubricant-infused surfaces with closed lifetime accounting
subfield: Surfaces, wetting, adhesion, and functional coatings
open: Preserve slipperiness through droplet shedding, shear, evaporation, absorption into substrates, and cleaning over a specified service life. Measure every lubricant-loss pathway and demonstrate a replenishment or retention strategy whose resource use is included in the performance claim.
status: Wong et al. demonstrated self-repairing lubricant-infused omniphobic surfaces in 2011. Initial pressure stability and scratch recovery do not resolve cumulative lubricant depletion during repeated use.
why: Supports durable anti-fouling coatings, condensation equipment, and low-adhesion medical interfaces.
key_works: T.-S. Wong et al. (2011), “Bioinspired self-repairing slippery surfaces with pressure-stable omniphobicity,” [DOI:10.1038/nature10447](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature10447).

title: Icephobicity after erosion, frost, and repeated icing
subfield: Surfaces, wetting, adhesion, and functional coatings
open: Maintain low ice adhesion after representative particle erosion, ultraviolet exposure, thermal cycling, and repeated frost/icing events. Establish accelerated tests that predict service performance rather than only reporting initial ice-shear measurements.
status: Golovin et al. demonstrated low-adhesion, mechanically durable icephobic elastomers in 2016, including approximately 3.6 ± 1 kPa adhesion for one formulation. Combined long-term exposure, variable ice morphology, and reliable scale-up remain unresolved.
why: Reduces deicing energy and maintenance for aircraft, wind turbines, and power infrastructure.
key_works: K. Golovin et al. (2016), “Designing durable icephobic surfaces,” [DOI:10.1126/sciadv.1501496](https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.1501496).

title: Broad-spectrum marine antifouling without persistent biocides
subfield: Surfaces, wetting, adhesion, and functional coatings
open: Prevent attachment and persistent growth across marine bacteria, algae, and macrofoulers during both stationary and moving service, without releasing persistent toxic agents. Demonstrate multiseason performance after abrasion and cleaning in distinct marine environments.
status: Non-biocidal amphiphilic and fouling-release coatings exist. A 2025 study followed a new coating over 1–50 weeks in artificial seawater and a Greek marine environment; broader organisms, climates, and service conditions still require validation.
why: Reduces vessel drag, cleaning costs, and environmental contamination.
key_works: P. Vourna, P. P. Falara, E. V. Hristoforou, and N. D. Papadopoulos (2025), “Corrosion and Antifouling Behavior of a New Biocide-Free Antifouling Paint for Ship Hulls Under Both Artificially Simulated and Natural Marine Environment,” [DOI:10.3390/ma18133095](https://doi.org/10.3390/ma18133095).

title: Selective polyolefin recycling with verified net benefit
open: Convert realistic polyethylene/polypropylene waste into defined polymer-building feedstocks with high carbon recovery, acceptable catalyst life, and independently measured energy and cost advantages over the relevant virgin process. Include sorting, purification, external reactants, and coproduct demand in the comparison.
status: Conk et al. demonstrated polyethylene-to-propylene chemistry in 2022 and broader polyolefin conversion using ethylene and heterogeneous base-metal catalysts in 2024. These advances leave feedstock variability and integrated industrial economics open.
why: Enables repeated use of the carbon in high-volume plastics.
key_works: R. J. Conk et al. (2022), “Catalytic Deconstruction of Waste Polyethylene with Ethylene to Form Propylene,” [DOI:10.1126/science.add1088](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.add1088); Conk et al. (2024), “Polyolefin waste to light olefins with ethylene and base-metal heterogeneous catalysts,” [DOI:10.1126/science.adq7316](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.adq7316).

title: Catalyst-tolerant processing of dirty mixed plastic waste
open: Process changing mixtures of polymers, dyes, stabilizers, fillers, food residues, and halogen-containing contaminants while retaining catalyst activity and useful product selectivity. Establish quantitative contaminant tolerance limits and regenerability using representative waste, rather than only model mixtures.
status: Sullivan et al. combined chemical oxidation and biological funneling for mixed plastics in 2022. Sustained operation under realistic impurity distributions, separation demands, and feed changes remains a distinct scale-up problem.
why: Reduces expensive presorting and avoids exporting contamination into recycled products.
key_works: K. P. Sullivan et al. (2022), “Mixed plastics waste valorization through tandem chemical oxidation and biological funneling,” [DOI:10.1126/science.abo4626](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.abo4626).

title: Closed-solvent separation of multilayer packaging
open: Separate changing postconsumer multilayer packages into reusable polymer fractions with demonstrated solvent recovery, adhesive/additive removal, retained molecular properties, and competitive total energy use. Validate the process against a specified heterogeneous waste stream at continuous pilot scale.
status: Walker et al. demonstrated solvent-targeted recovery and precipitation for selected multilayer materials in 2020, with nearly complete material recovery in their studied system. General feedstock variability and closed-loop process economics remain open.
why: Makes otherwise incompatible barrier-packaging layers recoverable at useful quality.
key_works: T. W. Walker et al. (2020), “Recycling of multilayer plastic packaging materials by solvent-targeted recovery and precipitation,” [DOI:10.1126/sciadv.aba7599](https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.aba7599).

title: Recovery of every useful fraction from elastane-containing textiles
open: Recover high-quality fibers or monomers from dyed, finished blends containing elastane without sacrificing the other valuable components or accumulating solvent waste. Quantify the destination and quality of each fraction across realistic blend ratios and aging histories.
status: Boschmeier et al. demonstrated recovery of pure PET from wool/PET/elastane blends in work published online in 2024 and in a 2025 issue. Recovering one intact fraction does not establish economical circularity for every constituent of diverse textiles.
why: Opens recycling routes for stretch clothing and mixed-fiber products.
key_works: E. Boschmeier et al. (2025), “Recovery of pure PET from wool/PET/elastane textile waste through step-wise enzymatic and chemical processing,” [DOI:10.1177/0734242X241276089](https://doi.org/10.1177/0734242X241276089).

title: Recycling without recirculating hazardous plastic chemicals
open: Identify and remove hazardous legacy additives and unintended reaction products while retaining useful polymer quality. Establish transferable chemical-screening and decontamination criteria for repeated recycling, including mixture exposures and contaminants lacking commercial standards.
status: The 2025 PlastChem analysis mapped 16,325 known plastic chemicals and highlighted major information gaps. Chemical inventories are a substantial partial result; they do not establish the safety of each recycled stream or supply universal decontamination chemistry.
why: Prevents increased recycled content from increasing hazardous chemical exposure.
key_works: L. Monclús et al. (2025), “Mapping the chemical complexity of plastics,” [DOI:10.1038/s41586-025-09184-8](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-025-09184-8).

title: Predicting complete polymer biodegradation across habitats
open: Predict time to mineralization, biomass incorporation, and residual micro/nanoplastic formation from polymer structure, formulation, geometry, and environmental conditions. Validate separately in soil, compost, freshwater, seawater, and sediment, including low-temperature and oxygen-limited conditions.
status: Chamas et al. compiled environmental degradation rates in 2020 and exposed large variability and data gaps. Mass loss, fragmentation, and industrial-compost certification do not by themselves establish complete biodegradation in other habitats.
why: Enables credible material selection and environmental persistence assessment.
key_works: A. Chamas et al. (2020), “Degradation Rates of Plastics in the Environment,” [DOI:10.1021/acssuschemeng.9b06635](https://doi.org/10.1021/acssuschemeng.9b06635).

title: Consistent humid-service performance of mycelium composites
open: Produce mycelium-based panels with reproducible stiffness, creep, thermal insulation, and dimensional stability across variable biological feedstocks. Demonstrate a specified humid-service lifetime, including mold susceptibility and wet–dry cycling, while preserving a credible end-of-life route.
status: Sharma and Le Ferrand reported mycelium grown on printed wood–PLA gyroid scaffolds in 2025, improving strength and other properties. Their controlled architectures and durability measurements are partial progress; long service under variable biological and environmental conditions remains unqualified.
why: Expands construction uses for low-temperature-grown, biobased materials.
key_works: D. Sharma and H. Le Ferrand (2025), “3D printed gyroid scaffolds enabling strong and thermally insulating mycelium-bound composites for greener infrastructures,” [DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-61369-x](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-61369-x).

title: Environmentally representative nanoplastic reference materials
open: Supply characterized, stable reference materials spanning irregular shapes, polymer chemistries, weathering states, and environmentally relevant size distributions, with interlaboratory recovery benchmarks in real matrices. Quantify particle number, mass, surface chemistry, and uncertainty on compatible scales.
status: Reference particles and metrology programs already exist, including NIST's microplastic and nanoplastic work. The remaining gap is representative weathered diversity and comparable matrix-specific measurement performance, rather than the first plastic-particle standard.
why: Makes exposure measurements and material-fragmentation studies comparable across laboratories.
key_works: NIST (ongoing; accessed 2026), “Microplastic and Nanoplastic Metrology,” [program](https://www.nist.gov/programs-projects/microplastic-and-nanoplastic-metrology); J. Pettibone et al. (2025), “Chemical heterogeneity observed in the development of photo-oxidized PET micro- and nanoparticle weathered controls,” [DOI:10.1039/D4EN00841C](https://doi.org/10.1039/D4EN00841C).

title: Integrated PFAS capture, regeneration, and verified destruction
open: Couple selective capture materials to regeneration and destruction for complex water, brine, or spent-sorbent streams while closing the fluorine mass balance. Demonstrate sustained operation without transferring unmeasured organofluorine into volatile products, sludge, or replacement sorbents.
status: Trang et al. mineralized selected perfluorocarboxylic acids in 2022; Yang et al. demonstrated phosphate-enabled mechanochemical destruction and fluoride reuse for multiple PFAS classes in 2025. Complex dilute streams and the full capture-to-destruction process remain distinct engineering gaps.
why: Converts temporary contaminant removal into verifiable permanent treatment.
key_works: B. Trang et al. (2022), “Low-temperature mineralization of perfluorocarboxylic acids,” [DOI:10.1126/science.abm8868](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.abm8868); L. Yang et al. (2025), “Phosphate-enabled mechanochemical PFAS destruction for fluoride reuse,” [DOI:10.1038/s41586-025-08698-5](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-025-08698-5).

title: Transmutation-aware fusion-alloy lifetime
subfield: Radiation, nuclear materials, and extreme environments
open: Predict the service life of a specified structural alloy under simultaneous fusion-spectrum neutron damage, helium and hydrogen production, temperature gradients, and stress. Validate predictions of swelling, embrittlement, and creep against irradiation histories outside the calibration set.
status: Recognized since early fusion-materials programs; mechanistic models and fission/ion experiments constrain individual effects, but reproducing their fusion-specific combination remains difficult.
why: Enables defensible component lifetimes and replacement schedules for fusion reactors.
key_works: J. Knaster, A. Moeslang, and T. Muroga (2016), “Materials research for fusion,” [DOI:10.1038/nphys3735](https://doi.org/10.1038/nphys3735).

title: Quantitative equivalence of surrogate irradiation
subfield: Radiation, nuclear materials, and extreme environments
open: Establish when ion, electron, or fission-neutron irradiation can quantitatively predict fusion-neutron material degradation, with explicit corrections for dose rate, implanted species, damage depth, and transmutation. Identify regimes where no such equivalence exists.
status: Decades of surrogate testing provide useful mechanism studies; matching displacements per atom alone does not match the resulting microstructure or gas production.
why: Makes accelerated testing informative before representative fusion exposures become widely available.
key_works: S. J. Zinkle and L. L. Snead (2014), “Designing Radiation Resistance in Materials for Fusion Energy,” [ORNL publication record](https://www.ornl.gov/publication/designing-radiation-resistance-materials-fusion-energy).

title: Tungsten survival under combined plasma and neutron loading
subfield: Radiation, nuclear materials, and extreme environments
open: Produce and qualify a tungsten-based plasma-facing component that retains acceptable erosion, cracking, thermal transport, and fuel retention under a declared reactor-relevant combination of plasma exposure, thermal cycling, and neutron damage.
status: Individual heat-flux and particle-exposure tests demonstrate substantial capabilities; the 2025 UK fusion-materials roadmap still identifies high-temperature and radiation-resistant materials as development needs. A universal component-lifetime record is not meaningful without the loading history.
why: Reduces divertor replacement, contamination, and reactor downtime.
key_works: UK Atomic Energy Authority (2025), “UK Fusion Materials Roadmap 2.0,” [roadmap and report](https://www.ukaea.org/about-ukaea/publications/uk-fusion-materials-roadmap/).

title: Predictive tritium release from breeding materials
subfield: Radiation, nuclear materials, and extreme environments
open: Predict tritium generation, trapping, release, and permeation in a specified breeding-material system as its microstructure evolves under irradiation. Demonstrate sustained recovery and thermal-mechanical performance across an agreed blanket operating envelope.
status: Ceramic and liquid breeder concepts have extensive laboratory histories; the 2025 UK roadmap retains breeding materials, coatings, and barriers as coordinated research priorities.
why: Supports a closed fusion-fuel cycle with controlled inventories and losses.
key_works: UK Atomic Energy Authority (2025), “UK Fusion Materials Roadmap 2.0,” [roadmap and report](https://www.ukaea.org/about-ukaea/publications/uk-fusion-materials-roadmap/).

title: Hermetic, irradiation-tolerant SiC-composite joints
subfield: Radiation, nuclear materials, and extreme environments
open: Join silicon-carbide composites into complex nuclear components while preserving hermeticity, strength, and thermal transport through irradiation and thermal cycling. Qualify both the joint and the inspection method for the intended service conditions.
status: The 2018 fusion-composite review documents substantial progress in fibers, composites, irradiation testing, and joining; successful specimens or larger components do not establish lifetime qualification for every joint architecture.
why: Extends the low-activation and high-temperature advantages of SiC beyond simple coupon geometries.
key_works: T. Koyanagi et al. (2018), “Recent progress in the development of SiC composites for nuclear fusion applications,” [DOI:10.1016/j.jnucmat.2018.06.017](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jnucmat.2018.06.017).

title: Predictive corrosion in flowing molten salts
subfield: Radiation, nuclear materials, and extreme environments
open: Predict selective dissolution, mass transfer, and component failure for alloys and coatings in a specified flowing molten salt with controlled impurities, redox state, and temperature gradients. Validate across laboratories and changing salt histories.
status: Decades of compatibility experiments exist; a 2026 review still identifies coupled effects of media and material state. Static immersion rankings alone do not establish loop-scale lifetime.
why: Enables durable molten-salt energy systems and high-temperature process equipment.
key_works: K. Su et al. (2026), “Molten Salt Corrosion in Energy Systems: A Comprehensive Review on the Effects of Media and Material States,” [DOI:10.1002/maco.70124](https://doi.org/10.1002/maco.70124).

title: Space-material lifetime from coupled exposures
subfield: Radiation, nuclear materials, and extreme environments
open: Predict optical, mechanical, and thermal-property drift of a specified spacecraft material from combined atomic oxygen, ultraviolet light, charged particles, thermal cycling, and contamination. Transfer ground-test predictions to independently observed orbital exposures.
status: NASA's 2025 MISSE report documents 365 flight samples across four experiments; these valuable exposures do not supply a universal acceleration law for arbitrary materials and orbits.
why: Supports longer missions and reduces overdesign and premature material degradation.
key_works: K. K. de Groh and B. A. Banks (2025), “Space Environmental Exposure of the MISSE 9-15 Polymers and Composites Experiment 1-4 (PCE 1-4),” [NASA/TM-20240000755/REV1](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20240000755).

title: Transferable prediction of waste-glass residual corrosion
subfield: Radiation, nuclear materials, and extreme environments
open: Predict the long-term residual dissolution rate of compositionally varied nuclear-waste glasses from evolving alteration-layer chemistry, pore transport, solution composition, and radiation history. Demonstrate transfer beyond the reference glass used to calibrate the model.
status: Gin and colleagues' 2020 work follows International Simple Glass for six years and resolves coupled hydrolysis/transport behavior; extrapolation across waste compositions and groundwater conditions remains open.
why: Reduces uncertainty in radionuclide-release assessments over geological times.
key_works: S. Gin et al. (2020), “Insights into the mechanisms controlling the residual corrosion rate of borosilicate glasses,” [DOI:10.1038/s41529-020-00145-2](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41529-020-00145-2).

title: Predicting resumption of waste-glass alteration
subfield: Radiation, nuclear materials, and extreme environments
open: Determine when secondary-phase formation destabilizes a protective alteration layer and accelerates nuclear-waste-glass dissolution. Predict induction times and acceleration magnitudes under independently specified water chemistry, temperature, and surface-area conditions.
status: Forty years of standardized durability testing are reviewed in 2021; alteration resumption is observed in some conditions and absent in others, preventing its treatment as a universal fixed stage.
why: Identifies conditions that could invalidate simple long-term durability extrapolations.
key_works: C. L. Thorpe et al. (2021), “Forty years of durability assessment of nuclear waste glass by standard methods,” [DOI:10.1038/s41529-021-00210-4](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41529-021-00210-4).

title: Durable funding for materials-data stewardship
open: Establish a sustained funding and governance model that pays for materials-data curation, correction, persistent identifiers, access, and preservation after individual grants end. Demonstrate continuity through personnel and funder turnover, including costly negative-result and provenance curation.
status: OECD's 2017 study identifies sustainability challenges across 48 research repositories; existing repositories demonstrate useful services, while the recurring-cost problem remains institution-dependent.
why: Prevents publicly funded observations from becoming unusable or disappearing.
key_works: OECD (2017), “Business models for sustainable research data repositories,” [DOI:10.1787/302b12bb-en](https://doi.org/10.1787/302b12bb-en).

title: Sustained access to shared materials instruments
open: Design and evaluate funding arrangements that cover maintenance, expert operators, consumables, and equitable external access for shared materials-characterization facilities. Resolve the gap between buying an instrument and sustaining reliable, affordable experimental capacity.
status: The 2019 US materials decadal survey documents access and maintenance pressures; shared centers provide partial solutions, but success depends on continuing operational support. This is a documented institutional problem, not a claim about a particular 2026 budget.
why: Makes advanced measurements reproducible and accessible beyond well-resourced laboratories.
key_works: National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine (2019), “Frontiers of Materials Research: A Decadal Survey,” [DOI:10.17226/25244](https://doi.org/10.17226/25244).

title: Funded access to fusion-spectrum irradiation
open: Deliver sustained, broadly accessible irradiation and post-irradiation testing capacity sufficient to qualify candidate fusion materials under representative neutron spectra. Solve the capital, operating, specimen-throughput, and international-access commitments together.
status: The need predates the 2016 fusion-materials review. The US Department of Energy's finalized 2026 fusion roadmap explicitly makes milestones contingent on future partnerships and appropriations; publishing a roadmap does not itself provide the required capacity.
why: Removes a shared bottleneck in experimentally validating component lifetimes.
key_works: Knaster, Moeslang, and Muroga (2016), “Materials research for fusion,” [DOI:10.1038/nphys3735](https://doi.org/10.1038/nphys3735); US DOE (2026), [finalized Fusion Science and Technology Roadmap announcement](https://www.energy.gov/articles/energy-department-releases-finalized-fusion-science-and-technology-roadmap-accelerate).

title: Shared pilot-scale materials qualification
open: Establish accessible pilot facilities where new materials can be produced, characterized, and independently qualified at application-relevant scale, with workable cost sharing, intellectual-property terms, and reproducible process records. Evaluate whether they shorten qualification for organizations lacking their own pilot plants.
status: The 2019 materials decadal survey recommends coordinated materials growth hubs and shared resources; individual foundries exist, but access and continuity remain uneven across material classes.
why: Connects laboratory discoveries to credible manufacturing and customer qualification.
key_works: National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine (2019), “Frontiers of Materials Research: A Decadal Survey,” [DOI:10.17226/25244](https://doi.org/10.17226/25244).

title: Phason-entropy stabilization of decagonal Al–Co–Cu
open: Determine whether, and by how much, phason entropy stabilizes decagonal Al–Co–Cu relative to crystalline approximants in the converged quasiperiodic limit. Separate phason, chemical, and vibrational entropy, then predict the equilibrium stability window without fitting its transition temperature.
status: Huang, Widom, and Mihalkovič’s 2024 calculations place their quasicrystal approximants at least about 3 meV per atom above crystalline competitors at zero temperature and predict entropy stabilization around 600–800 K. Experimental validation remains open; 2025 ground-state calculations for other binary quasicrystals also show why entropy stabilization should not be assumed universal.
why: It would establish which microscopic disorder stabilizes a real quasiperiodic solid and make its thermal processing predictable.
key_works: Y. Huang, M. Widom, and M. Mihalkovič (2024), “Simulated structure and thermodynamics of decagonal Al-Co-Cu quasicrystals,” [DOI:10.1103/PhysRevResearch.6.033145](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevResearch.6.033145); W. Baek et al. (2025), “Quasicrystal stability and nucleation kinetics from density functional theory,” [DOI:10.1038/s41567-025-02925-6](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41567-025-02925-6).

title: Phason jumps that actually transport atoms in Al–Pd–Ru
open: Establish which phason-related atomic rearrangements in Al–Pd–Ru produce irreversible long-range transport rather than local back-and-forth motion. The target is one quantitative account of jump statistics, tracer diffusion, and excess heat capacity on specimens with known composition and approximant content.
status: Nagai et al.’s 2024 molecular dynamics and heat-capacity measurements identified high-temperature aluminum jumps and linked diffusion to fluctuations in the higher-dimensional structural description. The remaining experimental task is to close the accounting between individual rearrangements, transport correlation factors, and bulk thermodynamics.
why: It would establish whether phason activity offers control of atomic transport independently of ordinary vacancy diffusion.
key_works: Y. Nagai, Y. Iwasaki, K. Kitahara, Y. Takagiwa, K. Kimura, and M. Shiga (2024), “High-Temperature Atomic Diffusion and Specific Heat in Quasicrystals,” [DOI:10.1103/PhysRevLett.132.196301](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.132.196301).

title: Direct observation of incipient kink nucleation in MAX phases
open: Observe the first irreversible event creating a kink band in a MAX-phase crystal under controlled basal compression. Discriminate pyramidal dislocation-loop nucleation from elastic buckling and ripplocation-based initiation, following the event into the eventual kink boundary.
status: Kink bands are established, but direct evidence identifying their earliest nucleation events remains elusive. Hossain and Ogata’s 2025 simulations of Ti₃SiC₂ propose pyramidal dislocation loops, lattice bending, and basal glide as a pathway to high-angle kink-band pairs; that pathway needs experimental discrimination from alternatives.
why: Incipient kinking controls damage tolerance and energy dissipation in layered structural ceramics.
key_works: R. Hossain and S. Ogata (2025), “Unveiling kink band formation mechanism in MAX phases,” [DOI:10.1038/s43246-025-00766-7](https://doi.org/10.1038/s43246-025-00766-7).

title: Same-specimen reconciliation of MXene hydroxyl assignments
open: Determine genuine hydroxyl termination abundance and geometry on Ti₃C₂Tₓ separately from intercalated water, adsorbed water, and oxidation products. Reconcile isotope-sensitive solid-state NMR and photoelectron spectroscopy on matched specimens with controlled hydration histories and a closed hydrogen inventory.
status: A 2020 NMR–DFT study assigned terminating hydroxyls and distinct water environments. A 2021 UPS/XPS study concluded that hydroxyls were not inherent terminations of its Ti₃C₂Tₓ surfaces. Reconciling these assignments through measured preparation and measurement histories remains open.
why: Surface proton identity changes interfacial reactions, ion binding, and the interpretation of computational MXene models.
key_works: T. Kobayashi et al. (2020), “Nature of Terminating Hydroxyl Groups and Intercalating Water in Ti₃C₂Tₓ MXenes: A Study by ¹H Solid-State NMR and DFT Calculations,” [DOI:10.1021/acs.jpcc.0c04744](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.jpcc.0c04744); L.-Å. Näslund et al. (2021), “Chemical Bonding of Termination Species in 2D Carbides Investigated through Valence Band UPS/XPS of Ti₃C₂Tₓ MXene,” [DOI:10.1088/2053-1583/ac1ea9](https://doi.org/10.1088/2053-1583/ac1ea9).

title: Termination-selected geometry of Janus MXene nanoscrolls
open: Demonstrate quantitative selection of nanoscroll radius, interlayer spacing, and handedness from measured termination asymmetry on individual Janus MXene flakes. Distinguish strain-driven rolling from adhesion, trapped reaction products, edge chemistry, and particle-induced deformation.
status: Scrolling itself is established. Rezaee et al.’s August 2026 preprint predicts termination-induced lattice mismatch of roughly 1–7%; simulations of particular 120 nm Ti₂C flakes give inner diameters near 7 nm or above 20 nm depending on termination combination. These are predictions awaiting experimental validation.
why: Predictable scrolling would enable chemically programmable nanocontainers and confined reaction environments.
key_works: S. Rezaee, F. Mohammad Dezashibi, Ould el Moctar, and H. Darban (2026), “Mechanisms of Nanoscroll Formation and Particle Encapsulation in Janus MXenes,” [arXiv:2608.12439](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12439), preprint.

title: Identifying the rate-controlling step in cold sintering
open: Predict when cold-sintering densification is limited by dissolution, transport through transient liquid, precipitation, or particle rearrangement using independently measured interfacial chemistry and local stress. Transfer the kinetic description between pressures, particle sizes, and solvent activities without refitting every condition.
status: Momjian, Mauro, and Randall’s 2025 relaxation model separates concurrent processes in ZnO densification and describes a broad range of tested conditions. This is a substantial material-specific advance; transferring independently determined rates between different solvent–ceramic systems remains open.
why: It would reveal which ceramics can densify at low temperature and which chemical or transport bottlenecks prevent it.
key_works: S. Momjian, J. C. Mauro, and C. A. Randall (2025), “Non-equilibrium thermodynamics and kinetics of the sintering process: A relaxation model describing cold sintering,” [DOI:10.1111/jace.70180](https://doi.org/10.1111/jace.70180).

title: Room-temperature relaxation of cold-sintered grain boundaries
open: Predict the chemical and electrical evolution of residual grain-boundary phases after cold sintering, including whether the dense ceramic has reached a stable final state at room temperature. Connect residual-solvent and precursor inventories to evolving barrier heights and equilibration times.
status: Hérisson de Beauvoir and Estournès reported in 2024 that cold-sintered ZnO with less than 1 wt% residual acetate could undergo nearly two orders of magnitude of resistivity increase during room-temperature aging. The atomistic pathways and relaxation laws governing this evolution remain unresolved.
why: It would make low-temperature ceramic processing compatible with reproducible electrical properties after storage.
key_works: T. Hérisson de Beauvoir and C. Estournès (2024), “Room temperature ZnO ageing after Cold Sintering Process: Grain boundaries evolution characterization by in situ electrochemical impedance spectroscopy,” [DOI:10.1016/j.jeurceramsoc.2024.02.014](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jeurceramsoc.2024.02.014).

title: Closing the vacancy inventory during metal exsolution
open: Determine where host-lattice defects created during metal exsolution go: retained point defects, reconstructed material around particles, surface sinks, or void volume. Close a quantitative cation–anion–volume balance through surface nucleation, buried nanoparticle formation, and particle migration.
status: Rosnes et al.’s 2026 study resolves multiple exsolution stages in a nonstoichiometric Cu-containing perovskite and discusses Schottky-defect annihilation. The observed stages do not yet supply a predictive defect inventory, particularly for stoichiometric hosts or changing surface-to-volume ratios.
why: Vacancy disposition determines whether exsolution produces useful supported catalysts or destabilizes the oxide host.
key_works: A. Rosnes et al. (2026), “Multiple Stages of Metal Exsolution from Nonstoichiometric Perovskites,” [DOI:10.1021/jacs.6c08762](https://doi.org/10.1021/jacs.6c08762).

title: Why mixed dislocations preferentially deliver exsolving ruthenium
open: Predict when moving mixed dislocations transport exsolving metal to an oxide surface, distinguishing that mechanism from segregation followed by diffusion along stationary dislocation cores. Determine the dependence on Burgers vector, line character, dopant chemistry, and redox history.
status: Choi et al.’s 2026 Ru-doped barium cerate study found about 75% of observed exsolved nanoparticles at mixed-dislocation ends, with none identified at the sampled pure edge or screw dislocations. Sampling and visibility limitations prevent treating this as a universal selection rule.
why: It could enable catalyst-particle positioning through deliberate control of dislocation populations.
key_works: S. Choi et al. (2026), “Dynamics of dislocation formations and their impacts on exsolution in Ru-doped perovskite oxide,” [DOI:10.1038/s41467-026-73457-7](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-73457-7).

title: Identity of the migrating nickel species in steam electrolysis
open: Determine the relative contributions of metallic surface diffusion, hydroxyl-containing volatile species, interfacial wetting changes, and electrochemical potential gradients to nickel redistribution in Ni–YSZ steam electrodes. Predict migration direction and rate from operating conditions and measured three-dimensional connectivity.
status: Pibulchinda et al.’s 2026 experiments compare electrode compositions at 800 °C, −1 A cm⁻², and 85% steam over 500 hours. Lower nickel content mitigated migration through changes associated with overpotential gradients and connected Ni–pore pathways, but did not uniquely identify the transported species.
why: Redistribution can remove nickel from the active electrochemical interface while leaving substantial nickel elsewhere in the electrode.
key_works: P. Pibulchinda et al. (2026), “Mitigating Ni migration in solid oxide electrolysis by altering Ni-YSZ electrode composition,” [DOI:10.1039/D6TA01398H](https://doi.org/10.1039/D6TA01398H).

title: Chemical versus oxygen-pressure-driven electrode delamination
open: Derive and experimentally distinguish chemical weakening from oxygen-activity-driven fracture at chromium-free LSM–YSZ and LSM–GdCeScSZ interfaces. Explain delamination at low inferred internal oxygen partial pressure as well as failure accompanying very high oxygen activity.
status: Kim et al. (2025) associate LSM–YSZ delamination with inferred internal oxygen partial pressure around 32,201 atm at 0.6 A cm⁻². LSM–GdCeScSZ also delaminated near 10⁻³ atm, without comparable intergranular fracture. These inferred oxygen activities must not automatically be interpreted as uniform mechanical cavity pressures.
why: It identifies when oxygen-transport improvements can prevent failure and when interface chemistry must change.
key_works: H. H. Kim et al. (2025), “Understanding delamination behavior of air electrode in solid oxide electrolysis cells through in situ monitoring of internal oxygen partial pressure,” [DOI:10.1016/j.cej.2024.158129](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cej.2024.158129).

title: Chromium-assisted reconstruction of LSCF–ceria interfaces
open: Establish the causal reaction sequence by which chromium contamination, strontium redistribution, and ceria-containing interlayers reconstruct an LSCF oxygen-electrode interface. Predict which reaction products remove adhesion or active pathways and which merely mark earlier damage.
status: Kindelmann et al.’s 2025 postmortem analysis examines a stack after approximately 93,000 hours at 700 °C and 0.5 A cm⁻². It identifies chromium-associated decomposition, substituted ceria-based nanoparticles, and gradual delamination; separating the reaction sequences and rates requires interrupted or time-resolved experiments.
why: It would explain when a nominally protective ceria interlayer participates in degradation.
key_works: M. Kindelmann, O. Guillon, J. Mayer, and N. H. Menzler (2025), “Atomic-scale insights into air electrode degradation after 10 years of fuel cell stack operation,” [DOI:10.1039/D5TA03917G](https://doi.org/10.1039/D5TA03917G).

title: Prescribing zeolite aluminum sites and aluminum pairs
open: Synthesize a zeolite with a specified distribution of aluminum among inequivalent tetrahedral sites and a specified population of aluminum pairs, while holding framework topology and bulk Si/Al ratio fixed. Prospectively select site populations and pair separations rather than only measuring them afterward.
status: This longstanding synthesis-control problem became more sharply measurable through Rzepka et al.’s 2025 anomalous X-ray diffraction determination of aluminum distributions in ZSM-5. Site mapping is a major advance, but it does not provide arbitrary control over occupancy, pairing, or redistribution during later treatment.
why: Identical bulk compositions can contain different acid-site arrangements and support different catalytic pathways.
key_works: P. Rzepka et al. (2025), “Aluminum distribution and active site locations in the structures of zeolite ZSM-5 catalysts,” [DOI:10.1126/science.ads7290](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.ads7290).

title: Molecular origin of zeolite pore-mouth resistance
open: Identify whether a measured surface barrier arises from blocked entrances, altered near-surface chemistry, structural disorder, or an intrinsic free-energy barrier at an open pore mouth. Independently measure surface resistance and intracrystalline diffusion, then predict how a selected surface modification changes both.
status: Surface and bulk resistance can mimic each other in uptake measurements. Liu et al.’s 2026 mordenite study improves transport and dimethyl-ether carbonylation through surface modification, while the molecular attribution and transferable prediction of these barriers remain incomplete.
why: It would distinguish inaccessible catalyst interiors from intrinsically slow chemistry.
key_works: H. Liu et al. (2026), “Reducing diffusion barriers of mordenite via surface modification to enhance dimethyl ether carbonylation,” [DOI:10.1016/j.ces.2026.123388](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ces.2026.123388).

title: Three-dimensional pore registry in nominal single-crystal COFs
open: Predict and control the lateral registry of successive layers throughout a two-dimensional covalent organic framework crystal. Reconstruct the actual three-dimensional pore network, identify growth conditions producing particular stacking faults, and predict their effect on molecular passage.
status: Kharel et al.’s 2025 imaging reveals widespread stacking disorder in nominal single-crystal COFs, including translations approaching half a unit cell. These exceed the small displacements commonly assumed in structural models; the growth-to-registry-to-transport relationship remains incomplete.
why: Sharp diffraction can conceal a pore network substantially different from the ideal channels used to predict separation or catalysis.
key_works: P. Kharel et al. (2025), “3D Imaging Reveals Widespread Stacking Disorder in Single Crystal 2D Covalent Organic Frameworks,” [DOI:10.1021/jacs.4c16207](https://doi.org/10.1021/jacs.4c16207).

title: Error correction before irreversible ketoenamine locking
open: Predict the kinetic window in which a β-ketoenamine COF can repair incorrect bonds before tautomerization locks them into the framework. Build a measured reaction-network model that selects additive acidity, concentration, and time-dependent conditions for a chosen monomer combination.
status: Van Voorthuizen et al. (2025) show that balancing additive pKₐ is crucial in TpPa synthesis, with selected organic bases improving crystallinity and porosity. Transfer across monomers requires a fuller account of competing imine exchange, nucleation, and irreversible locking.
why: It would reconcile chemical stability in the final framework with the reversible chemistry needed for ordered growth.
key_works: T. A. van Voorthuizen et al. (2025), “On the Importance of Balancing the pKₐ of the Additive in β-Ketoenamine COF Synthesis,” [DOI:10.1002/chem.202501512](https://doi.org/10.1002/chem.202501512).

title: Hydrogen-isotope selectivity above five above 200 K
open: Produce a regenerable solid with H₂/D₂ separation factor above five at temperatures above 200 K, retaining adsorption and desorption rates suitable for cyclic operation. Demonstrate the selectivity dynamically and quantify usable capacity and regeneration energy.
status: Yamauchi et al. explicitly identify this selectivity–temperature frontier. Their study, published online in 2025 and in a 2026 journal volume, reports a separation factor of 4.2 at 213 K, a 5.0 kJ mol⁻¹ isotope-dependent adsorption-enthalpy difference, and room-temperature chromatography. Room-temperature separation itself is already demonstrated.
why: Strong noncryogenic discrimination could reduce the energy and complexity of hydrogen-isotope processing.
key_works: T. Yamauchi et al. (2026), “Room-temperature chromatographic H₂/D₂ separation via a solid dihydrogen complex with balanced thermodynamics and kinetics,” [DOI:10.1039/D5GC04476F](https://doi.org/10.1039/D5GC04476F).

title: Strong intrinsic argon-over-oxygen recognition
open: Design an ambient-temperature physisorbent strongly favoring argon over oxygen while retaining reversible uptake. A proposed census target is Ar/O₂ selectivity of at least ten at 298–310 K and at least 0.5 mmol g⁻¹ argon working capacity between 1 and 0.1 bar; these are proposed thresholds, not community benchmarks.
status: Yan et al.’s 2025 MOF reports selectivity around 1.4 and argon uptake around 10 cm³ g⁻¹ at 308 K and 1 bar. Zhao et al. already demonstrate oxygen product purity above 99.99% with AlFUM; purity must be distinguished from recovery yield.
why: Stronger recognition could reduce sorbent inventories and gas-recycling burdens.
key_works: F. Yan et al. (2025), “An amino-functionalized ultra-micropore metal–organic framework using for argon/oxygen adsorption separation,” [DOI:10.1016/j.jiec.2025.01.013](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jiec.2025.01.013); S. Zhao et al. (2025), “Selective recognition of argon by an aluminum-based MOF for oxygen recovery from Ar/O₂ mixture under ambient conditions,” [DOI:10.1016/j.ces.2025.122130](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ces.2025.122130).

title: Mechanism-preserving acceleration of tin-whisker incubation
open: Develop an accelerated test quantitatively predicting incubation-time distributions and extreme whisker lengths in real plated tin finishes over service lifetimes. Preserve the governing stress-generation and mass-transport mechanism while accelerating it.
status: This decades-old reliability problem has established mitigation practices and accelerated tests. NIST investigates plating microstructure, intermetallic growth, and compressive stress; Zhang et al.’s 2025-online work supplies controllable atomized-tin whisker growth and graphene inhibition, but transferring its mechanisms and timescales to commercial plated interfaces remains open.
why: A predictive incubation law would make rare short-circuit risk measurable before years of storage or operation.
key_works: NIST, [“Lead-Free Surface Finishes for Electronic Components: Tin Whisker Growth”](https://www.nist.gov/programs-projects/lead-free-surface-finishes-electronic-components-tin-whisker-growth), research program; P. Zhang et al. (2025, online), “Inhibitory effect of graphene on tin whisker growth induced by atomized Sn,” [DOI:10.1016/j.matlet.2025.139631](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.matlet.2025.139631).

title: Premelting intermetallic precursors of zinc-induced steel embrittlement
open: Determine whether grain-boundary Fe–Zn intermetallics formed before zinc melts are necessary precursors, optional accelerators, or competing products during industrial liquid-metal embrittlement. Resolve their formation and mechanical effects on joining timescales and predict vulnerable grain-boundary characters.
status: Han et al. (2026) observe solid-state grain-boundary intermetallic precipitation below zinc’s melting temperature and associated ductility loss, without macroscopic liquid-metal-embrittlement cracking under those isolated conditions. Their causal contribution during rapid welding, subsequent liquid penetration, and fracture remains unresolved.
why: It could explain why protection aimed only at contact with molten zinc fails for some galvanized advanced high-strength steels.
key_works: S. Han, Y. Ikeda, L. Klusendorf, A. Das, and R. Maaß (2026), “Solid-state intermetallic grain-boundary precipitation as an early stage of liquid-metal embrittlement in advanced high-strength steels,” [DOI:10.1038/s41529-026-00851-3](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41529-026-00851-3).

title: GeTe resistance drift beyond a single structural-relaxation clock
open: Identify the microscopic processes producing both temperature-independent early drift and accelerated late drift in melt-quenched GeTe. Predict resistance from 10 ns to 1,000 s across temperature and quench rate, including increased drift coefficients after slower quenching.
status: Ballmaier, Walfort, and Salinga’s 2025 measurements span eleven time decades and approximately room temperature to 460 K. Submicrosecond behavior and late acceleration near the glass transition depart from familiar power-law models; the authors identify deficiencies in existing descriptions.
why: Predictive drift physics would improve analog-memory reliability and distinguish stable states from short observation windows.
key_works: J. Ballmaier, S. Walfort, and M. Salinga (2025), “Resistance Drift of Phase Change Materials Beyond the Power Law,” [DOI:10.1002/aelm.202400905](https://doi.org/10.1002/aelm.202400905).

title: The microscopic polarity bit in selector-only chalcogenide memory
open: Determine which atomic defect transformations store the polarity-dependent threshold-voltage state in single-chalcogenide X-point memories. Discriminate graded-bandgap, anisotropic-trap, and trap-delocalization descriptions under the same low-current programming conditions.
status: Fantini et al.’s 2026 graded-bandgap model reproduces several device trends through different defect transformations near the electrodes. Competing descriptions remain: segregation observed at high current does not explain all low-current devices, and some bilayer tests show opposite polarity dependence.
why: Identifying the stored physical variable would make memory-window, retention, and read-disturb predictions transferable between alloys and geometries.
key_works: P. Fantini et al. (2026), “Microscopic model of the operation of the single-chalcogenide X-point memory,” [DOI:10.1038/s43246-025-01044-2](https://doi.org/10.1038/s43246-025-01044-2).
aliases: Selector-only memory; self-selecting memory; single-chalcogenide X-point memory.

title: Predicting the sign reversal of illuminated-bias instability in IGZO
open: Predict when an amorphous In–Ga–Zn–O transistor’s threshold shift under negative-bias thermal illumination stress reverses from negative to positive. Connect hydrogen and oxygen chemical states, channel thickness, and stress history to the crossover time and both shift amplitudes.
status: Kim, Lee, and Choi reported this reversal in flexible top-gate devices in 2025, with stronger abnormal behavior in thicker channels. Spectroscopy associated it with hydrogen/oxygen-related states near the valence-band maximum; thickness optimization suppressed it, but the quantitative competition between defect reactions remains unresolved.
why: Predicting the sign of aging matters for display compensation and oxide-transistor circuits whose corrections can otherwise amplify drift.
key_works: D. Kim, K.-B. Lee, and B. Choi (2025), “Hydrogen and oxygen induced abnormal reliability degradation in flexible top-gate amorphous In-Ga-Zn-O thin-film transistors under negative bias thermal illumination stress,” [DOI:10.1016/j.mejo.2025.106902](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.mejo.2025.106902).

title: Eliminating discrete spectral jumps of hBN B centres
open: Identify and control the microscopic rearrangements making a B centre’s optical transition jump on microsecond-to-millisecond timescales. Sustain emission near the lifetime-limited linewidth while retaining coherent excitation and photon purity, without selecting only quiet intervals.
status: Gérard et al. demonstrated resonance fluorescence and high-visibility two-photon interference in 2026. The approximately 0.95 GHz time-averaged linewidth remained about ten times the 93 MHz Fourier limit, although dephasing between jumps was negligible. Suppressing intermittent environmental changes remains open.
why: Independent emitters must remain mutually resonant for scalable photonic interference and entanglement distribution.
key_works: D. Gérard et al. (2026), “Resonance fluorescence and indistinguishable photons from a coherently driven B centre in hBN,” [DOI:10.1038/s41467-026-68555-5](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-68555-5); J. Horder (2025), “Quantum photonics with the B centre in hexagonal boron nitride,” [doctoral thesis](https://opus.lib.uts.edu.au/handle/10453/196122).

title: Stable coherent NV centres within two nanometres of diamond surfaces
open: Demonstrate a nitrogen-vacancy centre 0.5–2 nm below a diamond surface that retains its useful charge state and the coherence protection predicted for surface-induced strain plus a weak static magnetic field. Independently establish depth and the surface electric- and magnetic-noise spectra.
status: Pershin et al.’s 2025 first-principles study proposes protection even near 1 nm depth, but favorable limits assume strong isotopic purification and sufficiently weak electric-field noise. Coherence demonstrations at larger shallow depths do not establish this ultrasmall stand-off regime.
why: This distance regime would strengthen coupling to individual external nuclear spins and molecular-scale magnetic structure.
key_works: A. Pershin, A. Tárkányi, V. Verkhovlyuk, V. Ivády, and A. Gali (2025), “A coherence-protection scheme for quantum sensors based on ultra-shallow single nitrogen-vacancy centers in diamond,” [DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-64771-7](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-64771-7).

title: Trap chemistry of optically written second-order nonlinearity in silicon nitride
open: Identify the atomic traps responsible for photogalvanically written second-order susceptibility in nominally centrosymmetric Si₃N₄. Predict how fabrication controls their density and distribution to obtain rapid, reproducible poling and long retention while preserving low optical loss.
status: Nitišs et al. established grating-formation rules and fitted thermal erasure to shallow traps around 0.44 eV in their 2020 publication. This constrains kinetics but does not uniquely assign the defects or establish a transferable connection between processing, trap chemistry, and grating lifetime.
why: Prescribed induced nonlinearity would support integrated frequency conversion and quantum-light generation.
key_works: E. Nitišs et al. (2020), “Formation Rules and Dynamics of Photoinduced χ⁽²⁾ Gratings in Silicon Nitride Waveguides,” [DOI:10.1021/acsphotonics.9b01301](https://doi.org/10.1021/acsphotonics.9b01301).

title: Experimental Purcell refrigeration below the rare-earth thermal-population limit
open: Demonstrate net laser refrigeration below liquid-nitrogen temperature using a cavity that preferentially enhances higher-energy fluorescence from a rare-earth-doped crystal. Include parasitic absorption, surface quenching, optical escape, and a calibrated heat load in the demonstration.
status: Ju et al.’s 2026 calculation uses measured Yb:YLF coefficients and predicts approximately 38 K for a nanocrystal near a cavity, compared with an experimental rare-earth refrigeration baseline of 87 K cited in that work. The lower temperature is a theoretical projection.
why: This regime could extend vibration-free optical refrigeration to detectors and quantum devices needing deeper cryogenic cooling.
key_works: P. Ju et al. (2026), “Purcell-enhanced optical refrigeration,” [DOI:10.1103/d7pk-hsry](https://doi.org/10.1103/d7pk-hsry), [arXiv:2404.19142](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.19142).

title: Predicting photodarkening-induced mode instability from pump history
