key_works: X. Li, Q. Liang, C. Liang, D. Wang, S. Li, and X. Ding (2026), “Fatigue resistant elastocaloric effect in TiNi via texture-precipitate synergy,” [DOI:10.1038/s41467-026-68835-0](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-68835-0).

title: Hundreds-second structural relaxation in magnetocaloric La(Fe,Si)₁₃
open: Determine whether the prolonged structural relaxation after a magnetic-field sweep stops is controlled by intrinsic nonthermal transformation kinetics, thermal lag, or their coupling. Predict the pronounced difference between field-application and field-removal branches using independently measured local temperatures and phase fractions.
status: Time-resolved synchrotron measurements in 2024 found relaxation lasting hundreds of seconds. Free-energy analysis revealed asymmetric barriers and behavior suggestive of nonthermal activation; a mechanism-discriminating account of that inference remains open.
why: Slow structural response can prevent a large equilibrium caloric effect from delivering useful cooling power.
key_works: A. Azevedo Beleza et al. (2024), “Structural dynamics of first-order phase transition in giant magnetocaloric La(Fe,Si)13: The free energy landscape,” [DOI:10.1016/j.mtphys.2024.101388](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.mtphys.2024.101388).

title: Non-Clausius–Clapeyron stress slopes in Ti–Al–Cr elastocaloric crystals
open: Explain why transformation-stress slopes reverse sign near 150 K in compression but near 200 K in tension in Ti₇₅.₂₅Al₂₀Cr₄.₇₅, while calorimetry retains a consistent transformation-entropy sign. Reconcile entropy, elastic moduli, phase fractions, and hysteretic stresses within equilibrium thermodynamics.
status: Song and colleagues measured cooling at 102 K in 2026, below the approximately 167 K cutoff inferred from a conventional stress-slope estimate. They explicitly leave tension–compression divergence and the microscopic origin of proposed B2 shear-modulus hardening unresolved; the discrepancy does not establish violation of the equilibrium Clausius–Clapeyron relation.
why: It would reveal which measured transformation stresses can serve as thermodynamic derivatives.
key_works: Y. Song et al. (2026), “Enhanced elastocaloric cooling beyond Clausius–Clapeyron limits,” [DOI:10.1038/s41467-026-72172-7](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-72172-7).

title: Predicting the first RF vortex from a real Nb₃Sn surface defect
open: Predict the first vortex-entry location and field from a measured three-dimensional Nb₃Sn defect map, including stoichiometry, embedded tin, grain-boundary grooves, and surface corrugation. Validate at the same locations under RF excitation.
status: Willson and colleagues combined microscopy and time-dependent Ginzburg–Landau simulations in 2024, showing strong interactions between defect composition and geometry. Subsequent thermal-groove modeling adds another contribution; prediction for interacting defects on an actual cavity surface remains unvalidated.
why: It would identify the few defects that control cavity performance.
key_works: S. A. Willson et al. (2024), “Impact of submicron Nb3Sn stoichiometric surface defects on high-field superconducting radiofrequency cavity performance,” [DOI:10.1103/PhysRevResearch.6.043133](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevResearch.6.043133); E. M. Lechner et al. (2024), “Analysis of Thermal Grooving Effects on Vortex Penetration in Vapor-Diffused Nb3Sn,” [arXiv:2409.01569](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.01569).

title: Buried-hydride vortex entry versus proximity breakdown in niobium
open: Determine whether buried niobium hydrides initiate high-field RF losses through vortex entry, loss of proximity-induced superconductivity, or coupled evolution. Relate known hydride depths and shapes to local dissipation and flux penetration in the same cryogenic state.
status: Cryogenic imaging and diffraction directly characterized nanometric hydrides in 2024. Harbick and colleagues’ 2026 computational study produces a subsurface-hydride vortex-entry interpretation of high-field Q-slope; direct local observations discriminating it from proximity breakdown remain needed.
why: It would specify whether processing should prevent precipitation or control precipitate geometry and superconducting surroundings.
key_works: Z. Sung et al. (2024), “Direct observation of nanometer size hydride precipitations in superconducting niobium,” [DOI:10.1038/s41598-024-77905-6](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-024-77905-6); A. Harbick et al. (2026), “A computational picture of hydride formation and dissipation in Nb SRF cavities,” [DOI:10.1088/1361-6668/ae4a52](https://doi.org/10.1088/1361-6668/ae4a52).

title: Full-cavity test of the superconducting–insulating multilayer field advantage
open: Demonstrate a complete superconducting–insulating–superconducting coating on a three-dimensional niobium cavity that increases usable RF field while preserving low dissipation. Isolate the multilayer screening benefit from thermal-processing and single-layer effects.
status: The enhancement proposal dates to 2006. SRF2025 reported substantial sample and coating progress, including an alumina-coated cavity retaining approximately 40 MV m⁻¹; a May 2026 study still describes full SIS implementations as limited to flat samples and identifies a coated single-cell cavity as a milestone.
why: It would test a long-standing route to higher-gradient accelerators.
key_works: A. Gurevich (2006), “Enhancement of rf breakdown field of superconductors by multilayer coating,” [DOI:10.1063/1.2162264](https://doi.org/10.1063/1.2162264); L. Preece et al. (2025), “SIS multilayer studies and status of the new cavity-coating system at University of Hamburg,” [DOI:10.18429/JACoW-SRF2025-TUA06](https://doi.org/10.18429/JACoW-SRF2025-TUA06); A. Gobeyn et al. (2026), [arXiv:2605.05505](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.05505).

title: Reversed odd–even acoustic selection rules in ultrathin lithium niobate
open: Identify the depth-dependent polarization and piezoelectric profile that reverses thickness-mode selection rules in approximately 67 nm lithium-niobate films. Distinguish graded surface damage from domain reversal and predict coupling after controlled surface treatments.
status: Xie and colleagues demonstrated resonances up to 220 GHz in 2025. Even-order modes became dominant as films thinned; surface measurements suggested a graded altered region, with approximately 5–6 nm indicated by reflectivity and approximately 20 nm affected by etching. Its piezoelectric profile remains undetermined.
why: It would enable deliberate sub-terahertz mode selection and identify damaging fabrication steps.
key_works: J. Xie, W. Wu, M. Shen, P. Fay, and H. X. Tang (2025), “Towards terahertz nanomechanics,” [DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-63561-5](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-63561-5).

title: Chemical identity of the Ga-site E1 trap in GaN and dilute AlGaN
open: Chemically identify the E1 donor trap, discriminating proposed carbon-on-gallium and molybdenum-on-gallium assignments. Reproduce alloy-neighbor splitting and transition energies while linking trap populations to independently controlled impurity incorporation.
status: High-resolution Laplace DLTS in 2025 showed E1 splitting in dilute AlGaN closely resembling that of known Fe-on-Ga defects. This strongly constrains the lattice site; hybrid-functional calculations narrow chemical candidates, but the impurity nucleus remains indirectly assigned.
why: It would connect trap suppression to specific contamination or precursor chemistry.
key_works: P. Kruszewski et al. (2025), “On the origin of the E1 electron trap level in GaN and dilute AlxGa1-xN films,” [arXiv:2506.10566](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.10566).

title: Carbon site versus growth-rate origin of the β-Ga₂O₃ 1.6 eV compensator
open: Determine whether the Eᶜ−1.6 eV acceptor in rapidly grown β-Ga₂O₃ is carbon on oxygen site I, carbon on site III, or another growth-correlated defect. Independently vary carbon supply and growth rate.
status: Ghadi and colleagues reported in June 2026 that this state accounts for more than 90% of compensation in their high-growth-rate series. Its concentration follows SIMS carbon, but precursor flow changes both carbon incorporation and growth rate; the paper explicitly leaves definitive assignment to experiments decoupling them.
why: It would permit faster growth of thick drift layers without compensating away their donors.
key_works: H. Ghadi et al. (2026), “Defect evolution and carrier compensation in high-growth rate MOCVD-grown β-Ga2O3,” [DOI:10.1063/5.0325051](https://doi.org/10.1063/5.0325051).

title: Which photoionized defects truncate the highest Cu₂O Rydberg states?
open: Identify the charged-defect species and photoionization pathways that erase high-principal-quantum-number Cu₂O exciton lines. Explain the different power sensitivities of P and D excitons together with optical purification and reionization dynamics.
status: A 2025 millikelvin study resolved n = 29 absorption below 1 μW cm⁻². Electric-field comparisons implicate photoionized impurities, and a 2026 purification study achieved 15 ns measurement resolution; the dominant charge-changing species behind the highest-n cutoff remain unassigned.
why: It would improve giant-exciton coherence and solid-state strong optical interactions.
key_works: J. Heckötter, D. Janas, M. Aßmann, and M. Bayer (2025), “Rydberg excitons in Cu2O at millikelvin temperatures,” [arXiv:2510.26966](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.26966); B. Panda et al. (2026), “Dynamics of Purification in Cu2O,” [DOI:10.1002/pssb.202500366](https://doi.org/10.1002/pssb.202500366).

title: The 1.5 eV lifetime-activation mechanism in BaTiO₃ capacitors
open: Identify the rate-limiting sequence producing approximately 1.5 eV lifetime activation in BaTiO₃ multilayer capacitors when oxygen-vacancy migration suggests roughly 1 eV. Connect ionic redistribution, electronic carrier processes, grain-boundary barriers, and failure statistics.
status: Chun and colleagues measured approximately 1.5 eV across three prototype capacitor systems in 2024 and proposed an electronic contribution. Its proximity to half the bandgap does not uniquely identify the mechanism or establish when the activation energy changes with field and compensation chemistry.
why: It would make accelerated lifetime extrapolation less vulnerable to changing failure mechanisms.
key_works: J. Chun, J. Heo, K. Lee, B. U. Ye, B. S. Kang, and S.-H. Yoon (2024), “Thermal activation energy on electrical degradation process in BaTiO3 based multilayer ceramic capacitors for lifetime reliability,” [DOI:10.1038/s41598-024-51254-w](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-024-51254-w).

title: Detecting oxygen interstitials proposed at neutral Er(Mn,Ti)O₃ walls
open: Quantify oxygen-interstitial excess and charge density at neutral Er(Mn,Ti)O₃ domain walls without changing their stoichiometry through beam exposure or vacuum. Correlate the inventory with reversible atmosphere-dependent conductivity at the same wall.
status: Richarz and colleagues demonstrated atmosphere-controlled wall conductivity in 2025, supported by calculations favoring oxygen-interstitial segregation. Atom-probe, time-of-flight SIMS, and electron-energy-loss measurements did not detect a significant wall oxygen anomaly, leaving a concrete sensitivity and measurement-perturbation frontier.
why: It would turn operational wall sensing into a chemically calibrated mechanism.
key_works: L. Richarz et al. (2025), “Ferroelectric Domain Walls for Environmental Sensors,” [DOI:10.1021/acsami.5c04875](https://doi.org/10.1021/acsami.5c04875); precursor [arXiv:2412.03691](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.03691).

title: Measuring the energy that actually reaches reacting powder in a ball mill
open: Establish the distribution of energy deposited in reacting powder during impacts, including cushioning, sliding, and evolving powder rheology. Create calibrated cross-mill measurements that predict conversion without a separately fitted energy-transfer factor for every apparatus.
status: A 2024 kinematic framework sought transferable milling specifications. Peterson’s 2025 correspondence identified reasons calculated maximum collision energies can substantially overestimate powder exposure; that distinction remains central to quantitative mechanochemical comparison.
why: It would support mechanochemical scale-up and comparisons of mechanical and thermal activation.
key_works: O. F. Jafter et al. (2024), “Navigating Ball Mill Specifications for Theory-to-Practice Reproducibility in Mechanochemistry,” [DOI:10.1002/anie.202409731](https://doi.org/10.1002/anie.202409731); G. I. Peterson (2025), “Responsible Use of Kinematic Models: Correspondence on ‘Navigating Ball Mill Specifications for Theory-to-Practice Reproducibility in Mechanochemistry’,” [DOI:10.1002/anie.202512324](https://doi.org/10.1002/anie.202512324).

title: Recovering the missing work density of anthracenophane composite actuators
open: Identify and remove the dominant losses between anthracenophane crystal transformation work and composite actuator output. A proposed milestone is tenfold higher work density than the reported composite while retaining its room-temperature reset time.
status: Lam and colleagues’ 2025 molecular designs reduced photodimer dissociation barriers by approximately 60% and enabled reset within minutes. Their composite’s estimated work density, 2.6 × 10³ J m⁻³, remained orders below ideal crystal predictions; conversion, orientation, and load transfer require quantitative separation.
why: It would convert large molecular strains into useful light-powered mechanical output.
key_works: K. Lam et al. (2025), “Photomechanical Anthracenophane Crystals: Theory, Experiment, and Composite Actuator Performance,” [DOI:10.1021/acs.cgd.5c00851](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.cgd.5c00851).

title: A kinetic law for the weak-light holding effect in 4F-9AC crystals
open: Explain quantitatively why a weak holding beam suppresses mechanical reset in photodimerized 4-fluoro-9-anthracenecarboxylic acid. Reproduce concentration-dependent nonexponential dissociation and mechanical recovery across pulse and holding-beam intensities.
status: Easley and colleagues documented the effect in 2020 and found simple first-order and autocatalytic descriptions inadequate. Stepwise DFT calculations in 2025 established thermodynamic cooperativity in photomechanical crystals but do not supply the required spatial kinetic law.
why: It would enable predictable optical holding and release in molecular actuators.
key_works: C. J. Easley et al. (2020), “Using light intensity to control reaction kinetics and reversibility in photomechanical crystals,” [DOI:10.1039/D0SC03557B](https://doi.org/10.1039/D0SC03557B); C. J. Perry and G. J. O. Beran (2025), “Investigating Cooperative Reactivity in Photomechanical Crystals Using First-Principles Density Functional Theory,” [DOI:10.1021/acs.cgd.5c00071](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.cgd.5c00071).

title: Predicting the crystallite-size cutoff for negative gas adsorption in DUT-49
open: Predict how finite-crystal size, shape, and surface termination suppress negative gas adsorption in DUT-49, including expelled-gas quantity and phase coexistence. Transfer independently determined microscopic parameters into a finite-crystal nucleation and propagation model.
status: Size-dependent pressure amplification was measured in 2018. By 2024, simulations described bulk thermodynamics and some finite MOF crystallites, while chemically accurate external surfaces and quantitative transfer between length scales remained explicit gaps.
why: It would determine whether pressure amplification survives particle manufacture and miniaturization.
key_works: S. Krause et al. (2018), “The effect of crystallite size on pressure amplification in switchable porous solids,” [DOI:10.1038/s41467-018-03979-2](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-018-03979-2); J. D. Evans and F.-X. Coudert (2024), “Challenges and Opportunities of Molecular Simulations for Negative Gas Adsorption,” [DOI:10.1021/accountsmr.4c00071](https://doi.org/10.1021/accountsmr.4c00071).

title: Fluoride-free silanol repair for zeolite-based microporous water
open: Remove internal silanol defects from silicalite particles while preserving external functionalization and micropore architecture through a fluoride-free treatment. Retain dry-reference oxygen capacity after aqueous dispersion and repeated cycling without generating substantial larger pores.
status: Calvin and colleagues already restored approximately full oxygen capacity using NH₄F treatment in 2026. Their stated limitations include hazardous reagents, external-surface changes, and larger-pore formation; an equally effective, selective alternative remains open.
why: It would improve aqueous gas carriers while preserving colloidal design and pore selectivity.
key_works: J. J. Calvin et al. (2026), “The Impact of Silanol Defects on the Properties of Zeolite-Based Microporous Water,” [DOI:10.1021/acs.jpcc.5c08300](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.jpcc.5c08300).

title: Bond-exchange pathway behind room-temperature oxygen scrambling in zeosils
open: Identify the site-specific bond-breaking and reformation pathways allowing room-temperature water to exchange oxygen with pure-silica zeolite frameworks. Predict when exchange remains reversible and when it produces persistent defects or degradation.
status: Kelly and colleagues observed framework isotope exchange in 2026 using NMR and neutron diffraction. Brako-Amoafo’s 2026 thesis reports topology- and silanol-dependent enrichment and improved dynamic NMR modeling, while identifying incomplete mechanistic understanding and extension to complex environments as remaining work.
why: It would change predictions of zeolite lifetime and water-mediated catalytic reconstruction.
key_works: N. L. Kelly et al. (2026), “Room-Temperature Framework Oxygen Isotope Exchange during Interaction of Water with Hydrophilic Pure-Silica Zeolites …,” [DOI:10.1021/jacs.5c23024](https://doi.org/10.1021/jacs.5c23024); D. Brako-Amoafo (2026), “Exploring zeolite-water interactions using a combined experimental-theoretical NMR approach,” PhD thesis, [DOI:10.17630/sta/1667](https://doi.org/10.17630/sta/1667).

title: Experimental vacancy-enabled escape from Y–Y proton traps in BaZrO₃
open: Test whether an oxygen vacancy between neighboring yttrium dopants permits protons to escape deep traps in partially hydrated BaZrO₃. Resolve mobility and proton concentration separately and determine whether the local mechanism forms a macroscopic conducting network.
status: Patel and colleagues predicted vacancy-position-dependent escape in September 2026 using a charge-aware foundation potential and migration calculations. Direct verification of the proposed local configuration and its conductivity benefit remains open.
why: Incomplete hydration could become a controllable transport variable rather than simply a conductivity penalty.
key_works: S. Patel et al. (2026), “Unraveling vacancy-modulated proton transport beyond trapping in partially hydrated Y-doped BaZrO3 using a charge-aware foundation potential,” [DOI:10.1038/s44456-026-00013-5](https://doi.org/10.1038/s44456-026-00013-5).

title: Observing lithium cage opening in MMIM–PF₆ plastic crystals
open: Measure lithium hopping and local molecular rearrangements together in lithium-doped dimethylimidazolium hexafluorophosphate plastic crystals. Identify which cage-breaking event enables a hop and whether lithium remains dynamically decoupled from matrix rotation across composition and temperature.
status: Park, Saito, and Sung’s 2026 hop-function analysis distinguishes rotational coupling of matrix ions from lithium transport. A direct experimental test of the predicted causal sequence remains needed; molecular rotation by itself does not identify the rate-limiting rearrangement.
why: It would distinguish conductivity-enhancing disorder from molecular motion that contributes little to ion transport.
key_works: H. Park, S. Saito, and B. J. Sung (2026), “Beyond the Paddle-Wheel Mechanism: Hop Function Analysis of Ion Transport in Organic Ionic Plastic Crystals,” [DOI:10.1021/jacs.6c04713](https://doi.org/10.1021/jacs.6c04713).

title: Joint explanation of giant in-plane permittivity and conductivity in confined water
open: Build a microscopic model reproducing both the dielectric response and electrical conductivity of water confined to approximately 1–2 nm. Predict thickness, frequency, and isotope dependences that distinguish proton defects, hydrogen-bond correlations, and interfacial polarization.
status: Wang and colleagues measured in-plane relative permittivity of order 10³ and conductivity of a few S m⁻¹ in 2025. These observations establish the phenomena; a jointly validated microscopic account of both responses remains the target.
why: It would provide reliable constitutive laws for nanofluidic channels and confined electrochemistry.
key_works: R. Wang et al. (2025), “In-plane dielectric constant and conductivity of confined water,” [DOI:10.1038/s41586-025-09558-y](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-025-09558-y); [arXiv:2407.21538](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.21538).

title: Why anomalous underscreening depends on probe size and waiting time
open: Explain why concentrated-electrolyte force measurements can produce apparent screening lengths differing from bulk optical measurements. Predict the effects of probe curvature, equilibration time, and approach speed, separating equilibrium screening from slowly relaxing interfacial structures.
status: Optical second-harmonic scattering in 2025 supported ordinary asymptotic underscreening. A September 2026 preprint reproduced anomalously long LaCl₃ force decay with AFM using larger probes, longer waiting, and slower approach, sharpening the question around geometry and relaxation.
why: It would establish which screening laws apply to concentrated electrochemical interfaces.
key_works: F. Rondepierre, P.-F. Brevet, and J. Duboisset (2025), “Asymptotic Underscreening in Concentrated Electrolytes Measured by Optical Second Harmonic Scattering of Water,” [DOI:10.1021/acs.jpclett.5c00037](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.jpclett.5c00037); T. Tilger et al. (2026), “Anomalously Large Screening Lengths in Highly Concentrated Electrolytes: A Matter of Experimental Conditions,” [arXiv:2603.08326v2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.08326v2).

title: Cell-free assembly of cable bacteria’s nickel–bis(dithiolene) nanoribbons
open: Reconstitute the identified nickel-organic ribbon architecture outside cable bacteria, including stacking and its stabilizing protein environment. Demonstrate long-range conductivity approaching native fibers and identify the biochemical steps controlling assembly.
status: Meysman and colleagues identified a nickel–bis(dithiolene)-based conductive architecture in 2026; native fibers can reach conductivities around 500 S cm⁻¹. This structure discovery narrows the remaining challenge to controlled synthesis and reconstitution.
why: It could provide a reproducible route to highly conductive biological electronics.
key_works: F. J. R. Meysman et al. (2026), “Highly efficient long-range conduction through a biosynthetic nickel-organic framework,” [DOI:10.1038/s41467-026-76989-0](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-76989-0).

title: A 100-second molecular magnetic memory at 100 K
open: Demonstrate a single-molecule magnet with zero-field relaxation time of at least 100 seconds at 100 K and useful remanence. This proposed milestone requires suppression of low-energy relaxation channels alongside a large reversal barrier.
status: A dysprosium amide–alkene complex achieved soft hysteresis up to 100 K in 2025. The authors’ August 2026 study emphasizes that this complex still relaxes within 100 seconds even at 2 K; newer cyclopentadienyl–amide magnets reach approximately 40 K under the 100-second blocking criterion.
why: It would connect elevated-temperature molecular magnetism with a concrete memory-retention specification.
key_works: J. Emerson-King et al. (2025), “Soft magnetic hysteresis in a dysprosium amide–alkene complex up to 100 kelvin,” [DOI:10.1038/s41586-025-09138-0](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-025-09138-0); J. Emerson-King et al. (2026), “Axial dysprosium cyclopentadienyl-amide single-molecule magnets with hysteresis up to 92 kelvin,” [DOI:10.1038/s41467-026-77104-z](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-77104-z).

title: Rapid bulk tetrataenite synthesis after the phosphorus-casting retraction
open: Produce a high-volume-fraction, well-ordered L1₀ FeNi bulk magnet on practical manufacturing timescales. Establish ordering and magnetic properties independently while excluding phosphide diffraction and surface-oxidation artifacts.
status: The 2022 rapid-casting claim was retracted; Houghton and colleagues’ 2025 reinterpretation found no supporting evidence for tetrataenite in those castings. Other work reported local ordering up to approximately 22 vol% after six weeks, leaving rapid extensive bulk ordering unresolved.
why: It would enable an iron–nickel permanent-magnet route with reduced rare-earth dependence.
key_works: O. S. Houghton et al. (2025), “Reinterpretation of Report of Tetrataenite in Bulk Alloy Castings,” [DOI:10.1002/advs.202408796](https://doi.org/10.1002/advs.202408796); L. H. Lewis et al. (2024), “Accelerating Nature: Induced Atomic Order in Equiatomic FeNi,” [DOI:10.1002/advs.202302696](https://doi.org/10.1002/advs.202302696).

title: Separating intrinsic Fe₁₆N₂ magnetization from interface enhancement
open: Establish the bulk-limit saturation magnetization of stoichiometric, well-ordered α″-Fe₁₆N₂, separating strain, nitrogen deficiency, interfaces, and minority phases. Reconcile absolute magnetometry with site- and depth-resolved moments.
status: The giant-moment controversy dates to the 1970s. A 2025 synthesis obtained approximately 97 wt% α″-Fe₁₆N₂ powder with 165 emu g⁻¹ magnetization; a 2026 report available online locates enhanced magnetization near film interfaces using neutron reflectometry.
why: It would establish which magnetization gains survive translation from films to bulk magnets.
key_works: T. Tsuchida et al. (2025), “Synthetic route for high-yield α″-Fe16N2 submicron-sized powder using CaH2 drying agent,” [DOI:10.1039/D4MA00961D](https://doi.org/10.1039/D4MA00961D); X. Hang et al. (2026), “Interfacial magnetization enhancement and the perpendicularly magnetized component in Fe16N2 thin films,” [DOI:10.1016/j.jmmm.2026.174468](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jmmm.2026.174468).

title: Experimental realization of the predicted tetragonal ZnFe magnet
open: Synthesize the particular tetragonal ZnFe phase proposed by computational screening and establish its structural stability and magnetic properties. Test the predicted combination of magnetization above 1 T, anisotropy above 0.5 MJ m⁻³, and Curie temperature above 1,200 K.
status: Jami, Bhagat, and Bhattacharya’s 2025 journal paper reports these predictions together with phonon and elastic stability calculations. Experimental realization remains open, and negative formation enthalpy alone does not establish stability against all competing phases.
why: It would test a specific rare-earth-free magnet candidate and the screening criteria that selected it.
key_works: J. Jami, N. Bhagat, and A. Bhattacharya (2025), “Data-driven high-throughput search for the accelerated discovery of rare-earth-free permanent magnets,” [DOI:10.1103/tppf-n3kb](https://doi.org/10.1103/tppf-n3kb); [arXiv:2507.01849](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.01849).

title: One-cycle lanmodulin separation of praseodymium from neodymium
open: Engineer an immobilized lanmodulin process separating Pr(III) from Nd(III) at useful loading, with high purity and recovery in one regeneration cycle. Establish performance on realistic mixed-metal feeds and retention of selectivity after reuse.
status: Diep and colleagues screened 621 lanmodulin orthologs in 2026 and demonstrated Pr/La separation above 99.9 mol% purity with 83% yield. Adjacent Tb/Dy separation was also achieved in 2026; Pr/Nd remains an explicit biological-separation development target.
why: It could reduce chemical separation stages for demanding rare-earth products.
key_works: P. Diep et al. (2026), “A family portrait of lanmodulin selectivity for enhanced rare-earth separations,” [DOI:10.1038/s41589-026-02176-3](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41589-026-02176-3); Ames National Laboratory, [“CMI Project 3.1.2: Biological separation of energy-critical rare earth elements”](https://www.ameslab.gov/cmi/cmi-project-biological-separation-of-energy-critical-rare-earth-elements).

title: Hydroxyl accessibility versus irreversible wood mechanosorption
open: Determine which stress-induced changes in cellulose hydroxyl accessibility cause reversible extra water uptake and which cause persistent interfibrillar slip. Predict residual strain and recovery from independently measured accessibility, spacing, and relaxation times.
status: Sun and colleagues’ 2026 measurements link tensile stress to enhanced sorption without corresponding crystalline-lattice expansion. A September 2026 stick–slip model reproduces cyclic responses through fitted parameters; connecting its slip thresholds to the measured molecular changes remains open.
why: It would improve predictions of permanent timber and paper distortion under moisture cycling.
key_works: F. Sun et al. (2026), “Tensile Stress Enhances Moisture Sorption by Increasing Cellulose Hydroxyl Accessibility in Wood Cell Walls,” [DOI:10.1021/acs.biomac.6c01305](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.biomac.6c01305); J. O. Amando de Barros and F. K. Wittel (2026), “The role of moisture gradients and time scales in wood mechanosorption,” [DOI:10.1007/s00226-026-01802-6](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00226-026-01802-6).

title: Molecular origin of locked compressive maturation stress in conifer wood
open: Establish how galactan, xylan, lignin, and bound water generate and retain compressive maturation stress. Manipulate wall chemistry or dehydration at matched microfibril angle and predict stress sign and magnitude from the resulting architecture.
status: Cresswell and colleagues’ 2025 study found reduced water content, porosity, and molecular mobility in compression wood, with disordered galactan. Their proposed combination of high microfibril angle, lignification, and dehydration does not yet apportion causal stress generation among those components.
why: It would explain timber warping and supply principles for prestressed plant-derived composites.
key_works: R. Cresswell et al. (2025), “The molecular architecture distinctions between compression, opposite and normal wood of Pinus radiata,” [DOI:10.3389/fpls.2025.1576928](https://doi.org/10.3389/fpls.2025.1576928).

title: Needle-punch reversal between permeability and capillary uptake
open: Predict when increased needle punching reduces a nonwoven’s saturated permeability yet increases through-thickness liquid uptake under partial saturation. Derive the law from three-dimensional pillar geometry and evolving saturation across compression and wetting histories.
status: Wegele and colleagues imaged multiphase distributions under load in 2024 and time-resolved transport in 2026. The results expose competing densification and out-of-plane pathway effects; transferable transport prediction across architectures remains beyond these observations.
why: It would connect manufacturing settings to absorbent textile, filter, and separator performance.
key_works: P. Wegele, T. Rosén, and D. Söderberg (2024), “Multiphase distribution in partly saturated hierarchical nonwoven fibre networks under applied load using X-ray computed tomography,” [DOI:10.1007/s00348-024-03869-y](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00348-024-03869-y); P. Wegele et al. (2026), “Time-resolved X-ray radiography of through-thickness liquid transport in partly saturated needle-punched nonwovens,” [DOI:10.1007/s00348-026-04201-6](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00348-026-04201-6).

title: Thickness and chemistry of lignin welds in hot-pressed paper
open: Measure the thickness, interpenetration, and chemistry of load-bearing lignin junctions after hot pressing. Separate polymer flow and interdiffusion from chemical bonding, then predict wet strength from measured junction properties.
status: Mattsson and colleagues’ 2026 tomography study examined pressing at 200 °C and 3.5 MPa for 0.05–30 seconds. Longer pressing improved wet mechanical response; the authors explicitly identify molecular bonding mechanisms and lignin-interface thickness as future work.
why: It would support water-resistant paper with controlled strength and lower processing severity.
key_works: A. Mattsson, A. Miettinen, T. Joelsson, G. Pettersson, P. Engstrand, and J. A. Ketoja (2026), “Stress-strain behavior and microstructural evolution of hot-pressed paper webs revealed by x-ray tomography,” [DOI:10.15376/biores.21.2.3718-3732](https://doi.org/10.15376/biores.21.2.3718-3732).

title: Adhesion-aware coarsening law for moderately wet foams
open: Predict bubble-size distributions and coarsening rates from independently measured interbubble adhesion, film geometry, and gas permeability. Include bubbles that lose contact with their neighbors without hiding adhesion effects inside an effective fitted permeability.
status: Requier and colleagues’ 2025 microgravity experiments show chemistry-dependent coarsening that film permeability alone cannot explain. Morgan and Cox’s 2026 mean-field model describes nonadhesive wet foams but reports discrepancies associated with omitted noncontacting bubbles; combining adhesion and contact loss remains open.
why: Foam lifetime and pore-size evolution could be predicted from formulation.
key_works: A. Requier et al. (2025), “Wet foam coarsening: More than film permeability,” [DOI:10.1016/j.jcis.2025.137825](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jcis.2025.137825); J. Morgan and S. Cox (2026), “Mean-field model for the bubble size distribution in coarsening wet foams,” [DOI:10.1039/D5SM01007A](https://doi.org/10.1039/D5SM01007A).

title: Direct test of through-thickness surfactant gradients before film rupture
open: Resolve vertical surfactant concentration profiles while a supported film thins and ruptures. Test whether measured diffusion and adsorption kinetics explain the predicted failure of vertically averaged descriptions.
status: Yang, Kumar, and Dutcher’s 2025 calculations predict strong gradients when diffusion lags advection or adsorption. Reduced adsorption generates stabilizing Marangoni stresses, causing averaged models to underestimate rupture time; simultaneous concentration, coverage, and rupture measurements remain the discriminating test.
why: It would identify when inexpensive thin-film models can reliably predict coating failure.
key_works: S. Yang, S. Kumar, and C. S. Dutcher (2025), “Vertical concentration gradients of soluble surfactants in the rupture of thin liquid films,” [DOI:10.1016/j.jcis.2025.01.234](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jcis.2025.01.234).

title: Lifetime law for transient partial coalescence of particle-filled droplets
open: Predict how many collisions or how much accumulated shear erase irregular shapes created by partial coalescence of particle-filled droplets. Distinguish permanent arrest from long-lived transients using particle loading, internal yielding, and shear history.
status: Vaswani and Velankar’s 2025 experiments used droplets containing more than 50 vol% silica. Partial coalescence followed a shear-rate reduction, but repeated collisions eventually restored smoother shapes; a predictive arrest-versus-relaxation boundary remains missing.
why: It would distinguish durable emulsion structures from temporary processing states.
key_works: J. Vaswani and S. S. Velankar (2025), “Particle-Filled Emulsion Drops Show Flow-Induced Partial Coalescence, but Only Transiently,” [DOI:10.1021/acs.iecr.5c02170](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.iecr.5c02170).

title: Local-thinning threshold for electrocoalescence of asphaltene-armored droplets
open: Predict the local thinning or defective-patch population required for electric-field rupture of an asphaltene-stabilized film. Transfer the criterion from planar films to curved droplet populations using measured interfacial rheology, adsorption, and field waveform.
status: Alicke, Jaensson, and Vermant’s 2025 experiments show that interfacial elasticity can preserve thick films despite applied fields. Demulsifiers restore electrical effectiveness through heterogeneous thinning; the quantitative link from patch structure to population-level coalescence probability remains open.
why: It would reduce empirical chemical dosing and electrical energy use in oil–water separation.
key_works: A. Alicke, N. O. Jaensson, and J. Vermant (2025), “Mechanistic Insights into Emulsion Destabilization by Electric Fields,” [DOI:10.1021/acs.langmuir.5c02307](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.langmuir.5c02307).

title: Boundary slip behind anomalous wet-granular strength curves
open: Determine when added liquid makes a granular material appear weaker because deformation moves to the wall rather than because bulk cohesion decreases. Predict the wall-slip–bulk-yield crossover from roughness, particle size, liquid morphology, and loading.
status: Chang and colleagues’ 2025 glass-bead experiments found shear stress decreasing with initial wetting and rising sharply near saturation. Competing boundary and bulk deformation explain the anomaly qualitatively; a transferable criterion separating their contributions remains open.
why: It would prevent apparatus-specific slip from being mistaken for a material strength law.
key_works: C. Chang, K. Ono, W. H. Schulz, and T. Yamaguchi (2025), “Anomalous Shear Stress Variation in Wet Granular Medium: Implications for Landslide Lateral Faults,” [DOI:10.1029/2024GL113816](https://doi.org/10.1029/2024GL113816).

title: Rate-dependent bridge rupture in viscous continuous phases
open: Measure a capillary-bridge rupture law spanning separation rate, viscosity ratio, wettability, and bridge volume for particles immersed in a viscous outer liquid. Transfer that law to network strength and yield strain under different mixing histories.
status: Haessig and colleagues’ 2025 experiments found that higher continuous-phase viscosity weakened capillary suspensions and reduced connectivity. Two-particle simulations associated higher viscosity with rupture at shorter separation; quantitative single-bridge experimental validation remains the missing link.
why: It would explain why changing a carrier liquid can undermine an otherwise unchanged capillary gel.
key_works: C. Haessig, J. Landman, E. Scholten, and A. Jarray (2025), “How bulk liquid viscosity shapes capillary suspensions,” [DOI:10.1016/j.jcis.2024.09.021](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jcis.2024.09.021).

title: Water-reservoir replenishment of bridges between protein particles
open: Measure water exchange between absorbing protein-particle interiors and external capillary bridges during deformation. Determine whether replenishment explains increased critical strain and recovery, independently of swelling, protein adhesion, and bridge-to-bridge redistribution.
status: Feichtinger and colleagues’ 2026 comparison found similar maximum strengths for protein and silica capillary gels but different deformation tolerance. Additional water increased critical strain and recovery; an internal-reservoir mechanism was proposed, while the required water flux during bridge extension remains unmeasured.
why: It would make food-grade capillary gels designable through particle porosity and hydration kinetics.
key_works: A. Feichtinger, G. Giménez-Ribes, J. Landman, and E. Scholten (2026), “The rheological behavior of oil-continuous capillary suspensions prepared with water-absorbing protein particles,” [DOI:10.1016/j.foodhyd.2025.111782](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.foodhyd.2025.111782).

title: Nonmicellar DMPE templating of cocoa-butter Form V
open: Identify the molecular surface structure by which dimyristoylphosphoethanolamine selects cocoa-butter Form V during cooling. Determine the headgroup arrangement and triacylglycerol adsorption geometry responsible for its additive specificity.
status: Stobbs and colleagues achieved suitable crystallization with 0.1 wt% DMPE under simple cooling without shear in 2025. Neutron scattering found no DMPE micelles, and infrared measurements did not establish a strong specific interaction; successful templating therefore precedes a resolved molecular mechanism.
why: It would make low-energy tempering transferable across variable cocoa-butter supplies and alternative fats.
key_works: J. A. Stobbs et al. (2025), “Dimyristoylphosphoethanolamine Addition During Chocolate Manufacture Promotes Proper Tempering under Simple Cooling Conditions without Shear,” [DOI:10.1021/acs.cgd.5c00575](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.cgd.5c00575).

title: Molecular trigger of two-mode corn-starch retrogradation
open: Identify the molecular event separating short- and long-term retrogradation in refrigerated corn-starch gels. Predict crossover time from amylose/amylopectin architecture, water state, and thermal history, distinguishing crystallization from solvent expulsion and stiffening.
status: Ninomiya and colleagues resolved two kinetic regimes in 2025, crossing near five days under their storage conditions. Separate Avrami fits describe the intervals; explaining the molecular switch is a follow-up problem inferred from the gap between those fitted regimes and structural mechanisms.
why: It would enable rational control of staling, texture, and water loss.
key_works: K. Ninomiya et al. (2025), “Analysis of Short- and Long-Term Two-Mode Retrogradation of Corn Starch During Refrigerated Storage,” [DOI:10.1002/cche.10883](https://doi.org/10.1002/cche.10883).

title: Mesoscopic origin of nonlinear scaling near the gluten gel point
open: Identify structures responsible for self-similar stress overshoots and post-cessation power-law relaxation in near-critical gluten gels. Distinguish cluster rearrangement from bond exchange and predict scaling across gelation state and shear history.
status: Louhichi and colleagues established the nonlinear scaling in 2024 and found that relaxation after flow cessation depends on preceding shear rate. They proposed changing mesoscopic dynamics, but the responsible structures were not directly resolved.
why: It would connect plant-protein formulation to processing memory and recovery.
key_works: A. Louhichi, M.-H. Morel, L. Ramos, and A. Banc (2024), “Scaling Properties of Gelling Systems in Nonlinear Shear Experiments,” [DOI:10.1021/acsmacrolett.4c00121](https://doi.org/10.1021/acsmacrolett.4c00121); [arXiv:2407.12367](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.12367).

title: Causal role of LRR connectors in reversible velvet-worm fibers
open: Demonstrate whether conserved leucine-rich-repeat proteins act as reversible connectors in velvet-worm slime’s fluid-to-fiber transition. Reconstitute the mixture and disrupt predicted binding surfaces to test assembly, mechanical performance, and recovery in water.
status: Hu, Baer, and colleagues identified conserved LRR proteins in 2025. Structural predictions suggest horseshoe-shaped dimers binding domains of larger slime proteins; these provide mutation targets, while causal reconstruction of the material transition remains open.
why: It could enable protein fibers and adhesives that disassemble and reprocess in water.
key_works: Z. Hu, A. Baer, et al. (2025), “Conserved leucine-rich repeat proteins in the adhesive projectile slime of velvet worms,” [DOI:10.1073/pnas.2416282122](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2416282122).

title: Identity of the mussel’s DOPA-rich vanadium-storage carrier
open: Identify and sequence the DOPA-rich protein storing vanadium in mussel-foot metal-storage particles. Determine binding stoichiometry, oxidation-state control, and transfer kinetics to byssal proteins, including prevention of premature crosslinking.
status: Jee and colleagues’ 2024 spectroscopy and calculations constrain vanadium uptake and storage. The study explicitly states that the DOPA-containing storage protein remains unidentified, preventing molecular reconstitution of this processing intermediate.
why: It would explain how biological fabrication separates metal acquisition, storage, and triggered curing.
key_works: S. Jee, M. Rammal, T. Priemel, D. S. Bohle, and M. J. Harrington (2024), “Vanadium uptake and storage in the fabrication and function of mussel byssus,” [DOI:10.1039/D4NJ02546F](https://doi.org/10.1039/D4NJ02546F).

title: Molecular and geometrical origin of hagfish-skein peeling resistance
open: Determine how much hagfish-skein unwinding resistance comes from molecular adhesive contacts and how much from coil geometry. Identify the adhesive and derive a salt- and rate-dependent peeling law predicting discrete force barriers.
status: Hossain and colleagues directly measured peeling forces in 2025, with a typical value near 6.8 nN, and showed that mucus is not required to initiate unwinding. The molecular identity and spatial distribution of the adhesive barriers remain unresolved.
why: It would enable compactly stored fibers that deploy rapidly under controlled flow.
key_works: M. T. Hossain et al. (2025), “Physics of unravelling and micromechanics of hagfish threads,” [DOI:10.1098/rsif.2025.0503](https://doi.org/10.1098/rsif.2025.0503); [arXiv:2506.07243](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.07243).

title: Cavitation-controlled size limit for ambient-dried silica monoliths
open: Determine when internal solvent cavitation relieves silica-aerogel drying stresses and when spatially heterogeneous cavitation promotes damage. Predict maximum crack-free monolith size and drying schedules from measured stiffening, transport, cavitation, and fracture properties.
status: Gonthier and colleagues’ 2024 tomography and scattering experiments detected vapor formation before maximum shrinkage, beginning near a 50% reduction in pore volume. The event is observed; the coupled nucleation, stress-redistribution, and size-scaling law remains unresolved.
why: Controlled cavitation could expand production of large aerogel components by ambient-pressure drying.
key_works: J. Gonthier, E. Scoppola, T. Rilling, A. Gurlo, P. Fratzl, and W. Wagermaier (2024), “Solvent Cavitation during Ambient Pressure Drying of Silica Aerogels,” [DOI:10.1021/acs.langmuir.4c00497](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.langmuir.4c00497).

title: Boron-carbide shock failure beyond reversible C–B–C chain bending
open: Determine which combination of deviatoric stress, strain rate, carbon occupancy, and chain defects converts crystalline boron carbide into irreversible amorphous shear bands. Connect the loss of dynamic strength to a measured atomic transformation and explain why quasihydrostatic chain bending can remain reversible.
status: A 2026 experiment supplied a stringent constraint on longstanding chain-collapse explanations: approximately B₁₃C₂ transformed from hR45 to mC60 between 78(2) and 90(3) GPa, bending C–B–C chains from 180° to 126.5(8)°, without amorphization. Slow decompression recovered the original phase; the connection to lower-pressure shock failure remains unresolved, with composition and loading conditions complicating comparison.
why: This would identify bonding configurations that improve impact resistance, beyond increasing quasistatic hardness.
key_works: Akun Liang et al. (2026), “High-pressure formation and characterization of a boron carbide polymorph featuring bent C–B–C chains,” *Physical Review B* 113, 104108, [DOI:10.1103/v5kf-svcz](https://doi.org/10.1103/v5kf-svcz).

title: A synthesis-path map for the competing structures called γ-alumina
open: Establish which γ-Al₂O₃ cation arrangements are selected by hydroxide dehydration, alloy oxidation, and subsequent annealing, and determine the kinetic paths between them. Predict preparation-dependent tetrahedral occupancy and vacancy ordering while reproducing NMR and diffraction on the same specimens.
status: Legrady et al. supported predominantly spinel-site Al and alternating tetrahedral/octahedral vacancy chains in 2025; Yang et al. proposed a lower-energy nonspinel model that year. Zuo et al. directly resolved octahedral-only Al in NiAl-oxidation-derived material in August 2026. A predictive preparation-to-structure map is the remaining problem inferred from these preparation-specific results.
why: Catalytic-site, transport, and thermal-stability predictions require the structure of the material actually produced.
key_works: M. B. Legrady, D. M. Dawson, P. B. Webb, and S. E. Ashbrook (2025), “Insight into the atomic-level structure of γ-alumina using a multinuclear NMR crystallographic approach,” [DOI:10.1039/D5SC01198A](https://doi.org/10.1039/D5SC01198A); X. Yang, C. Shang, and Z.-P. Liu (2025), “Resolving the atomic structure of γ-alumina: a non-spinel phase with a distorted anion lattice and three adjacent long channels,” [DOI:10.1039/D5TA01715G](https://doi.org/10.1039/D5TA01715G); S. Zuo et al. (2026), “Resolving the atomic structure of γ-alumina: Spinel framework with octahedral-only aluminum,” [DOI:10.1103/3byh-tzbz](https://doi.org/10.1103/3byh-tzbz).

title: Unrefined Co–B modulation in incommensurate Mg₁₊εCo₄B₄
open: Determine the positional modulation of the Co–B framework caused by its mismatch with the magnesium sublattice. Obtain a quantitative superspace displacement model consistent with electron-diffraction satellites and bulk scattering.
status: Oftedahl et al. established the compound and a powder-derived superspace model in December 2025. Additional electron-diffraction satellites indicated Co–B modulation that could not be refined from the available neutron and X-ray data; calculations on a 5:4 approximant do not determine that experimental modulation.
why: The actual modulation is needed to understand how the boride framework accommodates an incommensurate guest lattice and to test calculated stability and transport.
key_works: Paul Oftedahl et al. (2025), “Higher Dimensionality in the Mg–Co–B System: Synthesis and Structure of Incommensurate Composite Mg₁₊εCo₄B₄,” *JACS* 147, 47508–47522, [DOI:10.1021/jacs.5c16523](https://doi.org/10.1021/jacs.5c16523).

title: Chemical ordering of recovered cubic BC₂N
open: Determine the B/C/N occupation pattern in recovered cubic BC₂N, including whether apparently cubic specimens contain an ordered network, chemical disorder, or nanoscale intergrowths. The assignment must jointly explain chemical contrast, diffuse scattering, and mechanical properties.
status: Synthesis preceded unambiguous atomic assignment by decades. Rao et al.’s 2024 paper, published online in 2023, explicitly identified the elusive experimental structure as a limitation while calculating sharply different bonding and phonon transport in candidate polymorphs. Discriminating experimental assignment remains the target.
why: A verified structure is necessary to determine which combination of hardness, heat conduction, and dopant incorporation this material can support.
key_works: Y. Rao, Y. Wu, C. Y. Zhao, and S. Ju (2024), “Heterogeneous C–C bonding induced anomalous phonon transport in superhard BC₂N polymorphs,” *Acta Materialia* 262, 119454, [DOI:10.1016/j.actamat.2023.119454](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.actamat.2023.119454).

title: Freestanding boroxol B₂O₃ monolayers
open: Release a crystalline boroxol-network B₂O₃ monolayer from its growth substrate and determine whether its predicted rippled state survives as an intact suspended membrane. Measure corrugation and elasticity while separating intrinsic rippling from transfer damage.
status: Zio et al. synthesized the supported two-dimensional polymorph in 2025. Zhang et al. predicted in 2026 that a flat freestanding sheet is dynamically unstable but a rippled configuration is stable, lowering calculated energy by approximately 8 meV per B₂O₃ unit. Experimental release and validation remain the follow-up implied by these results.
why: This would establish a chemically distinct oxide membrane and test stabilization of atomically thin networks by ring topology.
key_works: T. Zio et al. (2025), “Two-dimensional diboron trioxide crystal composed by boroxol groups,” *Science* 390, 95–99, [institutional record](https://iris.cnr.it/handle/20.500.14243/578781); X. Zhang, Y. Lei, Y. Zhang, and C. He (2026), “Rippling-induced stabilization and property modulation in freestanding two-dimensional B₂O₃,” [DOI:10.1063/5.0324393](https://doi.org/10.1063/5.0324393).

title: An alteration-free Curie temperature for greigite
open: Determine greigite’s intrinsic Curie temperature while demonstrating that Fe₃S₄ remains the magnetic phase throughout the measurement. Resolve whether reported transitions belong to greigite or thermally generated products, including compositional dependence.
status: Wang et al. reported approximately 677 K in 2010. Nevertheless, Roberts’s *Mineral Magnetism* chapter, published online in January 2026, still treats the intrinsic value as unknown because greigite commonly alters around 220–350 °C before the anticipated transition. Reconciling the positive report with phase-resolved thermal stability is the specific gap.
why: The answer affects sedimentary magnetic records and assessments of sulfide magnetic materials.
key_works: J. Wang, S.-H. Cao, W. Wu, and G.-M. Zhao (2010), “The Curie temperature and exchange energy between two sublattices in half-metallic greigite Fe₃S₄,” [arXiv:1012.2364](https://arxiv.org/abs/1012.2364); A. P. Roberts (2026 online), “The Iron Sulphides: Greigite,” *Mineral Magnetism*, [DOI:10.1017/9781108935630.016](https://doi.org/10.1017/9781108935630.016).

title: The predicted Besnus-like transition of 6C pyrrhotite
open: Establish whether phase-pure antiferromagnetic 6C pyrrhotite undergoes the proposed low-temperature symmetry-lowering transition. Measure its order parameter and atomic displacements, or identify energetic and compositional constraints that prevent the symmetry-allowed transition.
status: Haines et al.’s analysis, first posted in 2019, predicted a Besnus-like transition specifically in 6C pyrrhotite, distinct from the familiar 4C transition and proposed spin-flop behavior of 3C/5C. The phase-specific experimental test remains the outstanding target; symmetry analysis alone does not establish that a transition occurs.
why: It would test coupling between vacancy order and magnetic symmetry and improve low-temperature mineral identification.
key_works: C. R. S. Haines, C. J. Howard, R. J. Harrison, and M. A. Carpenter (2019/2020), “Group-theoretical analysis of structural instability, vacancy ordering and magnetic transitions in the system troilite (FeS)–pyrrhotite (Fe₁₋ₓS),” [arXiv:1901.04756](https://arxiv.org/abs/1901.04756), [DOI:10.1107/S2052520619014197](https://doi.org/10.1107/S2052520619014197).

title: Completing dolomite cation ordering at low temperature
open: Reproduce conversion of disordered Ca–Mg carbonate into demonstrably ordered dolomite at low temperature and determine the time-dependent ordering mechanism. Use ordering-sensitive diffraction to distinguish the product from protodolomite and mixed carbonates.
status: Ordering remains a separate component of the historical dolomite problem. Zhang et al. emphasized in 2026 that ambient laboratory products still fail to reproduce diagnostic ordering reflections, while isotope evidence from Neogene dolomites supported recrystallization-associated ordering at inferred temperatures of 16–32 °C. A reproducible laboratory pathway and kinetic law remain missing.
why: This would distinguish original crystallization conditions from later reorganization in dolomite-based environmental records.
key_works: P. Zhang, K.-J. Huang, D. Feng, L. Ma, W. Xu, and W. Yan (2026), “Ancient massive dolomites: The present is the key to the past,” *Sedimentary Geology* 498, 107080, [DOI:10.1016/j.sedgeo.2026.107080](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.sedgeo.2026.107080).

title: Hydrogen solubility and solute trapping in laser-welded AlSi10Mg
open: Measure hydrogen solubility in the relevant solid and liquid states of AlSi10Mg and determine nonequilibrium partitioning during laser-weld solidification. Predict when hydrogen remains trapped and when it nucleates interdendritic gas pores.
status: Kramer et al. explicitly identified this alloy’s hydrogen solubility as unknown in January 2026. In-process drying reduced hydrogen by approximately 25% and prevented weld porosity, although pure-aluminum equilibrium estimates still implied supersaturation; 50 kHz X-ray imaging localized pore formation near the solidification front. The empirical remedy leaves alloy-specific thermodynamic and kinetic data missing.
why: Such data would replace alloy-inappropriate assumptions with transferable welding limits.
key_works: S. Kramer et al. (2026), “Investigation of the formation and reduction of hydrogen porosity during laser welding of additively manufactured AlSi10Mg parts,” [DOI:10.1007/s00170-025-17198-9](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00170-025-17198-9).

title: Matrix-solute-controlled incubation of tin pest
open: Predict distributions of β-Sn-to-α-Sn incubation times from solute concentrations inside the tin matrix, residual stress, and second-phase partitioning. Explain why nominally similar alloys transform after very different delays and establish conditions supporting long service-life predictions.
status: Michalcová et al. followed five historical-organ-pipe analogues for up to 100 days in 2026. Retained stress accelerated transformation, and substantial bulk Pb did not guarantee protection when alloy constituents partitioned into separate phases. Proposed low-level Zn segregation could not be resolved by EDS; the work leaves matrix chemistry and long-latency prediction incompletely connected.
why: This would improve preservation of tin artifacts and cold-storage reliability of tin-rich electronics.
key_works: A. Michalcová, Š. Msallamová, E. Gavel, D. Fink, and P. Jánošíková (2026), “Influence of Low Zn Concentrations on Behavior of Historical Organ Pipes and Its Model Analogs,” [DOI:10.3390/met16020241](https://doi.org/10.3390/met16020241); D. Hillman, R. Wilcoxon, and A. Wieland (2022), “An Examination of the Tin Pest Phenomenon Over a 10-Year Period,” *Journal of Electronic Materials* 51, 6492–6502; University of Maryland CALCE, [“Tin Pests”](https://calce.umd.edu/tin-pests).

title: Direct electron-wind force measurements on aluminum dislocations
open: Measure the current-induced force on identified edge dislocations in aluminum and test its predicted magnitude and direction dependence. Isolate the component that reverses with current while controlling Joule heating and thermal expansion.
status: Gurrutxaga-Lerma’s March 2026 first-principles treatment predicted electron-wind stresses of order MPa at current densities of 10⁸–10⁹ A m⁻², with electron drag much smaller than phonon drag in the studied systems. Those predictions provide quantitative targets for separating competing electroplastic contributions experimentally.
why: This would establish when electrical pulses directly control plastic flow at technologically relevant stress scales.
key_works: B. Gurrutxaga-Lerma (2026), “Ab initio theory of electron drag and wind forces on dislocations: Bridging quantum transport and electroplasticity,” *Physical Review Materials* 10, 033803, [DOI:10.1103/t697-7fn5](https://doi.org/10.1103/t697-7fn5).

title: Avoiding reduction arrest in partially molten, gangue-bearing iron ore
open: Design ore microstructures and gangue chemistry that preserve hydrogen access and oxide reducibility through the partially molten regime. Predict when dense iron and silicate phases arrest reduction, then prevent the arrest across realistic feedstock variation.
status: Mohanta et al. mapped hydrogen reduction from 900 to 1590 °C in 2025 and found a strong slowdown around 1100–1400 °C, associated with dense metallic product layers and less-reducible gangue-derived phases. A transferable strategy for avoiding this experimentally identified bottleneck remains an engineering follow-up.
why: The bottleneck can erase expected productivity gains from increasing reduction temperature.
key_works: R. K. Mohanta, D. Fisher, Y. Korobeinikov, Q. Hong, C. Muhich, S. Sridhar, and N. Leick (2025), “Bridging the Gap in Carbon Free Iron Making: How Hydrogen Affects the Reduction of Iron Ore between 900 and 1590 °C,” [DOI:10.1021/acssuschemeng.5c03402](https://doi.org/10.1021/acssuschemeng.5c03402).

title: Pressure-aware prevention of iron-whisker defluidization
open: Demonstrate a pressure–temperature–gas-composition trajectory that prevents whisker entanglement throughout hydrogen reduction of iron-ore fines while maintaining high metallization. It must tolerate ore variation and realistic residence-time distributions in a continuously operating bed.
status: Zhou et al. achieved 95.26% metallization at 575 °C with 60 vol% hydrogen for 60 minutes in 2025. Murakami et al. found in 2026 that increased pressure extends the whisker-forming region toward lower temperatures and proposed a three-stage morphology-control sequence; robust continuous-bed implementation remains to be demonstrated.
why: Preventing interparticle hooking could widen the practical temperature and throughput range of fine-ore reduction.
key_works: T. Zhou, Y. Sun, Y. Han, and Y. Li (2025), “Hydrogen-based fluidization direct reduction of high purity iron concentrate: Experimental optimization and mechanism analysis,” [DOI:10.1016/j.mineng.2025.109273](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.mineng.2025.109273); T. Murakami, N. Toyoshima, D. Maruoka, and E. Kasai (2026), “Morphology Control of Metallic Iron Formed by Hydrogen Reduction of Iron Oxide,” [DOI:10.2355/isijinternational.ISIJINT-2025-330](https://doi.org/10.2355/isijinternational.ISIJINT-2025-330).

title: Pyrrhotite concrete damage without faster intrinsic oxidation
open: Explain why pyrrhotite-bearing aggregates can cause severe concrete deterioration when controlled alkaline oxidation rates do not support intrinsically faster reaction than pyrite. Predict damage from reaction locations, secondary precipitation, transport, and stress rather than sulfur inventory alone.
status: Clos et al.’s 2026 comparison concluded that pyrrhotite’s damaging role cannot simply be attributed to faster intrinsic high-pH oxidation. A separate 2026 electrochemical study examined aggregate size, sulfide content, and mineral source; the quantitative connection from these chemical differences to damaging expansion remains incomplete.
why: This would improve aggregate qualification and discrimination between superficially similar sulfur-bearing materials.
key_works: H. Clos, L. Santos, K. Wille, and M. Chrysochoou (2026), “Oxidation mechanisms and kinetics of pyrite and pyrrhotite in alkaline solutions,” [DOI:10.1016/j.cemconres.2026.108339](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cemconres.2026.108339); M. Ojo et al. (2026), “Mechanisms of pyrrhotite-induced concrete deterioration: A controlled electrochemical study of aggregate size, sulfide content, and mineral source,” [DOI:10.1016/j.cemconres.2026.108210](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cemconres.2026.108210).

title: Mechanism-preserving ozone acceleration of pyrrhotite deterioration
open: Develop an ozone-based accelerated test whose reaction products, precipitation locations, and damage rankings agree with natural pyrrhotite deterioration in concrete. Determine when ozone dose, humidity, or specimen dimensions change the mechanism instead of merely accelerating it.
status: NIST’s 2026 conference contribution reported that 500 ppb ozone at 40% relative humidity for 14 days produced tarnish without further visible reaction in thin mortar tiles. Higher ozone exposure at 70% humidity produced sulfate crusts and gypsum needles; development of a validated accelerated method remains explicitly unfinished.
why: A trustworthy accelerated screen could shorten aggregate qualification and investigations of affected buildings.
key_works: M. Mengason, P. Dixon, A. Carey, O. Dehwah, and S. Watson (2026), “Ozone as an oxidant for accelerated testing of pyrrhotite-induced concrete degradation,” [NIST conference record](https://www.nist.gov/publications/ozone-oxidant-accelerated-testing-pyrrhotite-induced-concrete-degradation), [DOI:10.17605/OSF.IO/7Y4SG](https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/7Y4SG).

title: Decades-long ferrihydrite persistence in asbestos-body coatings
open: Determine which silicate binding, incorporated elements, and fluid-cycling conditions stabilize ferrihydrite in mineral-fiber coatings for decades. Predict conversion to goethite and associated surface redox changes during repeated acidic and near-neutral exposures.
status: Di Carlo’s March 2026 doctoral research found variable ferrihydrite/goethite proportions using synchrotron Fe spectroscopy. Its public abstract proposes silicate binding and incorporation of biological-environment elements as stabilizers, without resolving their causal contributions; the full thesis is embargoed until March 2027.
why: The mechanism would connect a specific metastable coating to retained fibers’ long-term surface chemistry and biopersistence.
key_works: M. C. Di Carlo (2026), “Dissolution in simulated lung fluids and surface reactivity of mineral fibres of environmental and health interest,” doctoral thesis, Sapienza University of Rome, [public research abstract](https://tesidottorato.depositolegale.it/handle/20.500.14242/362829).

title: Tin–oxo insolubility before dense network formation
open: Determine the intermolecular connectivity and developer interactions that make irradiated n-butyltin–oxo cages insoluble after modest ligand loss. Identify the roles of covalent bridges, aggregation, and trapping of intact cages at the dissolution threshold.
status: Sadegh et al.’s 2026 TinOH measurements found maximum film retention near 45 mJ cm⁻² and estimated only approximately 2.2 lost butyl groups per cage there. Extensive three-dimensional crosslinking is therefore unnecessary, while direct structural evidence for the connections between cages remains missing.
why: A molecular dissolution law would make sensitivity improvements more predictable.
key_works: N. Sadegh, J. Haitjema, Y. Zhang et al. (2026), “Extreme ultraviolet induced reactions of tin–oxo cage photoresists,” [DOI:10.1039/D5TC04167H](https://doi.org/10.1039/D5TC04167H).

title: Absolute low-energy electron reaction data for specified EUV resists
open: Build calibrated datasets of electron-energy-dependent reaction cross sections, charge lifetimes, and branching yields in chemically specified condensed EUV resists. Include uncertainty and conversion dependence so electron generation, bond cleavage, and solubility change can be modeled separately.
status: Bespalov et al. studied tin-resist reactions with 2–38 eV electrons in 2020. Brainard’s public September 2026 AVS abstract still identifies electron counts, lifetimes, and reaction cross sections as poorly known; a quantitative material-resolved dataset remains missing.
why: Such data would make lithography simulations chemically testable and reduce reliance on fitted effective reaction parameters.
key_works: I. Bespalov et al. (2020), “Key Role of Very Low Energy Electrons in Tin-Based Molecular Resists for Extreme Ultraviolet Nanolithography,” [DOI:10.1021/acsami.9b19004](https://doi.org/10.1021/acsami.9b19004); R. Brainard (2026), “EUV Resists: Chemistry, Mechanisms and Challenges,” [public AVS abstract EUV-MoA-1](https://www.avssymposium.org/AVS2026/Sessions/Schedule/89752).

title: Residue-free EUV-triggered dry depolymerization of PPA resists
open: Design a polyphthalaldehyde architecture and EUV exposure/development cycle that removes exposed material completely by volatilization while preserving unexposed features. Suppress secondary monomer and radical reactions that generate nonvolatile residue.
status: PPA lithography dates to the 1980s. Naqvi et al. found in 2025 that cyclic PPA and a phthalaldehyde–propanal copolymer respond strongly to EUV, but neither achieved complete dry removal under the tested conditions; spectroscopy supports secondary chemistry and increasing crosslinking at higher doses.
why: Complete dry development could eliminate capillary-collapse constraints without requiring a separate photoacid component.
key_works: B. A. Naqvi, J. Schwartz, A. Engler, P. A. Kohl, S. De Gendt, and D. De Simone (2025), “Analysis of EUV induced depolymerization and side reactions of polyphthalaldehydes for dry develop EUV resist applications,” [DOI:10.1039/D4TC05250A](https://doi.org/10.1039/D4TC05250A).

title: Humidity-triggered crystallites in indium-nitrate resists
open: Identify the crystalline phase and hydrolysis/condensation sequence responsible for nanoscale bumps in humidly processed indium-nitrate films. Predict their onset from water activity and processing history while preserving radiation sensitivity.
status: A public 2026 abstract reports smooth films through 35% relative humidity and 19 nm electron-beam-patterned lines with 2 nm line-edge roughness at 25%. It explicitly leaves the molecular role of absorbed water unresolved; the quoted dimensions are electron-beam results.
why: A chemical explanation could turn a narrow environmental process window into a predictable formulation.
key_works: M. A. Patel, C. R. Allen, R. Nam, M. Valdez, K. Brenner, and J. W. P. Hsu (2026), “Effect of processing environment on film morphology and resist characteristics of indium nitrate photoresists,” [DOI:10.1117/12.3090475](https://doi.org/10.1117/12.3090475); C. Allen et al. (2026), “The Role of Environmental Humidity During Processing on the Properties of Indium Nitrate Sol-Gel EUV Resists,” [public AVS abstract EUV-MoA-7](https://www.avssymposium.org/AVS2026/Sessions/Schedule/89752).

title: Reactive sites that escape DMATMS inhibition
open: Identify and block the minority silica sites that remain reactive after dimethylaminotrimethylsilane treatment. Predict residual alumina nucleation density from site populations and precursor chemistry, including growth below ordinary ellipsometry sensitivity.
status: Kim et al.’s June 2026 industrial-laboratory abstract reports approximately 2 nm of nucleation delay and vapor-phase-decomposition mass-spectrometry sensitivity below 0.0001 nm equivalent thickness. It attributes failure mainly to incompletely passivated sites, leaving their identity and elimination as the sharper targets.
why: Sparse parasitic nuclei can defeat self-aligned deposition while average growth appears negligible.
key_works: J. Kim, D. Hausmann, A. Fox, F. Preischel, H. Parala, and A. Devi (2026), “Impact of Aluminum Precursor on Selective Dielectric on Metal Deposition,” [ALD/ALE 2026 abstract AS-TuP-8](https://avssymposium.org/ALD2026/Sessions/Schedule/86867).

title: Byproduct-controlled alumina nucleation on rutile
open: Derive a cycle-resolved kinetic model of how ALD-generated isopropanol occupies and vacates TiO₂(110) defects, then changes subsequent nucleation. Predict growth from byproduct exposure and purge history.
status: Jones et al. showed in 2025 that isopropanol pretreatment improves nucleation reproducibility, with partially reversible binding at oxygen vacancies and calculated site-specific adsorption thermodynamics. Closing the time-dependent feedback between product generation, site occupancy, and new nuclei is an inferred follow-up to those results.
why: It would explain recipe sensitivity to reactor history and evolving surface populations.
key_works: J. C. Jones, J. Xu, C. Yan et al. (2025), “Probing the Effects of Dimethyl Aluminum Isopropoxide Surface Reaction Byproducts on Atomic Layer Deposition Nucleation,” [DOI:10.1021/acsami.5c00901](https://doi.org/10.1021/acsami.5c00901).

title: Electro-optic versus photoplastic birefringence in AlGaAs mirrors
open: Identify the microscopic process converting photocarriers into changed birefringence in GaAs/AlGaAs mirror coatings. Distinguish electric-field-induced electro-optic response from illumination-assisted stress relaxation and predict wavelength, power, and relaxation-time dependence.
status: Ma et al.’s 2026 study supports one-photon excitation above the GaAs gap and two-photon excitation below it, followed by slower carrier-related dynamics. Empirical response modeling and noise cancellation are demonstrated, but electro-optic and photoplastic routes remain competing explanations.
why: Removing the material response would reduce precision-cavity noise without continual cancellation.
key_works: C. Y. Ma, J. Yu, T. Legero, S. Herbers, D. Nicolodi, M. Kempkes, F. Riehle, and U. Sterr (2026), “Photo-birefringent effects in crystalline AlGaAs mirror coatings,” [arXiv:2602.04724](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.04724).

title: Changed absorption above the amorphous-silicon annealing optimum
open: Determine whether defect-assisted absorption, incipient crystallization, or changes in Urbach-tail disorder explain the altered near-infrared absorption trend after high-temperature annealing of a-Si coatings. Suppress the responsible structural changes while preserving low mechanical loss.
status: Diksha et al.’s 2025 study found correlation between absorption and Urbach energy through approximately 400 °C, followed by a changed trend. Tested substrate hydroxyl content and substantial additional oxygen incorporation were excluded as explanations; the structural mechanism remains undetermined.
why: Residual absorption heats cryogenic mirrors and can prevent use of otherwise mechanically quiet coatings.
key_works: D. Diksha, A. Amato, V. Spagnuolo, S. Roorda, M. Chicoine, I. W. Martin, and J. Steinlechner (2025), “Urbach tails and optical absorption of amorphous silicon coatings,” [DOI:10.1088/1361-6382/ae153f](https://doi.org/10.1088/1361-6382/ae153f).

title: Optically usable crystalline titania–tantala with low cryogenic loss
open: Determine whether crystallized Ti-rich titania–tantala can retain its low mechanical loss while meeting mirror-grade scattering and absorption requirements. Establish the phase and grain-size window in a reflective multilayer.
status: Murray et al. reported a large cryogenic loss reduction in 2025 for their nominally 75%-Ti cation mixture after crystallization at 500 °C. Its loss was below that of either separately crystallized constituent, while optical scattering was explicitly left as a potentially decisive limitation.
why: This tests whether controlled crystallization can produce useful high-index precision-optics layers.
key_works: P. G. Murray, J. Steinlechner, H. N. Isa et al. (2025), “Mechanical loss reduction at low temperature after crystallization in a titania-tantala film,” [DOI:10.1103/PhysRevD.111.042005](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevD.111.042005).

title: A crystalline-silicon top layer that closes the cryogenic absorption budget
open: Realize a complete a-Si/SiN mirror stack with a transferred crystalline-silicon top layer that jointly meets 1–5 ppm absorption and the intended cryogenic thermal-noise budget. Control implantation damage, oxide removal, and bonding interfaces.
status: Diksha et al.’s 2026 analysis predicts that one crystalline top layer reduces absorption from approximately 27 to 13.5 ppm at 2 µm, still above the requirement. An implanted prototype with an optically fitted 83 nm silicon layer was characterized; the complete low-absorption, low-noise mirror remains the engineering target.
why: This could make silicon-based reflective stacks compatible with cryogenic interferometer operation.
key_works: D. Diksha, I. El Ouedghiri-Idrissi, L. Massaro, A. Amato, J. Woehler, I. W. Martin, and J. Steinlechner (2026), “Crystalline toplayer concept for absorption reduction,” [DOI:10.1088/1742-6596/3177/1/012108](https://doi.org/10.1088/1742-6596/3177/1/012108).

title: Unaccounted channel-mobility loss after nitric-oxide annealing
open: Identify the states and scattering processes accounting quantitatively for low inversion-channel mobility in NO-annealed 4H-SiC MOSFETs. Reconcile local trap spectroscopy with transport, distinguishing oxide traps, interface states, above-band-edge states, and nontrapping scattering.
status: Wen, Tsui, and Cheung found in 2025 that filling traps over 10–500 ns reduced mobility by less than 10% in their devices, insufficient to explain the full deficit. Ono et al. imaged NO-associated submicrosecond traps in 2026; their existence alone does not establish transport dominance.
why: This would direct interface treatments toward the defects that actually limit power-device efficiency.
key_works: Y.-X. Wen, B.-Y. Tsui, and K. P. Cheung (2025), “Impact of near interface defects on NO annealed SiC MOSFET mobility,” [DOI:10.1016/j.microrel.2025.115841](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.microrel.2025.115841); T. Ono et al. (2026), “Individual characterization of fast-responding trap states at the NO-annealed SiO₂/4H–SiC interfaces,” [arXiv:2605.27041](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.27041).

title: Emergent structural transition in magnetite trimeron-hopping models
open: Derive the first-order Verwey structural transition and its approximately hundredfold conductivity change from one dynamical Fe₃O₄ model. Produce the cubic time-averaged high-temperature structure and transport discontinuity without externally switching between separately assigned transport regimes.
status: The transition dates to 1939. Fominykh and Stegailov’s 2026 calculations reproduce conductivity on both sides using approximately 0.15 eV nonadiabatic and 0.06 eV adiabatic hopping barriers, but their 112-atom, picosecond trajectories do not develop the cubic structural transition.
why: This would connect microscopic transport to the collective physics governing transition temperature and hysteresis.
key_works: N. Fominykh and V. Stegailov (2026), “Polaron transport and Verwey transition in magnetite,” [DOI:10.1103/fphl-8mzy](https://doi.org/10.1103/fphl-8mzy), [arXiv:2604.20642](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.20642); J. P. Attfield (2022), “Magnetism and the Trimeron Bond,” [DOI:10.1021/acs.chemmater.2c00275](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.chemmater.2c00275).

title: SrTiO₃ thermal Hall recovery without longitudinal-conductivity recovery
open: Identify the strain or defect distribution that suppresses transverse phonon transport in SrTiO₃ while scarcely changing longitudinal heat conduction. Predict the effects of air annealing and ferroelastic domain arrangement on the same material.
status: SrTiO₃’s phonon thermal Hall effect was reported in 2020. A 2026 study measured Hall angles up to 0.3% at 9 T in high-quality crystals and recovery to approximately 0.1% after annealing disordered crystals, with little longitudinal-conductivity change. The specific suppressing disorder remains unidentified.
why: Identifying this channel would make a highly specimen-dependent transverse heat response controllable.
key_works: Q. Xiang, X. Li, X. Guo, K. Behnia, and Z. Zhu (2026), “Phonon thermal Hall effect: the roles of disorder, annealing, and metallic contacts,” [DOI:10.1038/s41535-026-00876-6](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41535-026-00876-6); X. Li, B. Fauqué, Z. Zhu, and K. Behnia (2020), “Phonon thermal Hall effect in strontium titanate,” [DOI:10.1103/PhysRevLett.124.105901](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.124.105901).

title: Reversible mechanical poling of metallic LiOsO₃
open: Reverse LiOsO₃’s polar distortion with a calibrated strain gradient while retaining metallic conduction. Establish reversible domain switching and its nucleation-and-motion threshold, distinguishing switching from elastic displacement under load.
