status: A 2021 first-principles proposal estimated a homogeneous-switching critical bending radius near 118 Å and identified experimental switching as the next target. Domain-wall nucleation and octahedral-tilt-gradient contributions were omitted; the radius remains a model estimate, with experimental realization of this proposal unconfirmed.
why: Mechanical control could provide a switchable structural state despite electric-field screening in a metal.
key_works: A. Zabalo and M. Stengel (2021), “Switching a Polar Metal via Strain Gradients,” [DOI:10.1103/PhysRevLett.126.127601](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.126.127601), [arXiv:2007.11857](https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.11857).

title: Two directional BKT scales at EuO/KTaO₃ with finite coupling
open: Explain different apparent BKT transition temperatures along different current directions at EuO/KTaO₃(111), despite finite coupling across the interface. Distinguish multiple ordering scales from directional transport crossovers and predict the low-current limit.
status: Huang et al. reported fitted scales of 1.15 and 1.23 K in one 2026 device, with directional differences persisting toward zero bias. Proposed superconducting stripes remain hypothetical, and tested nanowire and higher-order interstripe-coupling explanations fail particular observations.
why: This would determine what form of spatial superconducting organization the transport measurements actually imply.
key_works: Z. Huang et al. (2026), “Directional-dependent Berezinskii–Kosterlitz–Thouless transition at EuO/KTaO₃(111) interfaces,” [DOI:10.1038/s42005-026-02628-1](https://doi.org/10.1038/s42005-026-02628-1).

title: The normal-state memory carrier in 4Hb-TaS₂
open: Identify the magnetic state that stores field-training information above 4Hb-TaS₂’s superconducting transition and later determines spontaneous vortex density. Test whether interactions among correlated Star-of-David clusters provide the required memory.
status: Magnetic training of the eventual vortex phase was demonstrated in 2022. In 2026, STM on lightly Se-substituted 4Hb-TaS₁.₉₉Se₀.₀₁ found locally nonsuperconducting paramagnetic clusters and short-range spatial correlations, but their responsibility for collective magnetic memory remains unresolved.
why: The answer would identify a degree of freedom that stores magnetic information before superconducting coherence appears.
key_works: E. Persky et al. (2022), “Magnetic memory and spontaneous vortices in a van der Waals superconductor,” [DOI:10.1038/s41586-022-04855-2](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-022-04855-2); P. Wu et al. (2026), “Unveiling the landscape of Mottness and its proximity to superconductivity in 4Hb-TaS₂,” [DOI:10.1038/s41467-026-75274-4](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-75274-4).

title: Microscopic source of π Josephson links in 4Hb-TaS₂
open: Determine whether π-shifted Little–Parks oscillations originate from intrinsic superconducting phase structure or negative interlayer Josephson coupling mediated by correlated clusters. Measure the local coupling sign while controlling cluster filling and relative layer orientation.
status: Approximately half the rings in the 2024 study showed π-shifted oscillations. The 2026 spectroscopy supplies a concrete alternative involving spin-dependent tunneling between rotated superconducting layers; its coupling sign and responsibility for the ring response remain unestablished.
why: This would clarify the pairing information contained in a phase-sensitive signature and guide intentional π-junction design.
key_works: A. Almoalem et al. (2024), “The observation of π-shifts in the Little-Parks effect in 4Hb-TaS₂,” [DOI:10.1038/s41467-024-48260-x](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-024-48260-x); P. Wu et al. (2026), “Unveiling the landscape of Mottness…,” [DOI:10.1038/s41467-026-75274-4](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-75274-4).

title: Is chlorine responsible for GaN’s slow RL1 red luminescence?
open: Identify the atomic defect producing the approximately 1.8 eV RL1 band in conductive HVPE-grown GaN. Determine whether chlorine is a constituent or a growth-process correlate, reproducing the band’s kinetics through controlled impurity introduction.
status: RL1 was distinguished from fast red centers by at least 2016, and its chemical identity remains unresolved in the 2025 specialist assessment. A mean hole-capture coefficient of approximately 2.9 × 10⁻⁷ cm³ s⁻¹ at 100 K is already measured and provides a quantitative constraint.
why: Chemical identification would make this growth-related recombination channel controllable.
key_works: M. A. Reshchikov et al. (2017), “Evaluation of the concentration of point defects in GaN,” [DOI:10.1038/s41598-017-08570-1](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-017-08570-1); M. A. Reshchikov (2025), “Luminescence Properties of Defects in GaN: Solved and Unsolved Problems,” [DOI:10.3390/solids6030052](https://doi.org/10.3390/solids6030052).

title: Atomic identity of GaN’s optically generated GL1 giant trap
open: Determine which defect produces the excitation-dependent GL1 green band and unusually efficient electron capture after optical activation. Resolve its atomic structure and charge-state sequence.
status: Work in 2014–2016 established characteristic kinetics and proposed a carbon assignment. The 2023 and 2025 assessments nevertheless identify GL1’s origin as unresolved; superlinear excitation dependence and temperature-dependent capture remain important constraints.
why: This would identify a light-activated carrier sink capable of dominating high-purity GaN at low defect concentrations.
key_works: M. A. Reshchikov et al. (2016), “Optically generated giant traps in high-purity GaN,” [DOI:10.1103/PhysRevB.93.081202](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevB.93.081202); M. A. Reshchikov (2023), “On the Origin of the Yellow Luminescence Band in GaN,” [DOI:10.1002/pssb.202200488](https://doi.org/10.1002/pssb.202200488).

title: Chemical identity of GaN’s multiband RY3 center
open: Identify the RY3 defect responsible for coupled red and yellow emissions. Test whether Fe is required and, if so, distinguish isolated substitutional Fe from an Fe-containing complex.
status: The 2019 measurements established dramatically different red and yellow lifetimes, approximately 10 ns and hundreds of microseconds, and an approximately 0.06 eV redistribution barrier. The 2025 assessment notes Fe correlations but also conductive Fe-containing specimens lacking RY3, leaving the chemical assignment tentative.
why: A chemical assignment would turn a multiband fingerprint into a growth and compensation-control strategy.
key_works: M. A. Reshchikov et al. (2019), “Unusual properties of the RY3 center in GaN,” [DOI:10.1103/PhysRevB.100.045204](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevB.100.045204); M. A. Reshchikov (2025), “Luminescence Properties of Defects in GaN…,” [DOI:10.3390/solids6030052](https://doi.org/10.3390/solids6030052).

title: Diamond’s candidate 584.5 nm oxygen-pair center
open: Determine the atomic geometry, charge state, and optical cycle of the 584.5 nm center formed in oxygen-implanted diamond. Establish whether it contains two oxygen atoms and which vacancy arrangement stabilizes it.
status: Neugebauer et al. reported the center in 2026 after approximately 1500 °C annealing. Emission increased with implantation fluence to a power between 1.5 and 1.9, suggesting an oxygen pair; the proposed O₂Vₓ composition and microscopic structure remain unconfirmed.
why: A structural assignment would expand the chemically understood family of diamond emitters and explain annealing-induced oxygen-defect conversion.
key_works: P. Neugebauer et al. (2026), “Oxygen in diamond: Thermal stability of ST1 spin centres and creation of oxygen-pair complexes,” [DOI:10.1016/j.diamond.2026.113395](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.diamond.2026.113395), [arXiv:2601.04418](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.04418).

title: Uniform donor control after local n-type conduction in cubic BAs
open: Establish reproducible, spatially uniform n-type doping in cubic boron arsenide with controlled carrier density, then form intentionally positioned p–n junctions. Determine the donor and compensation chemistry behind existing patchy n-type behavior.
status: Work published online in 2025 and in a 2026 issue established local n-type regions using four electrical and scanning methods and reported minority-carrier diffusion lengths up to 33 µm. Si on the B site is a donor candidate, but demonstrated doping is inhomogeneous and carrier-density control remains a bottleneck.
why: Controlled junctions are needed to combine BAs’s thermal properties with active electronic functions.
key_works: J. Kierdaszuk et al. (2026), “Evidence of n-type Doping in Cubic Boron Arsenide,” [DOI:10.1002/adma.202514590](https://doi.org/10.1002/adma.202514590).

title: Bright cyclazine J-aggregates retaining singlet–triplet inversion
open: Realize a structurally characterized cyclazine J-aggregate with enhanced radiative brightness and an experimentally measured inverted singlet–triplet gap. Demonstrate both properties in the same aggregate while resolving aggregation-induced quenching and excited-state reordering.
status: Ghosh and Bhattacharyya’s 2026 calculations predict that J-dimer geometry mixes local excitation into the lowest singlet and increases oscillator strength relative to monomers and H-dimers. Experimental realization of that particular bright, inverted-gap aggregate remains the target.
why: Low radiative strength can erase the practical triplet-harvesting advantage of inverted-gap emitters.
key_works: A. P. Ghosh and K. Bhattacharyya (2026), “Unlocking Brightness in Inverted Singlet–Triplet Systems via J-Aggregate Formation,” [DOI:10.1021/acs.jpca.5c07712](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.jpca.5c07712).

title: An 800-hour Me-PTCDI monolayer continuous-wave laser
open: Reach an output half-life of at least 800 hours in an hBN-encapsulated Me-PTCDI monolayer laser, matching the eight-hour benchmark in pump intensity relative to threshold, temperature, and the 50%-output criterion. Preserve low-threshold coherent lasing by suppressing the residual irreversible degradation channel; this is a proposed census milestone of approximately 100-fold lifetime improvement.
status: Zhang et al. demonstrated room-temperature, optically pumped continuous-wave lasing in 2026 with thresholds of 1.4–3.4 W cm⁻² and an operating half-life up to eight hours. Suppressed triplet accumulation and hBN heat removal provide the partial result.
why: Much longer operating life would support practical molecularly thin laser devices.
key_works: L. Zhang et al. (2026), “Continuous-wave organic laser enabled by monolayer molecular crystal,” [DOI:10.1038/s41467-026-73984-3](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-73984-3).

title: Passivation transmitting both carrier polarities at singlet-fission silicon interfaces
open: Make an ultrathin organic–silicon interlayer that suppresses surface recombination while efficiently transferring both constituents of a singlet-fission triplet exciton into silicon. Demonstrate a net benefit on a high-efficiency cell architecture.
status: Nagaya et al.’s 2025 device reported a model-inferred peak charge-generation yield of 138 ± 6% per tetracene-absorbed photon using an approximately 15%-efficient silicon baseline. McNab et al.’s September 2026 analysis identifies the combined passivation and dual-polarity transport requirement; its above-33% back-contact efficiencies are simulations.
why: The interface could transfer demonstrated molecular multiplication to efficient silicon photovoltaics.
key_works: N. Nagaya et al. (2025), “Exciton fission enhanced silicon solar cell,” [DOI:10.1016/j.joule.2025.101965](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.joule.2025.101965); S. McNab et al. (2026), “Silicon Solar Cell Design for >30% Efficiency via Singlet Fission,” [arXiv:2609.10979](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.10979); A. J. Baldacchino et al. (2025), “Singlet Fission c-Si Solar Cells: Beyond Tetracene,” [DOI:10.1021/acsenergylett.5c01930](https://doi.org/10.1021/acsenergylett.5c01930).

title: The geometric-motion limit of pentacene triplet-pair decorrelation
open: Determine when nuclear motion in a covalently linked pentacene dimer can destroy singlet admixture in a bound triplet pair before decay. Derive a criterion involving geometry-dependent exchange, structural dynamics, and triplet migration.
status: Atandrita Bhattacharyya’s public July 2026 thesis-colloquium abstract reports persistent intermediate optical polarization despite substantial nuclear reorganization. In those strongly coupled dimers, effective decorrelation driven by THz motions was slower than rotational-diffusion times of 0.2 ns and longer, so decay prevailed. The negative result is specific to the studied bound pairs.
why: Fast pair formation produces little benefit if two usable triplets never emerge.
key_works: A. Bhattacharyya et al. (2026), “Persistent singlet electronic character in the multiexcitonic triplet-pair state of strongly coupled pentacene singlet fission dimers,” [arXiv:2606.09130](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.09130); A. Bhattacharyya (2026), [IISc thesis-colloquium abstract](https://sscu.iisc.ac.in/thesis-colloquium-on-the-formation-and-evolution-of-the-correlated-triplet-pair-state-in-singlet-fission-insights-from-polarization-controlled-impulsive-optical-spectroscopy/).

title: Molecular connectivity behind native suberin lamellae
open: Determine the covalent connections and packing that produce suberin’s native lamellar repeat, including links between aliphatic components, aromatics, and the surrounding cell wall. Predict spacing and barrier properties from a chemically specified architecture.
status: Daraspe et al.’s 2025 cryogenic tomography resolved approximately 5–7 nm lamellae in hydrated Arabidopsis roots without heavy-metal staining. Opposed hydroxy-fatty-acid units are a proposed explanation of the spacing, while polymer connections and integration into the wall remain explicitly unresolved.
why: A molecular design rule for this thin biological barrier could inform drought resilience and degradable barrier films.
key_works: J. Daraspe, E. Bellani, D. De Bellis, C. Genoud, and N. Geldner (2025), “Targeted imaging of specialized plant cell walls by improved cryo-CLEM and cryo-electron tomography,” [DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-66410-7](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-66410-7).

title: Silicon-sensitive dAnk control of diatom silica pores
open: Determine how dAnk proteins couple silicon availability to silica-deposition-vesicle organization and pore formation in *Thalassiosira pseudonana*. Predict normal pores, large gaps, or poreless silica from genotype and silicon supply.
status: Aram et al. showed in July 2026 that dAnk-mutant phenotypes depend strongly on silicon availability, with structures ranging from large gaps to poreless coverage. Cryogenic tomography revealed altered vesicle organization; the molecular coupling behind this context-dependent morphogenesis remains unresolved.
why: The missing rule limits biological programming of hierarchical silica porosity.
key_works: L. Aram, N. Varsano, O. Brontvein et al. (2026), “The morphogenetic activity of dAnk genes in the diatom *Thalassiosira pseudonana* is sensitive to Si availability,” [DOI:10.1038/s42003-026-10583-4](https://doi.org/10.1038/s42003-026-10583-4).

title: Sequence-mixture synergy in silicatein-mediated nanoceria synthesis
open: Identify which silicatein variants and mixture ratios cause enhanced ceria formation in evolved sequence populations. Use purified variants and defined mixtures to separate cooperative templating, catalytic chemistry, phase organization, and protein-abundance effects.
status: Vigil et al. screened approximately 100,000 variants and obtained populations producing roughly four times the wild-type ceria yield in 2025. Multiple sequences and truncations persisted, some catalytic-triad substitutions retained mineralization, and individual-variant characterization was explicitly unfinished.
why: Resolving cooperation would make mineral-producing protein systems reproducible and transferable.
key_works: T. N. Vigil, M.-J. C. Rowson, A. J. Frost, A. R. Janiga, and B. W. Berger (2025), “Directed Evolution of Silicatein Reveals Biomineralization Synergism between Protein Sequences,” [DOI:10.1021/acsomega.4c06359](https://doi.org/10.1021/acsomega.4c06359).

title: Oxygen control of magnetosomes after the NsrR negative result
open: Identify the sensing and regulatory processes translating oxygen and redox conditions into magnetite formation in *Magnetospirillum gryphiswaldense*. Determine whether control is distributed and manipulate mineralization independently of growth and iron uptake.
status: A 2026 re-evaluation found no evidence that the putative nitric-oxide sensor NsrR is a key magnetosome regulator, challenging the earlier proposed mechanism. Other redox-related regulators influence production without explaining the complete oxygen response; a single replacement master regulator is not established.
why: Predictable oxygen control is needed for reproducible magnetic-nanoparticle fermentation and transfer of mineralization pathways.
key_works: A. Woller, R. Uebe, and D. Schüler (2026), “No evidence for the putative nitric oxide sensor NsrR as a key regulator of magnetosome formation in *Magnetospirillum gryphiswaldense*,” [DOI:10.1093/nar/gkaf1422](https://doi.org/10.1093/nar/gkaf1422).

title: Hydrogen blockade of magnetite formation despite continued iron storage
open: Determine why hydrogen suppresses magnetite mineralization in *Desulfovibrio magneticus* RS-1 while permitting growth and iron storage. Identify the inhibited reaction or redox state and restore mineralization under hydrogen.
status: A December 2025 study used 5% hydrogen to suppress magnetosomes and a switch to nitrogen to synchronize their formation. Hydrogen-grown cells doubled in approximately six hours versus eight under nitrogen, retained ferrosome production, and showed no broad reduction in magnetosome-protein abundance; the mineralization-specific inhibition mechanism remained unresolved.
why: A reversible switch downstream of iron uptake could separate biomass production from nanoparticle nucleation.
key_works: V. V. Russell, A. T. Iavarone, E. Ozyamak, C. Grant, and A. Komeili (2025), “A network of coiled-coil and actin-like proteins controls the cellular organization of magnetosome organelles in deep-branching magnetotactic bacteria,” [DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-66326-2](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-66326-2).

title: How woven fibrils become a butterfly single gyroid
open: Determine how precursor fibrils assemble into a single-gyroid topology in *Parides sesostris* wing scales and become the mature network. Identify fibril composition and membrane or protein templates, then reproduce the topology-preserving transition.
status: Jessop et al.’s 2025 developmental imaging revealed a woven fibrillar precursor to the adult gyroid. Perturbed development could preserve fibrous structures with blue reflection; the weaving rule, detailed molecular composition, and conversion mechanism remain open.
why: Fibril-based assembly could provide a manufacturing route to three-dimensional photonic networks.
key_works: A.-L. Jessop, P. L. Clode, M. Saunders et al. (2025), “Hierarchical woven fibrillar structures in developing single gyroids in butterflies,” [DOI:10.1073/pnas.2507297122](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2507297122), [arXiv:2504.03459](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.03459).

title: Species-dependent selection of gyroid handedness
open: Explain how molecular chirality, growth direction, and cellular boundaries select gyroid handedness in butterfly scales. Predict species-dependent enantiomer populations and demonstrate a perturbation that reverses or tunes them.
status: A 2025 study classified more than 200 *Teinopalpus imperialis* crystals as left-handed, whereas *Parides sesostris* contained a strongly biased mixture of both hands. Orientation correlations constrain possible mechanisms but do not identify the causal amplification from molecular chirality to the network.
why: Predictable handedness would enable controlled polarization responses in chiral photonic materials.
key_works: M. Inoue, K. Saito, H. Aoyama, H. Inoue, R. Ohnuki, and S. Yoshioka (2025), “Study on the chirality of gyroid photonic crystals in butterfly wing scales,” [DOI:10.1038/s41598-025-05750-2](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-05750-2).

title: Guanine cargo import into acidic iridosomes
open: Identify the transporters or cargo-delivery pathways accumulating guanine or its precursors inside iridosomes without premature precipitation elsewhere. Measure the transported species and flux, linking delivery to pH and supersaturation.
status: Work published online in 2025 established protonated amorphous guanine accumulation in acidic developing iridosomes but explicitly left import unresolved. An April 2026 study identified Rab32a, Ap3m2, and Hps5 as necessary organelle regulators, without identifying a guanine-selective transporter or measuring guanine-cargo flux.
why: Controlled substrate delivery is essential for engineering intracellular optical crystals.
key_works: Z. Eyal, R. Deis, A. Gorelick-Ashkenazi et al. (2025 online; 2026 issue), “pH variations enable guanine crystal formation within iridosomes,” [DOI:10.1038/s41589-025-02020-0](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41589-025-02020-0); A. Gorelick-Ashkenazi et al. (2026), “Lysosome-related organelles orchestrate guanine crystal formation in pigment cells,” [DOI:10.1073/pnas.2524305123](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2524305123).

title: Metabolic selection of yeast guanine spherulites versus nanoplates
open: Determine how perturbing **HPT1** and **GUD1** changes the chemistry selecting guanine-crystal morphology in *Saccharomyces cerevisiae*. Connect purine flux, impurities, vacuolar pH, and supersaturation to branching and plate growth.
status: Janssen et al. demonstrated genetic size-and-shape control in 2026; at 4.5 hours, wild-type and **hpt1Δ** populations had median crystal diameters of approximately 485 and 761 nm. The authors lacked a definitive morphological mechanism, and attempted fluorescent vacuolar-pH measurements did not yield a specific signal.
why: A predictive mechanism could turn yeast into a tunable organic-crystal manufacturing platform.
key_works: J. N. Janssen, Y. Fishman, Y. Li et al. (2026), “Biosynthesis and Genetic Tuning of Guanine Crystals via Metabolic Engineering of Yeast,” [DOI:10.1002/anie.6259849](https://doi.org/10.1002/anie.6259849).

title: Mechanical function of brominated tyrosine crosslinks in spongin
open: Establish how brominated di- and trityrosine crosslinks change hydrated spongin’s stiffness, dissipation, fatigue resistance, and chemical stability. Vary crosslink chemistry while controlling collagen organization sufficiently to isolate the contribution.
status: A 2025 study identified collagen-like components and brominated tyrosine crosslinks and modeled selected crosslinks in collagen-mimetic systems. Their possible mechanical role in the native fibrous network was explicitly left open.
why: This could explain the durability of a halogen-rich extracellular skeleton and suggest new wet protein materials.
key_works: H. Ehrlich, I. Miksik, M. V. Tsurkan et al. (2025), “Discovery of mammalian collagens I and III within ancient poriferan biopolymer spongin,” [DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-57460-y](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-57460-y).

title: The missing chemical driver of natural-rubber storage hardening
open: Identify the latex-derived constituents and reaction network responsible for storage hardening after controlled removal or retention of proteins and metal ions. Reconstitute the effect from purified components and predict gel formation and viscosity evolution.
status: Chanpaka, Suchiva, and Wirasate’s 2026 phase-transfer study found that residual bonded proteins and the examined Mg, Ca, and Fe ions did not significantly account for hardening under its conditions. The result narrows familiar explanations and implicates other non-rubber constituents, without excluding context-dependent protein or metal contributions elsewhere.
why: Identifying the reaction would enable targeted stabilization of a major renewable industrial elastomer.
key_works: B. Chanpaka, K. Suchiva, and S. Wirasate (2026), “Phase transfer study on the effects of metal ions on storage hardening of natural rubber,” [DOI:10.1016/j.rinma.2025.100872](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.rinma.2025.100872).

title: Does Payne softening fluidize interparticle glassy rubber?
open: Observe directly whether segmentally slow rubber between nearby silica particles becomes dynamically mobile during Payne softening. Measure local polymer dynamics and filler connectivity simultaneously to separate this contribution from contact rupture and chain detachment.
status: Hart et al.’s 2025/2026 study used interface-sensitive neutron measurements and mechanics to connect glassy interparticle layers, reinforcement, and reduced Payne softening after steric stabilization. The remaining discriminating test is strain-resolved observation of segmental mobilization in the same material volume as stiffness falls.
why: Causal separation of microscopic dissipation channels would improve low-loss rubber formulation.
key_works: J. M. Hart, W. D. Carswell, V. García-Sakai et al. (2025 online; 2026 issue), “Structural and Dynamic Origins of Payne Effect Reduction by Steric Stabilization in Silica Reinforced Poly(butadiene) Nanocomposites,” [DOI:10.1002/pc.70163](https://doi.org/10.1002/pc.70163).

title: Hydration-resolved prediction of counterion-induced PSS flexibility
open: Predict how counterion valence and identity change polystyrene-sulfonate flexibility and scattering correlations using explicit polymer and ion hydration. Reproduce the concentration-scaling crossover and predict new counterions without independently refitting effective charge.
status: A 2025 reanalysis found that the correlation-peak concentration exponent changes from approximately one-half to one-third with counterion conditions, accompanied by increased chain flexibility. The evidence points toward hydration, but a transferable microscopic prediction remains beyond the reported empirical relationships.
why: Ion-specific predictions would reduce experimental screening needed to control polyelectrolyte conformation.
key_works: J. F. Douglas, F. Horkay, and Y. Zhang (2025), “Influence of counterion valency on the scattering properties of highly charged polyelectrolyte solutions revisited,” [DOI:10.1063/5.0292505](https://doi.org/10.1063/5.0292505).

title: The local dielectric profile behind polyzwitterion charge asymmetry
open: Determine the molecular dielectric environment and unequal counterion binding around a polyzwitterion’s two charges, then predict electrophoretic response across salts and nanopores. Separate effective polymer charging from electroosmotic transport.
status: Lee and Muthukumar demonstrated opposite-direction transport of chemically distinct neutral polyzwitterions in 2025 and proposed dielectric-gradient-driven counterion asymmetry. Their interpretation inferred a local dielectric constant near 28; independently calculated dielectric profiles and fuller electroosmotic treatment remain outstanding.
why: This would make nominally neutral polymers more predictable in separations and nanopore sensing.
key_works: Y. Lee and M. Muthukumar (2025), “Charge symmetry breaking in neutral polyzwitterions,” [DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-58928-7](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-58928-7).

title: Experimental verification of short-chain-seeded shear bands
open: Test whether pre-existing short-chain-rich regions determine where shear bands nucleate in chemically uniform bidisperse entangled melts. Measure pre-flow composition, subsequent band locations, and chain migration while controlling wall and free-edge effects.
status: Ma et al.’s 2025 simulations compared chains of lengths 200 and 400 with a monodisperse length-300 reference. They linked persistent bands and a broad stress plateau to short-chain-rich soft regions, disentanglement, and migration; a composition-resolved experimental test remains the next step.
why: Structural precursors could make unstable processing flows predictable from molecular-weight distribution and spatial history.
key_works: L.-C. Ma, Y.-J. Ruan, Y.-Y. Lu, and L.-J. An (2025), “Structural Origins of Shear Banding in Bidisperse Polymer Melts,” [DOI:10.1007/s10118-025-3421-8](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10118-025-3421-8).

title: Cates–Candau ring-driven shear thickening in living micelles
open: Establish whether reversibly linked micellar rings cause shear thickening and long-lived thermal memory just below overlap in the proposed Cates–Candau regime. Measure ring populations and linking–unlinking kinetics together with nonlinear rheology, or quantitatively exclude the mechanism.
status: The scenario was explicitly proposed as speculative in 2001. A 2026 Brownian-dynamics study connected molecular timescales to linear rheology in unentangled living-micelle models containing linear and ring aggregates; experimental closure of the nonlinear ring-linking hypothesis remains separate.
why: It could explain slow collective memory and increased flow resistance in nominally dilute surfactant solutions.

title: The transient p53 oligomer selecting a finite cluster radius
open: Identify the transient oligomeric species proposed to maintain finite p53-rich clusters and measure the formation, diffusion, and dissociation rates selecting their radius. Perturb oligomer lifetime and quantitatively predict the size response.
status: Primary experiments established mesoscopic p53-rich clusters and their role in amyloid nucleation in 2021. A 2025 synthesis describes radii near 45 ± 5 nm for 2 µM R248Q p53 at 15 °C and a transient-oligomer mechanism, but decisive species identification and kinetic accounting remain unresolved.
why: This would explain protein assemblies that persist at finite size without ordinary macroscopic coarsening.
